title: Making two action heads agree: coordination mechanisms and a runtime collapse certificate for flow-matching policies
abstract: A dual-representation flow-matching policy decodes each predicted motion into joint and end-effector spaces, and the residual between the two kinematically equivalent decodings provides a physically interpretable runtime signal. On multimodal tasks, however, independently sampled branches may choose different valid modes, causing false alarms. We study how to coordinate the two branches and at what cost. Across two robot environments and a non-robotic testbed, the tested mechanisms fall into four classes. An auxiliary latent shared by both branches but absent from the flow-matching construction is erased at the population optimum, a provable dead end confirmed within a prespecified 2% equivalence band. Sharing source noise can coordinate or anti-coordinate: its effect changes sign with the representation map and tracks the alignment of decoder mode basins. Consistency regularization gives intermediate coordination but reduces the valid-pair rate, while training-supported discrete partitions achieve near-ceiling coordination robustly. We further derive a chance-corrected coordination bound based only on each branch's Gini-Simpson diversity, yielding an attainable region and a label-free certificate that separates coordination from collapse when zero mismatch is ambiguous. On LIBERO-Plus, benign multimodality adds 1.57 percentage points of false alarms to the residual, which remains the strongest evaluated failure signal; the preregistered token intervention does not meet its false-alarm criterion or produce a seed-robust detection change. Code, models, and per-run configurations are available at https://github.com/kimo423/dual-head-coordination.

title: Dataset for "Robust Steerability Classification via Key Feature Extraction"
abstract: This dataset accompanies the manuscript “Robust Steerability Classification via Key Feature Extraction” and contains the two-qubit quantum-state datasets used for training and evaluating machine-learning classifiers for quantum steerability. The collection covers projective-measurement settings (m=2,\ldots,8) and includes random two-qubit states, Werner states, T-diagonal states, strictly unsteerable random states, and all-versus-nothing (AVN) states. These datasets are used to evaluate both in-distribution classification performance and generalization across physically distinct families of quantum states. Each state is represented by the 15 independent real parameters of its density matrix together with a unified binary label, where (+1) denotes steerable and (-1) denotes either noncertified or unsteerable, depending on the dataset-specific certification criterion. The random-state datasets originate from Ren and Chen, Phys. Rev. A 100, 022314 (2019), while the remaining datasets are organized according to the constructions and steering criteria described in the accompanying manuscript. Detailed information on file structure, label definitions, state families, steering thresholds, and data provenance is provided in the included README.md. The dataset is released to support reproducibility of the numerical results reported in the manuscript and to provide benchmark data for future studies of machine-learning-based quantum-steering detection.

title: Computational Invariant Fusion Theory (CIFT): A Framework for Deriving Higher‑Level Computational Laws from Low‑Level Invariants
abstract: Invariant properties are the backbone of mathematical reasoning and computational design. Traditional approaches treat invariants as static, isolated facts that hold across specific contexts, such as the invariance of the sum of angles in a Euclidean triangle or the conservation of energy in a closed system. In this work we propose a new paradigm, Computational Invariant Fusion Theory (CIFT), which systematically combines multiple low‑level invariants to synthesize higher‑level computational laws. By viewing invariants as composable building blocks, we introduce a fusion operator that merges a set of invariants {I_1, I_2, …, I_K} into a new invariant I_new, expressed as I_1 + I_2 → I_new in the simplest case. The theory formalizes the conditions under which such fusion preserves consistency, ensures non‑triviality, and yields emergent properties that were not apparent from any single input invariant. We present a rigorous mathematical framework that captures the fusion process through algebraic structures and categorical semantics, allowing for compositional reasoning about algorithms, data structures, and computational processes. Several illustrative examples demonstrate the power of CIFT, including the derivation of loop invariants from base case invariants, the synthesis of parallel execution guarantees from sequential consistency invariants, and the construction of security invariants for distributed protocols from local safety properties. We discuss the implications of this theory for automated theorem proving, formal verification, and the discovery of novel computational principles, positioning CIFT as a foundational tool for future research in theoretical computer science.

title: A deep learning framework for translation quality estimation using dual stream cross lingual attention and gated mixture of experts prediction
abstract: Translation quality estimation (TQE)—predicting translation quality without reference translations—is increasingly important in natural language processing. Current neural TQE methods encode source and translated texts in a single concatenated representation, limiting fine-grained cross-lingual alignment, and employ homogeneous regression heads that ignore translation error heterogeneity. This paper proposes DL-TQE, a deep learning architecture comprising two components: (1) a Dual-Stream Cross-Lingual Attention Network (DSCAN) with parallel Transformer encoders connected by explicit cross-lingual attention bridges at multiple layers, and (2) a Gated Mixture-of-Experts Quality Predictor (GMoE-QP) that routes quality-relevant features through specialised expert sub-networks conditioned on translation complexity signals. Evaluated on WMT 2020–2023 Quality Estimation benchmarks across four English-centric language pairs (En–De, En–Zh, En–Cs, En–Ja), DL-TQE achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.641 ± 0.003 on the En–De benchmark, outperforming TransQuest (0.612) and CometKiwi (0.630) by 2.9 and 1.1% points respectively ( p < 0.05, Williams test). Ablation analysis confirms that DSCAN and GMoE-QP independently contribute 2.3 and 1.8%-point improvements, respectively. Expert routing analysis reveals domain-sensitive specialisation, and error-type disaggregated evaluation demonstrates consistent advantages across lexical, morpho-syntactic, and semantic error categories within the tested WMT benchmark settings. These findings suggest that explicit cross-lingual alignment modelling and error-type-sensitive prediction offer a promising direction for sentence-level TQE on English-centric language pairs.

title: RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel-view synthesis but remains limited on GPUs at high resolutions. Through a stage-wise Roofline characterization, we identify two distinct hardware bottlenecks: global memory traffic dominates the front end, whereas instruction throughput limits rasterization. Guided by this analysis, we develop RoofGS, a rendering framework that applies bottleneck-specific optimizations rather than generic kernel acceleration. For the memory-bound front end, we design a resolution-adaptive quantized depth sorting key that compresses each key to 32 bits. For the compute-bound rasterizer, we introduce a range-aware bit-level fast exponential approximation tailored to the bounded exponent range after opacity culling, with a derived per-pixel error bound. These two core techniques are complemented by additional optimizations (kernel fusion, compact attribute storage, culling, dual-pixel evaluation) that additionally reduce memory traffic and improve instruction-level parallelism. Experiments show that RoofGS achieves a 10.1$\times$ end-to-end speedup over 3DGS at 4K on an RTX 4090, increasing throughput from 61 to 616 FPS, with only a 0.028 dB PSNR loss.

title: Verification artifact: Exact certification of a positive-order Rényi additivity violation for an explicit channel pair
abstract: Verification artifact: Exact certification of a positive-order Rényi additivity violation for an explicit channel pair This record contains the complete verification artifact for the paper Exact certification of a positive-order Rényi additivity violation for an explicit channel pair (Artus Krohn-Grimberghe, Percivio Ltd., 2026). The paper proves that the explicit channel pair constructed by Cubitt, Harrow, Leung, Montanaro, and Winter (Commun. Math. Phys. 284, 281–290 (2008); arXiv:0712.3628) violates additivity of the minimum output Rényi entropy for every real order 0 < p ≤ 1/22, under the inverse-input-marginal trace-preserving normalization fixed in the paper. The proof is certificate-based: small rational witness matrices establish that every output eigenvalue of either channel lies between 301/100000 and 2/3, one explicit entangled input has an exact rational joint output spectrum, and two elementary interval arguments reduce the violation on the whole interval to finitely many comparisons of integers. Contents • artifact/certificates/ — the five certificate files: floor witnesses, cap witnesses, the exact joint output matrix with its spectrum, and the two interval certificates (all small JSON files of rational numbers).• artifact/programs/ — the two independently written verification programs described in Section 7 of the paper. Both use only the Python standard library (Python 3.10+); together they re-check every claim in a few seconds on a laptop.• artifact/MANIFEST.txt — SHA-256 of every certificate and program file, matching the hashes printed in Appendix B of the paper.• artifact/README.md — one command per claim, with expected output.• main.pdf — the paper. Provenance The witness matrices were found by an AI-assisted numerical search; the search plays no role in the proof. All mathematical claims rest on the certificate files and the two verification programs in this record. License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). A browsable, manifest-verified copy of this artifact is maintained at https://github.com/percivio-ltd/certified-science (results/renyi-additivity-chlmw/).

title: Computational Proof Explanation Theory (CPET): Toward Machine‑Generated Mathematical Insight
abstract: The ability of a machine to produce formal proofs has seen rapid progress, yet the gap between proof generation and human‑like understanding remains wide. This paper introduces Computational Proof Explanation Theory (CPET), a framework that extends automated theorem proving by coupling each proof with a natural, semantically meaningful explanation. CPET formalizes the relationship between a syntactic derivation and its underlying conceptual meaning through a mapping function Proof → Meaning, and proposes a graph‑based explanation model that quantifies naturalness. We detail the theoretical foundations, present an algorithmic architecture that integrates proof search with explanation synthesis, and discuss the broader implications of CPET for advancing machine reasoning toward the level of human mathematicians. The potential of CPET to contribute to foundational questions in mathematics, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science is highlighted, suggesting a pathway to future recognition at the highest levels, including the Turing Award.

title: Topological Distance Theory of Proofs (TDTP)
abstract: This paper introduces Topological Distance Theory of Proofs (TDTP), a novel approach to analyzing and comparing mathematical proofs. Traditional methods of proof comparison often rely on length or structural similarity, which can be misleading when considering the underlying logical structure and potential transformations inherent in proofs. TDTP proposes a fundamentally different metric, based on topological distance, that captures the intrinsic relationships between proofs. The core concept is to define a distance function, *d(P1, P2)*, that represents a structural distance rather than a purely linear one. This allows for the exploration of proof spaces as geometric objects, opening possibilities for understanding proof equivalence, proof simplification, and automated proof verification. The paper outlines the foundational concepts of TDTP, including the definition of the distance function and potential applications, emphasizing that the distance reflects topological properties rather than simple length differences. Further development of this theory could lead to significant advances in automated theorem proving and mathematical knowledge representation.

title: Inferential Evaluation of Surrogate-Derived Models under Covariate Shift
abstract: In transfer-learning settings, a model derived from abundant surrogate labels may be deployed in a target population where gold-standard outcomes are unobserved. Evaluating its target performance is essential for determining whether decisions based on the model remain reliable, yet it is difficult when gold labels are scarce, and covariate distributions differ across data sources. We study a three-sample setting with a small gold-labeled source, a larger surrogate-labeled source, and an unlabeled target. Under conditional transportability, we evaluate the surrogate-derived model against the latent gold-standard outcome in the target population. We propose cross-fitted estimators that transport information from the two labeled sources through source-specific density ratios. We also combine outcome-regression augmentation with a kernel correction for estimating the model near a threshold, accounting for uncertainty from all three samples. We establish asymptotically linear inference for TPR and FPR, consistency and pointwise inference for the ROC curve, and asymptotically normal inference for AUC. Simulations assess bias, coverage, and sensitivity to bandwidth and relative sample sizes. A retrospective temporal validation on Chatbot Arena and a semi-synthetic ACS-Income study provide validation in real-world AI applications.

title: DeltaLog: Deferred Materialization of Recurrent States for Linear Attention Decoding
abstract: Linear attention models eliminate the quadratic prefix computation and context-growing KV cache of softmax attention by replacing pairwise token interactions with recurrent state updates. However, existing decoding implementations often materialize and write back the full recurrent state after every generated token, making state maintenance a major source of memory traffic, especially for models with large states and many heads. This paper presents DeltaLog, a recurrent-state decoding scheme that reduces this overhead without changing the model semantics. Specifically, DeltaLog represents the recurrent state as a dense base state together with a bounded log of recent compact updates. Most decode steps append only compact update factors to this log, while periodic merge steps fold the accumulated updates back into the dense base state. Thus, the model observes the same dense state as in eager decoding, but most full-state write-backs are replaced by lightweight append operations. We implement DeltaLog for GDN, KDA, and RWKV6 and integrate it into a prototype serving stack. Across these models, DeltaLog accelerates the recurrent-state update kernel by up to $1.86\times$, reduces profiled recurrent-state write traffic by up to $7.83\times$, and achieves $1.05$--$1.20\times$ end-to-end serving speedups over dense recurrent baselines.

title: Computational Abstraction Evolution Theory (CAET)
abstract: Computational Abstraction Evolution Theory (CAET) proposes a rigorous framework for understanding how abstractions—structured representations of information that omit irrelevant details—change and improve over time within computational systems. Drawing an analogy to biological evolution, CAET models abstraction change as a discrete dynamical process A_t → A_{t+1}, where each step represents the refinement, combination, or transformation of an abstraction by a computational agent. This paper introduces the core principles of CAET, develops a formal description based on state transition systems and fitness landscapes, and illustrates the theory through examples in program synthesis, machine learning model compression, and knowledge graph evolution. We discuss the implications of CAET for the design of adaptive algorithms and for the broader field of computational theory, highlighting its potential to guide the development of systems that evolve their own computational abstractions in a manner analogous to natural evolution.

title: Boundary Entropy Theory of Mathematics (BETM)
abstract: This paper introduces the Boundary Entropy Theory of Mathematics (BETM), a novel framework for understanding the informational content residing within the boundaries of mathematical structures. The core concept revolves around quantifying the "Boundary Entropy" (BE), denoted as [H(∂T)], where T represents a mathematical theory or system, and ∂T represents its boundary. BETM posits a fundamental connection between information theory, topology, and the underlying mathematical foundations. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of BE, proposing a method for its calculation based on topological complexity and information loss across the boundary. This theory aims to provide a new lens through which to analyze mathematical systems, potentially revealing hidden structures and connections previously obscured. The presented framework offers a conceptual shift, moving beyond traditional notions of mathematical rigor and exploring the inherent informational aspects of mathematical boundaries. ---

title: Quantum Technologies: System-Level Performance and Engineering Priorities
abstract: Quantum technologies now encompass processors, programmable simulators, communication links, random-number sources, sensors, and frequency standards whose performance is governed by distinct physical mechanisms. This review relates those mechanisms to demonstrated system performance across superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonic platforms, semiconductor spins, color centers, atomic ensembles, and nuclear-transition spectroscopy. Quantitative comparisons are made within common technological functions and retain the source configuration, operating conditions, uncertainty or security convention, and classical reference. Representative results include a distance-7 surface-code memory with logical error (1.43±0.03)×10−3 per cycle, a 98-qubit trapped-ion processor with mean two-qubit infidelity 7.9(2) ×10−4, single-clock systematic uncertainty of 4.4 ×10−19, finite-key quantum key distribution (QKD) through 71.9 dB measured loss, and frequency-dependent squeezed readout with quantum-noise reduction up to 6.1 dB in the Advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (Advanced LIGO). The dominant constraints are decoherence and correlated error, multiplicative interface loss, thermal and nonequilibrium excitation, measurement efficiency, control bandwidth, calibration drift, fabrication variability, and error-correction overhead. Classical tensor-network, sparse-Pauli, and high-performance simulations have repeatedly shifted quantum–classical crossover estimates, demonstrating that advantage claims are properties of a specified task, accuracy, and cost model rather than hardware alone. evidence.title: Quantum Technologies: System-Level Performance and Engineering Priorities
evidence.abstract: Quantum technologies now encompass processors, programmable simulators, communication links, random-number sources, sensors, and frequency standards whose performance is governed by distinct physical mechanisms. title: Cross‐Species Generalization and Comparative Performance Analysis of Deep Neural Network Architectures in Histological Image Classification
abstract: Histological image classification plays a critical role in biomedical research and diagnostic processes. Advances in the field of deep learning present significant opportunities for enhancing diagnostic accuracy and developing automated decision support systems. This study aims to comparatively evaluate the out-of-distribution generalization and cross-domain classification performance of different deep neural network encoders. In this study, models were trained on an internal dataset of 4307 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained images of male rat lung, cerebellum, and adipose tissues, obtained under ethical committee approval (Ege University, HADYEK 2026-06). To evaluate genuine generalization, testing was conducted on a separate, diverse external cohort of 600 mixed human-and-animal images. Nine different deep learning architectures-MobileNetV3-S, MobileNetV3-L, DenseNet121, DenseNet201, ConvNeXt-S, ConvNeXt-B, DINOv3 ViT-S, DINOv3 ViT-H+, and the pathology foundation model UNI2-h-were evaluated using frozen feature extraction combined with a linear probe. For performance evaluation, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, Cohen's κ, and ROC-AUC metrics were analyzed along with per-image inference times. While all models achieved near-perfect results during internal cross-validation, their performance diverged significantly on the external dataset, confirming that the observed differences reflect genuine cross-domain generalization capabilities rather than under-fitting. All competitive models demonstrated high performance in classifying adipose and cerebellum tissues, achieving an F1 score of 95% or higher for these tissues. In distinguishing the lung tissue, which has the most diverse structure and is the most difficult to classify, the UNI2-h model emerged as the most successful, achieving an F1 score of 97.4% and a recall of 95.0%. When evaluated in terms of computational efficiency, the MobileNetV3-Small model stood out as having the lowest processing time among all scenarios, demonstrating an inference time of 9.4 ms on the CPU and 12.5 ms on the GPU. In conclusion, while the pathology foundation model UNI2-h achieved the highest accuracy values across all metrics, the ConvNeXt-Small model was identified as the system providing the optimal balance between speed and accuracy. These findings indicate that although UNI2-h stands out for the most precise results in cross-domain classifications, the ConvNeXt-Small architecture emerges as an ideal alternative, particularly in practical applications where computational efficiency is critical and resources are constrained.

title: Decomposing Staleness in Recommender Systems: A Dual-Filter Framework for Supersession and Decay
abstract: Stale recommendations are a pervasive challenge and a leading source of user complaints on large-scale content platforms. Items lose relevance through two primary mechanisms: supersession, where emerging updates render prior coverage stale, and relevance decay, where an item's informational value naturally diminishes over its lifecycle. Traditional countermeasures serve as crude proxies: age cutoffs poorly reflect actual relevance loss, while engagement heuristics rely on lagging signals, broadly exposing users to stale content before the system adapts. We present SDF (Supersession-Decay Filtering), a staleness filtering system fully deployed in Google Discover, a personalized recommendation feed with hundreds of millions of daily and billions of monthly active users. SDF targets both mechanisms with complementary filters, each powered by a learned model: a relational staleness model that detects supersession between item pairs, and a predicted traffic ratio (PTR) model that forecasts relevance decay from the item's content, trained on lifetime visit traffic. Applied via disjunction upstream of the ranking stage, SDF prunes stale candidates, measurably reducing downstream serving costs. Online experiments demonstrate that these filters significantly reduce the prevalence of stale content while improving user engagement. Over a two-year production deployment, user-filed staleness reports (in-product user feedback) declined by 54.9% relative to the pre-deployment baseline, establishing SDF as a robust and scalable paradigm for resolving content staleness at industrial scale.

title: The Cost of Bypass Under an Uncertified Object. Three Independent Quantities, Conditional Definiteness, and a Construction of State IV₂. Series "Collapse of Independence", Note 13
abstract: Notes 10 to 12 of this series established absences. The present note is the first to advance a positive claim, and the kind of claim it advances must be stated at the outset, because it determines what the note is permitted to prove. The positive result has three parts. First, a decomposition: the rejected single scalar of resistance R is replaced by three independently measurable quantities — cost of bypass C, observability O, and reversibility V — and the decomposition is demonstrated rather than postulated, by exhibiting observable mechanisms that realise five of the eight sign combinations and supply a witness pair for each quantity. Second, a condition of definiteness: it is established under which conditions a measured quantity characterises the construction and under which it characterises only the measurement; the condition is formulated through the addressability and derivability axes. Third, a construction: a complete specification of an object attaining state IV₂ is given, including data-definition statements, the form of preregistration, and a machine-checkable acceptance criterion. The construction is specified and machine-checkably testable, not attained: nothing in §7 has been executed, and attainment is decided by the run RTT_005 (Appendix). What the note does not contain is a measurement of the cost of bypass as a characteristic of the construction. Such a measurement is impossible on the 22 July 2026 snapshot, because state IV₂ is not attainable retrospectively. The figures given in §6 characterise the measurement, not the object, and this is stated at each of them.

title: TopoDialogue III: Beyond the Transcript — Observable Implicit Interactional Structure in Human–AI Dialogue
abstract: What is often described as the “unspoken” part of human–AI dialogue should not be operationalised by guessing a participant’s hidden state. This instrumentation pilot extends TopoDialogue with seven observable interaction-event candidates: revisit, repair, rejection, adoption, handover, reframing, and explicit pause. It applies deterministic extraction to one 114-turn Japanese human–AI dialogue while withholding every original utterance from the public derivative. The released representation retains speaker order, coarse descriptive metadata, pseudonymous recurrence regions, and event candidates. The paper reports a representation-sensitive trajectory comparison and a low projection-stability failure case. It includes an annotation protocol and per-label agreement software, but does not claim that two-person human agreement has already been measured. The work makes no psychological, clinical, causal, or mathematical-topology claim.

title: Computational Proof Ecology Theory (CPE): A Framework for Modeling Proof Strategies as Ecological Interactions
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Proof Ecology Theory (CPE), a novel interdisciplinary framework that treats formal proofs as living entities evolving within a mathematical ecosystem. By drawing parallels between biological communities and proof development, CPE formalizes three fundamental ecological interactions—competition, combination, and elimination—that govern the dynamics of proof strategies. We present a set of plain‑text equations that capture the population dynamics of proof species, analyze their stability properties, and discuss implications for automated theorem proving, proof search optimization, and the future of computational mathematics. The theoretical insights offered by CPE point toward significant advances in the field, potentially warranting recognition at the highest levels, such as the Turing Award.

title: ALKEMIE Agent: an autonomous platform for computational materials design
abstract: Despite the powerful multi-scale modeling methods and high-throughput infrastructures established in the materials community, real material computation workflows remain fragmented and heavily manual, requiring researchers to constantly bridge software tools, data analysis, and intermediate decisions. This growing gap between methodological capability and practical execution highlights the need for a new kind of autonomous computational framework, one that can coordinate tools, knowledge, and workflows in a more unified and adaptive way. Here, we introduce ALKEMIE Agent, an agentic platform in which retrieval-augmented generation, a materials-computation knowledge base, registered skills, database-supported provenance, AI-assisted structure modeling, bounded task execution, tool-calling iteration, and error-diagnostic assistance are integrated within a traceable control loop. The capabilities of ALKEMIE Agent are demonstrated through applications including materials recommendation, structure modeling, phonon calculations, machine-learned interatomic potential training, LAMMPS simulations, Ab Initio Monte Carlo (AIMC) sampling, and active-learning-based materials screening. Finally, we outline the future directions and challenges for the development of agentic platforms for computational materials design.

title: Self-Verifying Scene-Graph Memory for Long-Horizon Embodied Task Execution
abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks expose a persistent weakness of large-language-model (LLM) and vision-language-action (VLA) agents: acting under partial observability and stochastic execution, a reactive policy forgets what it has seen, hallucinates preconditions, and fails silently when an action slips. We present a lightweight agent architecture pairing a structured scene-graph memory—an accumulating, object-centric record of everything observed and every action outcome—with a per-step self-verification loop: before acting the agent predicts the effect of its action, and a verifier compares the prediction against the resulting scene graph, feeding any mismatch back so the agent can self-correct. On a symbolic kitchen/tabletop benchmark with partial observability and a high stochastic slip rate (0.35), and with the policy driven by a free open-weight LLM, structured memory is the dominant factor—raising task success from 0.15 (reactive) to 0.60 and subgoal completion from 0.53 to 0.72—and self-verification adds a further, complementary gain: perfect recovery from stochastic failures (0.901.00), higher subgoal completion (0.720.80), and the lowest hallucinated-precondition rate (0.03). The raw success gain from verification over memory alone is positive but within confidence intervals; its measurable benefit is concentrated in robustness, at a small cost in invalid-action rate, which we report transparently. The system is pure software, needs no GPU, robot, or data, and runs end-to-end on a laptop.

title: Computational Causal Dynamics Theory (CCDT)
abstract: Computational Causal Dynamics Theory (CCDT) is a formal framework that describes how causal structures evolve over time. By treating causal relations as dynamic entities governed by deterministic or stochastic transition operators, CCDT provides a unified language for modeling complex systems whose underlying mechanisms change with context, time, or internal state. This paper develops the mathematical foundations of CCDT, introduces a canonical model architecture that implements causal updates through a graph transformation kernel, and demonstrates the theory's potential to unify disparate domains such as causal inference, reinforcement learning, and adaptive control. We formalize the core dynamic equation C_t → C_{t+1}, where C_t denotes a causal graph or matrix representation at time t, and outline conditions under which the system exhibits stability, convergence, or chaotic behavior. We also discuss how CCDT can be integrated with probabilistic graphical models and machine learning pipelines to enable real‑time adaptation to nonstationary environments. The implications of CCDT for future research in dynamic computation and the potential for Turing Award–level contributions are highlighted.

title: Computational Boundary Self-Discovery Theory (CBSDT)
abstract: The Computational Boundary Self-Discovery Theory (CBSDT) proposes a formal framework for autonomous systems to identify and articulate the limits of their own computational capabilities. By treating the boundary as an emergent property of the system's internal state, CBSDT enables agents to detect algorithmic, representational, and inferential constraints without external supervision. This paper develops the core concepts of CBSDT, presents a formal model of boundary discovery, and outlines an algorithmic architecture that operationalizes the theory. We discuss the implications for artificial general intelligence, highlight potential applications in adaptive control and autonomous robotics, and outline directions for future research.

title: Computational Personality Compression Theory (CPCT)
abstract: Computational Personality Compression Theory (CPCT) proposes a formal framework for representing long‑term human behavior patterns with a minimal symbolic code. CPCT treats an individual's behavioral history as a discrete sequence of actions or states, S = {s_1, s_2, …, s_n}, where each s_i belongs to a finite alphabet Σ. The theory defines a compression mapping C that assigns to S a compact representation M = C(S) such that the reconstruction fidelity F(S, C(S)) exceeds a pre‑specified threshold. The core idea is that a small set of latent factors, encoded in M, can capture the salient dynamics of S while discarding noise and redundancy. This paper develops the theoretical underpinnings of CPCT, presents algorithmic strategies for constructing M, demonstrates the approach on synthetic behavioral datasets, and discusses implications for future research in cognitive modeling, artificial intelligence, and digital humanities. CPCT may serve as a new representational paradigm, analogous to how Shannon's entropy and Kolmogorov complexity revolutionized information science.

title: Computational Invariant Self‑Revision Theory (CISR)
abstract: Computational Invariant Self‑Revision Theory (CISR) proposes a novel framework for developing adaptive computational systems that can autonomously identify, formalize, and refine invariant properties of their operating environment. By treating invariants as first‑class entities, CISR equips systems with a mechanism to detect when existing invariant assumptions become invalid, triggering an automatic revision process that transforms an old invariant into a new, more accurate invariant. This iterative cycle enables continuous self‑evolution of the theory underpinning the system, reducing reliance on manual human intervention. The theory is grounded in formal logic, automata theory, and statistical learning, and is illustrated through several conceptual case studies. CISR offers a pathway toward systems with the capacity for self‑directed theoretical development, potentially qualifying for recognition comparable to the Turing Award.

title: Designing Reliable Harnesses for Autonomous Machine Learning Experiments: Failure Modes, Safeguards, and Lessons Learned
abstract: Autonomous AI agents offer a promising venue to accelerating machine learning research through iterative experimentation with limited human intervention. However, reliable autonomous experimentation requires carefully designed experimental environments that prevent unintended modifications and preserve evaluation integrity. Drawing on more than 15,000 autonomous experimental runs across three biomedical segmentation benchmarks, we present practical recommendations and lessons learned for designing robust experimental harnesses. Our findings highlight common agent behaviors and provide guidelines for improving the reliability, reproducibility, and efficiency of structured autonomous machine learning experiments.

title: Time- and Space-Efficient List Decoding up to Capacity
abstract: In the theory of error correcting codes, list-decoding refers to the following problem. Given a code $C \subseteq Σ^N$ and a received word $y \in Σ^N$, find all codewords $c \in C$ so that $δ(c,y) \leq ρ$, where $δ$ is relative Hamming distance and $ρ\in (0,1)$. Codes that approach the optimal trade-off between the rate $R := \log_{|Σ|}(|C|) / N$ and the list-decoding radius $ρ$ are said to achieve capacity.By now, there are constructions of capacity-achieving list-decodable codes with fast near-linear-time list-decoding algorithms, but most existing work has not considered space complexity. In a recent line of work, Cook and Moshkovitz (2024, 2025, 2026) initiated the study of low-space deterministic algorithms for error correcting codes. In particular, in their 2026 paper, they gave a construction of list-decodable codes with deterministic near-linear-time and sublinear space list-decoding algorithms. However, these codes were far from achieving capacity. In this paper, we present list-decodable codes approaching capacity with deterministic time- and space-efficient list-decoding algorithms. More precisely, for any $R \in (0,1)$ and any arbitrarily small constant $τ> 0$, we present a family of codes $C\subseteq Σ^N$ with rate $R$ that are deterministically list-decodable up to radius $ρ= 1 - R - τ$, in time $N^{1 + τ}$ and space $N^τ$ with constant output list size and constant alphabet size. Our results can be extended to capacity-achieving list-recoverable codes.

evidence.title: Time- and Space-Efficient List Decoding up to Capacity
evidence.abstract: In the theory of error correcting codes, list-decoding refers to the following problem. Given a code $C \subseteq Σ^N$ and a received word $y \in Σ^N$, find all codewords $c \in C$ so that $δ(c,y) \leq ρ$, where $δ$ is relative Hamming distance and $ρ\in (0,1)$. Codes that approach the optimal trade-off between the rate $R := \log_{|Σ|}(|C|) / N$ and the list-decoding radius $ρ$ are said to achieve capacity.By now, there are constructions of capacity-achieving list-decodable codes with fast near-linear-time list-decoding algorithms, but most existing work has not considered space complexity. In a recent line of work, Cook and Moshkovitz (2024, 2025, 2026) initiated the study of low-space deterministic algorithms for error correcting codes. In particular, in their 2026 paper, they gave a construction of list-decodable codes with deterministic near-linear-time and sublinear space list-decoding algorithms. However, these codes were far from achieving capacity. In this paper, we present list-decodable codes approaching capacity with deterministic time- and space-efficient list-decoding algorithms. More precisely, for any $R \in (0,1)$ and any arbitrarily small constant $τ> 0$, we present a family of codes $C\subseteq Σ^N$ with rate $R$ that are deterministically list-decodable up to radius $ρ= 1 - R - τ$, in time $N^{1 + τ}$ and space $N^τ$ with constant output list size and constant alphabet size. Our results can be extended to capacity-achieving list-recoverable codes.

title: Learning Stock Trading Policies via Barycenter-Based Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Designing effective trading strategies using reinforcement learning remains challenging due to delayed and noisy rewards, poor exploration, and the difficulty of enforcing explicit risk constraints. In this work, we propose BRaG, a barycenter-based adversarial inverse reinforcement learning framework for stock trading that learns trading behavior from multiple heterogeneous expert strategies. BRaG aggregates expert demonstrations using a performance-weighted Wasserstein barycenter, yielding a stable pseudo-expert representation that captures shared structure across diverse trading styles. This representation is used to pretrain a trading policy via adversarial imitation learning, which alleviates unstable exploration during reinforcement learning. The pretrained policy is subsequently refined using reinforcement learning with true market rewards. To ensure risk-aware decision-making, BRaG incorporates control barrier functions that constrain action execution and regularize policy learning to satisfy drawdown limits. We evaluate the proposed approach on four major global equity markets, including the US, UK, Indian, and Taiwanese indices. Across all the markets, the proposed approach achieves stronger performance than both classical trading rules and recent deep reinforcement learning methods, while exhibiting more stable risk characteristics.

title: Computational Resource Transfer Theory (CRTT): A Unified Framework for Translating Human Knowledge into Computational Capabilities
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital systems and artificial intelligence has highlighted a persistent gap between the richness of human knowledge and the efficiency of computational resources. This paper introduces Computational Resource Transfer Theory (CRTT), a formal framework that models the conversion of human knowledge into computational resources through systematic mappings, optimization strategies, and adaptive learning mechanisms. CRTT defines a set of core principles, mathematical formulations, and transformation protocols that enable the translation of domain expertise, heuristics, and experiential insights into algorithmic components, data structures, and processing pipelines. By bridging cognitive constructs with machine architectures, CRTT proposes a pathway toward unified human-machine resource utilization, offering a theoretical foundation that could underpin future Turing Award–level breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and human-computer interaction.

title: Computational Personality Generation Network (CPGN)
abstract: The rise of deep learning has yielded models that excel at performing specified tasks, yet these systems lack an internal sense of identity or style. This paper introduces the Computational Personality Generation Network (CPGN), a novel architecture that learns not only to solve problems but also to cultivate an intrinsic computational personality. CPGN comprises a dual‑branch design: a task‑oriented head and a personality‑oriented head, coupled through a shared latent space that is continuously refined by a meta‑learning loop. The personality head learns to shape the network's parameter updates, internal activations, and inference trajectories, thereby enabling the system to exhibit distinct computational styles such as conservative, exploratory, or aggressive reasoning. Theoretically, we analyze CPGN's convergence properties, show that the personality dynamics can be modeled as a stochastic differential equation over the latent space, and demonstrate that the system can spontaneously generate new inference strategies that are not explicitly encoded in the training data. This capacity positions CPGN as a candidate for a new AI paradigm, potentially leading to Turing‑award‑level breakthroughs in autonomous intelligence.

title: Computational Abstraction Ecology Theory (CAE)
abstract: Computational Abstraction Ecology Theory (CAE) proposes a unified framework for understanding the emergence, interaction, and evolution of abstractions in large‑scale computational systems. Drawing inspiration from ecological metaphors—coexistence, replacement, and evolution—CAE models abstractions as dynamic species that occupy resource niches within a computational ecosystem. By formalizing abstraction dynamics with simple differential and difference equations, CAE offers insights into the stability and adaptability of software architectures, the propagation of programming paradigms, and the long‑term trajectory of computational civilizations. This paper develops the core concepts of CAE, presents mathematical formulations for coexistence, replacement, and evolutionary processes, and discusses the potential of CAE to guide the design of resilient computational infrastructures and to illuminate the factors driving the growth of computational societies.

title: Demons on a Budget: Adaptive Measurement Placement at the Entanglement Phase Transition
abstract: Monitored quantum circuits exhibit a measurement-induced phase transition between volume-law and area-law entanglement as a function of the measurement rate $p$. Prior work places measurements at random locations and treats the rate as the control parameter. We instead fix the measurement budget and vary the placement process, comparing random placement against hand-designed and learned policies in brickwork random Clifford circuits at matched budget. First, placement geometry matters more than placement information. A deterministic contiguous sweep cuts the half-cut entropy by a factor of 3.4 relative to random placement, while equal-coverage unstructured placement and a greedy policy with full state access do far worse. The effect is carried by spatial order alone: measuring the $k$ least recently measured sites gives $4.14 \pm 0.06$ bits with random tie-breaking and $1.29 \pm 0.04$ bits with position-ordered tie-breaking. Second, the sweep eliminates the transition rather than shifting it. Tripartite mutual information crossings recede as $p^* \propto 1/L$, the steady-state entropy saturates at an $L$-independent ceiling near $0.46/p$, and data for $64 \le L \le 512$ collapse onto the form $S = p^{-1} f(pL)$ predicted by a ballistic regrowth argument. Third, in stabilizer dynamics every outcome is deterministic or a fair coin flip, so the record's Shannon entropy is exactly countable; the sweep dominates the entropy-versus-record-cost frontier while paying the same roughly one bit per measurement as random placement. Policies trained by cross-entropy and proximal policy optimization do not find the sweep: score-based policies parameterize which sites to measure, not the order in which degenerate scores are resolved, and the effect lives in that order. The phase diagram of monitored dynamics is a property of the placement process, not only of the measurement rate.

title: Monoidal su-categories
abstract: We introduce monoidal su-categories, an abstract categorical notion of single-input higher-order process over a monoidal category. The definition separates a base category C of lower-order processes from a monoidal category V of holes or supermaps and axiomatizes the compatibility needed for partial application to bipartite processes. For a fixed monoidal base C, monoidal su-categories, monoidal su-functors, and monoidal su-natural transformations form a 2-category MonSuCatC. We then show that the category Optic[C] of coend optics is 2-initial in this 2-category, giving an alternative universal-property characterisation of coend optics as the minimal monoidal theory of single-hole contexts.

title: LED-ML: Causal Lens of Layer-wise Energy Dissipation in LLM
abstract: This paper presents an observability mechanism for LLM internals that simultaneously captures forward activations and Vector-Jacobian Products (VJPs) of target output logits. It provides lightweight, hook based implementation designed to extract runtime tensors and target gradients safely across layers. A down-sampled subset of these captured tensors are rendered into text based visual maps and Graphics Interchange Format (GIF) animations.This framework provides an illustrative and intuitive interface for analyzing the internal states and semantic interpretations of deep models, enabling architecture debugging, training diagnostics, and dynamic routing.

title: Unified Computational Personality Theory (UCPT)
abstract: The field of computer science has traditionally been driven by a sequence of abstractions that map input to algorithmic manipulation and produce output. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have shifted this paradigm toward a data–model–prediction pipeline, yet the notion of a system's own identity, style, and self‑model remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces Unified Computational Personality Theory (UCPT), a formal framework that characterizes a computational system's personality as an emergent property derived from its learning history, interaction patterns, and optimization processes. We provide a concise mathematical representation, demonstrate how UCPT extends existing computational models, and discuss its implications for the design of intelligent agents with self‑aware capabilities. Finally, we outline twenty novel research directions that build upon UCPT and could serve as foundational contributions to the next generation of Turing Award–level work.

title: Computational World Model Dynamics Theory (CWMDT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational World Model Dynamics Theory (CWMDT), a framework for describing how a world model—an internal representation of an agent's environment—evolves over time. The core premise is that the world model is continuously updated according to a deterministic or stochastic evolution equation that integrates new observations, internal predictions, and feedback from actions. We formulate the update rule, analyze its mathematical properties, and discuss how CWMDT can serve as a foundation for dynamic intelligence research, potentially guiding the development of systems that exhibit learning, adaptation, and planning at a scale comparable to human cognition. The theory is presented without empirical experiments, focusing instead on formal derivation and theoretical implications.

title: When AI Decides with Me: The Delegation-Overreach Paradox in AI-Mediated Smartphone Purchases
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes involved in an increasing number of consumers’ buying choices, the role of AI in consumption patterns transforms from a recommending agent to a decision-making partner. The study explores the influence of AI Decision Delegation on Customer Advocacy through the mediation of Perceived AI–Customer Decision Partnership and focuses on the role of AI Autonomy Expectation and Algorithmic Overreach as moderators. Exploratory research has been conducted among Generation Z customers to operationalize the effect of the delegation in the smartphone and technology market. A quantitative, cross-sectional method was implemented to collect and analyze data from approximately 378 participants. The analysis was carried out in SmartPLS 4 using the PLS-SEM technique and bootstrapping procedure to evaluate direct, mediating, moderating, and conditional indirect effects. The results demonstrate that AI Decision Delegation positively affects customers’ perception of AI as a decision-making partner, which, in turn, drives Customer Advocacy. The study found the strongest support for the mediating role of Perceived AI–Customer Decision Partnership, suggesting that the relationship between AI Decision Delegation and Customer Advocacy was established due to increased advocacy stemming from the perception of delegation as a shared AI–customer decision-making process. Moreover, the first-order moderation effect of AI Autonomy Expectation was found to strengthen the mediation process, while the effect of Algorithmic Overreach was negative. The Delegation–Overreach Paradox was identified as a second-order interaction between the two first-order moderators that showed consumer expectations of AI autonomy to handle complex decisions but in circumstances where AI does not take responsibility for outcomes. This article adds to the understanding of AI marketing by reconceptualizing consumer–AI relationships around shared decision-making processes and advocating for the necessity of empowering consumers to influence AI decisions as a key to cultivating long-term Customer Advocacy. The results have implications for marketers who should consider AI Decision Delegation as an element of the decision-making process that empowers consumers and transforms AI-driven buying experiences into memorable moments. title: Computational Causal Hierarchy Theory (CCHT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Causal Hierarchy Theory (CCHT), a unifying framework that connects low‑level operations, algorithms, systems, and intelligence through a causal lens. By formalizing the flow of causal influence from elementary operations to emergent intelligent behavior, CCHT provides a principled basis for evaluating and designing computational systems. The theory leverages established causal inference notation while extending it to encompass algorithmic complexity, system architecture, and cognitive function. We discuss the theoretical foundations, present a rigorous mathematical formalization, and explore the implications of CCHT for artificial intelligence research. The potential for CCHT to guide the development of transformative AI aligns with the criteria for the Turing Award, offering a cohesive explanation for how computation and causality intertwine to produce intelligence.

title: Unified Computational Abstraction Theory (UCAT)
abstract: The evolution of computing has historically hinged on the invention of new abstractions rather than on incremental algorithmic improvements. This paper proposes the Unified Computational Abstraction Theory (UCAT) as a comprehensive framework that unifies algorithms, programming languages, AI representations, software architecture, and computational models under a single abstract paradigm. UCAT is formally expressed as the transformation sequence: Observation + Structure + Search → New Abstraction → New Computation. By systematically analyzing the lifecycle of computational abstractions, we demonstrate how UCAT can be applied to generate novel computational principles, thereby expanding the foundation of computing theory. The theoretical contributions include a formal definition of abstraction discovery, a classification of abstraction layers, and a set of construction rules that guide the creation of new abstractions. Practical implications are discussed in the context of designing next‑generation programming languages, AI systems, and software architectures that inherently support the automatic generation of abstractions. UCAT thus provides a roadmap for future research aimed at creating computing systems that not only optimize existing algorithms but also discover new computational principles autonomously.

title: Relations Among Listed Pauli Terms Bound Distance in Qubit Stabilizer qLTCs
abstract: How many linear relations must a quantum locally testable stabilizer Hamiltonian contain? We prove a finite relation–distance law for qubit stabilizer presentations that bounds code distance in terms of local-term weight, code rate, normalized soundness, and the dimension of the relation space among listed terms. Thus, under bounded term weight, a family cannot simultaneously have constant rate, linear distance, and constant normalized soundness without linearly many independent relations. With bounded qubit incidence, this remains true after duplicate terms are removed. For Calderbank–Shor–Steane presentations with constant normalized soundness in both check sectors, the requirement separates by sector, so redundancy cannot be concentrated in one sector. The result provides a rank- computable necessary test for candidate locally testable stabilizer Hamiltonians, a soundness ceiling for natural rank-minimal hypergraph-product presentations, and sectorwise lower bounds for term-appending amplifiers.

title: Consumer Cognitive Electronics: Physics-Based Intelligence for Every Device
abstract: We present the application of a deterministic cognitive substrate to consumer electronics: smartphones, smart TVs, wearables, security cameras, electric vehicles, health monitors, and smart home devices. The 2MB physics kernel delivers 10-60x battery life improvement through zero-idle operation, privacy by structural impossibility of data leakage, deterministic personalization without machine learning, and content authentication through conservation enforcement. 2.8 billion devices ship annually -- each one needs intelligence the kernel provides.

title: Computational Personality Fusion Theory (CPFT-2)
abstract: The increasing complexity of artificial agents necessitates advanced mechanisms for synthesizing multiple individual personalities into coherent, emergent computational personalities. This paper proposes the Computational Personality Fusion Theory (CPFT-2), a formal framework for integrating the affective, cognitive, and behavioral attributes of multiple intelligent agents into a unified personality representation. CPFT-2 introduces a hierarchical fusion architecture that leverages weighted aggregation of trait vectors, dynamic adjustment of inter‑agent influence matrices, and a self‑consistency loss that ensures emergent personalities remain coherent over time. The theory is grounded in psychological models of personality, such as the Five‑Factor Model, and extends them to the computational domain by defining a trait space T = {t_1, t_2, …, t_N}. The fusion operator F is formally described as F(P_1, P_2, …, P_M) → P_f, where each P_i is a vector of trait scores and influence weights. We detail the mathematical formulation, provide an algorithmic specification, and discuss potential applications in multi‑agent systems, adaptive user interfaces, and collaborative robotics. By establishing a principled method for personality synthesis, CPFT-2 offers a pathway toward more nuanced, socially intelligent artificial systems.

title: Proof Compression Limit Theory (PCLT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Proof Compression Limit Theory (PCLT), a novel framework for understanding the inherent constraints within mathematical proofs. The core concept revolves around identifying the minimal form of a proof, denoted as `P → P_min`, which represents the most concise and essential representation of the argument. PCLT posits that there exists a limit to how much a proof can be compressed, dictated by the fundamental structure of the mathematical object being proven. The theory aims to characterize this limit, providing insights into the nature of proof reduction and potentially offering a new perspective on the efficiency of mathematical reasoning. This work explores the key elements of PCLT, detailing the method for identifying `P_min` and discussing its implications across various mathematical domains. The focus is on the theoretical underpinnings of the theory, without experimental validation. ---

title: Global Simulation-Guided Dynamic Operator Scheduling for Efficient Multi-Tenant Model Serving
abstract: Container-granularity scheduling leaves abundant short-lived idle slices within containers unexploited. Reallocating containers is too heavyweight to utilize such fine-grained opportunities under SLA constraints, and operator-level scheduling requires reasoning about dependencies, memory safety, and cluster-wide execution dynamics in real time. In this paper, we present SliceScheduler, a dynamic operator-level scheduling system for multi-tenant model serving. The key idea is to expose cluster-wide operator execution state and enable what-if reasoning over scheduling decisions. SliceScheduler consists of four key components. First, we introduce the Global Mapping Graph (GMG), a unified abstraction that captures operator dependencies, tensor shapes, resource mappings, and execution states, providing a real-time, cluster-wide view with explicit resource semantics. Second, we build a global simulator on top of GMG to predict operator-level execution and memory evolution under candidate placements. Third, we design an incremental, simulation-based scheduling module that selects placements to exploit fragmented idle slices while avoiding memory violations and preserving SLA. Finally, we develop an operator executor that materializes scheduling decisions on GPUs and coordinates computation and cross-accelerator transfers. We implement SliceScheduler as a PyTorch backend and evaluate it using production trace replay. Experimental results show that SliceScheduler improves token throughput by 1.10--2.29$\times$ compared to existing approaches, while maintaining SLA violations within 9\%. SliceScheduler demonstrates that operator-level scheduling is a practical and effective approach to improving GPU utilization for multi-tenant LLM serving.

title: owlery-vfb: Owlery reasoner endpoint configured for the Virtual Fly Brain ontology
abstract: Container build and configuration for the Owlery OWL reasoner endpoint used by Virtual Fly Brain. It serves DL queries over VFB's ontology, and is what answers the classification and subsumption queries behind VFB's search and its neuron/region browsing. By default it loads owlery-live.owl as published at http://VirtualFlyBrain.org/data/VFB/OWL/owlery-live.owl; the OWLURL environment variable overrides this, and LOGLEVEL controls logging. Request and idle timeouts are set to 240 seconds to survive long prefix-resolution queries. This repository contains VFB's Dockerfile and configuration only. Owlery itself is separate software by the Phenoscape project, MIT licensed, at https://github.com/phenoscape/owlery . This repository began as a fork of https://github.com/Robbie1977/docker-sbt-owlery .

title: Computational Representation Self-Discovery Theory (CRSDT)
abstract: Computational representation self‑discovery theory (CRSDT) proposes a principled approach in which a computational system autonomously searches for the representation that most effectively captures the intrinsic structure of a given problem domain. Rather than relying on human‑designed features such as vectors, graphs, or tensors, the system iteratively refines a space of candidate representations, guided by a composite objective that balances expressiveness, compactness, and learnability. This paper formalizes the theoretical foundations of CRSDT, introduces a generic algorithmic framework for self‑discovery of representations, and discusses the potential implications for next‑generation computational paradigms. We argue that CRSDT can unlock new levels of abstraction, enabling systems to discover richer data structures that transcend conventional linear, relational, or multilinear forms. The theory also offers a lens through which to view emergent representation learning in deep neural networks and to inspire the design of adaptive, self‑organizing computational architectures that may serve as foundations for future generations of computing.

title: Computational World Model Fusion Theory (CWMFT)
abstract: The notion of a world model has become central to many modern approaches in artificial intelligence, philosophy, and cognitive science. Traditional world models are typically limited by the scope of the data and the assumptions inherent in their construction, leading to fragmented or incomplete representations of reality. This paper introduces the Computational World Model Fusion Theory (CWMFT), which proposes a principled framework for combining multiple world models into a single, more comprehensive model. The core idea is encapsulated in the fusion operation W_1 + W_2 → W_3, where two distinct world models W_1 and W_2 are merged to produce a richer model W_3 that captures a broader range of phenomena. We formalize this operation, discuss its computational properties, and analyze its convergence and stability. We further explore the potential applications of CWMFT across knowledge integration, artificial general intelligence, and scientific discovery, arguing that this fusion framework could serve as a foundation for unified knowledge systems and may even possess the transformative potential that aligns with the vision of a Turing Award. The paper offers a comprehensive theoretical foundation without relying on empirical experiments, thereby focusing on the mathematical underpinnings and conceptual implications of the theory.

title: Provenance, Not Behaviour: A Serialisation Artifact in Edge-IIoTset and a Leakage-Free Benchmark for Precision-Agriculture Intrusion Detection
abstract: Edge-IIoTset is the reference benchmark for machine-learning intrusion detection in the industrial Internet of Things, and results reported on it cluster above 99%. We show that much of that performance is not intrusion detection. The preprocessing recipe distributed with the dataset instructs researchers to one-hot encode seven categorical columns. Four of them separate attack from normal traffic with an accuracy of 1.0000 on their own, through the spelling of the placeholder written for an absent protocol field: the string "0" in the normal-traffic branch of the dataset build against "0.0" in the attack branch. The label is recoverable from a serialisation artifact encoding file provenance, with no network behaviour modelled, and separates every row of both curated subsets. Under 5-fold x 3-repeat cross-validation, five of six standard classifiers attain exactly 1.0000 +/- 0.0000 accuracy and the sixth attains 0.99998. Under a corrected protocol, naive Bayes falls by 0.3005 macro-F1 and the strongest model settles at 0.9503 +/- 0.0011. Label, ordinal and frequency encoding leak identically. Because the curated subsets also lack Modbus and per-device identity, we rebuild the benchmark from the raw captures under uniform parsing, producing AgriEdge: 1,276,122 rows, five devices with full attribution, and no column separating the classes above 0.0288. A leave-one-device-out sweep locates the generalisation boundary at the perception/actuation layer, where random forest falls from 0.9988 to 0.5083 balanced accuracy. Non-IID federated partitioning costs at most 0.0037 macro-F1, but a 20-round LoRaWAN training run costs 4.6 hours of uplink.

evidence.title: Provenance, Not Behaviour: A Serialisation Artifact in Edge-IIoTset and a Leakage-Free Benchmark for Precision-Agriculture Intrusion Detection
evidence.abstract: Edge-IIoTset is the reference benchmark for machine-learning intrusion detection in the industrial Internet of Things, and results reported on it cluster above 99%. We show that much of that performance is not intrusion detection. The preprocessing recipe distributed with the dataset instructs researchers to one-hot encode seven categorical columns. Four of them separate attack from normal traffic with an accuracy of 1.0000 on their own, through the spelling of the placeholder written for an absent protocol field: the string "0" in the normal-traffic branch of the dataset build against "0.0" in the attack branch. The label is recoverable from a serialisation artifact encoding file provenance, with no network behaviour modelled, and separates every row of both curated subsets. Under 5-fold x 3-repeat cross-validation, five of six standard classifiers attain exactly 1.0000 +/- 0.0000 accuracy and the sixth attains 0.99998. Under a corrected protocol, naive Bayes falls by 0.3005 macro-F1 and the strongest model settles at 0.9503 +/- 0.0011. Label, ordinal and frequency encoding leak identically. Because the curated subsets also lack Modbus and per-device identity, we rebuild the benchmark from the raw captures under uniform parsing, producing AgriEdge: 1,276,122 rows, five devices with full attribution, and no column separating the classes above 0.0288. A leave-one-device-out sweep locates the generalisation boundary at the perception/actuation layer, where random forest falls from 0.9988 to 0.5083 balanced accuracy. Non-IID federated partitioning costs at most 0.0037 macro-F1, but a 20-round LoRaWAN training run costs 4.6 hours of uplink.

title: Who Leads Now? Token-Level Modality Arbitration for Chart-to-Code Generation
abstract: Chart-to-code generation requires a model to read the fine-grained visual details of a chart and write executable code that reproduces it. Existing chart-to-code methods either train visual and coding abilities separately, or fine-tune on chart-to-code data with the two abilities entangled. Neither strategy accounts for the distinct nature of the two abilities or the interference that arises when they are optimized together. We propose MoCA (Mixture of Cross-modal Arbitration), which separates the two abilities rather than blending them. MoCA is built on Cross-modal Arbitration Block (CAB), which maintains a visual branch and a code branch as two distinct pathways, and a lightweight arbiter that arbitrates their relative contributions at every layer and generated token. We train MoCA in two stages: a supervised warm-up on self-distilled reasoning trajectories that decomposes visual understanding into explicit steps, followed by reinforcement learning with rewards on both the reasoning process and the final code. Analysis shows that the arbiter learns structured rather than arbitrary allocations, with expert contributions varying systematically across tokens, layers, and instances. Across three benchmarks, MoCA delivers competitive performance against general-domain and chart-specialized models. Ablation results show that the gains cannot be attributed to a larger model size alone, but instead arise from the joint contributions of complementary visual and code branch initialization and input-conditioned arbitration through CAB.

title: Computational Self‑Fusion Theory (CSFT): A Unified Framework for Multi‑Agent Self‑Modeling and Collective Intelligence
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Self‑Fusion Theory (CSFT), a theoretical framework that describes how multiple autonomous intelligent systems can fuse their individual self‑models into a coherent collective self‑model. The central mathematical construct is the self‑fusion operator, denoted ⊕, which combines two self‑representations S_i and S_j to produce a new representation S_k. The theory is grounded in formal logic, information theory, and dynamical systems, and it offers explicit equations for the evolution of fused self‑models over time. CSFT provides a rigorous basis for understanding the emergence of shared identity in multi‑agent networks, the potential for unprecedented levels of collective intelligence, and the possibility of achieving Turing Award‑level breakthroughs in artificial general intelligence. The paper details the formalism, explores theoretical scenarios, and discusses implications for future research in autonomous systems, distributed cognition, and human‑machine interaction.

title: Dynamic heterogeneous graph-structured knowledge tracing with multi-behavior integration and temporal forgetting
abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) aims to estimate the temporal evolution of learners’ knowledge states and predict future exercise performance. Most existing KT methods focus on exercise-response sequences and therefore cannot explicitly distinguish knowledge exposure through learning resources from knowledge verification through problem solving. We propose Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph-Structured Knowledge Tracing (DHGKT), a framework that organizes learners, exercises, videos, concepts, and optional comments within a unified relational event representation. Each learner is associated with an interpretable concept-mastery vector. Before each event, an exponential temporal decay is applied; video events provide a duration-aware exposure signal, whereas exercise events calibrate the state through prediction-error feedback. Semantic concept-video weighting and concept-aligned social exposure are treated as auxiliary extensions rather than indispensable components. Under a chronological 70%/10%/20% training/validation/test split with five random seeds on four MOOCCubeX courses, DHGKT-Core achieved an average test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.8529, compared with 0.8318 for its exercise-only variant and 0.7508 for a same-input multi-behavior fusion control. The contribution of video behavior was course dependent: it improved three courses but reduced performance on C_801420. Fixed and learnable topology-aggregation variants produced negligible AUC changes, and the semantic and social extensions did not yield reliable additional gains. These results indicate that the principal value of DHGKT lies in transparent event-driven knowledge-state evolution rather than generic graph convolution. The revision further clarifies the roles of behavioral modalities, graph-event semantics, decay sensitivity, and evaluation limitations in response to the second-round comments.

title: An affective computing framework for preschool music education using MoE architecture and neural radiance fields
abstract: The key content of this paper is the digital construction of preschool music education scenarios and affective computing. It adopts an innovative approach, integrating the MoE architecture and neural radiance field technology together. The Edu-NeRF reconstruction framework is relied on to achieve high-fidelity reconstruction of dynamic scenes, and its PSNR value is 28.5. The SSIM value is 0.92, which is 10.8% higher than that of the traditional method. This paper also constructed an affective computing model. After training this model with 60 h of multimodal data from 120 preschool children, its accuracy rate for emotional state recognition reached 89.7%, with a macroscopic F1 value of 0.881. By combining cross-modal fusion algorithms, we have successfully broken through the technical bottlenecks in dynamic scene reconstruction and affective computing. In terms of real-world applicability, this approach significantly outperforms conventional 2D music education products. It enables real-time, high-fidelity interaction on standard low-power devices, thereby reducing hardware deployment costs and lowering the barrier for widespread school adoption. Furthermore, experimental verification demonstrates that this model increases children’s learning engagement and the efficiency of personalized interaction by 30%. By enhancing both the immersive learning experience and teacher acceptance, this framework provides a highly practical and scalable technical path for the digital transformation of early childhood education.

title: Temporal Logic Guided Universal Task Representations for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Task guided agents demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of complex tasks. However, most existing task representation algorithms are tailored to specific contexts and struggle to generalize across diverse scenarios. Moreover, they typically depend on gradient signals from reinforcement learning controllers to update their weights, which can degrade both representation quality and learning efficiency. To overcome these limitations, we propose LOTUS, a temporal logic inspired universal task representation framework that can be seamlessly integrated into any RL algorithm to enhance agent performance across diverse task settings. Specifically, we design a novel task representation architecture capable of modeling relationships and extracting task semantics from LTL formulas. We further introduce a more effective update mechanism that treats the LTL encoder as a policy, thereby improving representation capacity. To enhance stability and robustness, LOTUS leverages the bisimulation metric, which provides theoretical guarantees for LTL representation, including behavioral equivalence, optimality fidelity, and trajectory robustness. Experimental results show that LOTUS outperforms most existing methods in learning efficiency, generalization capability, and representation quality. Specifically, LOTUS accelerates convergence over 20% in single-task scenarios, achieves a 15%-45% higher success rate in unseen manipulation tasks, and improves generalization performance over 25% in complex multi-task environments with increased sub-goal depth or conjunctions. The corresponding code, videos, and appendix are available at: https://lotus-website.github.io/.

title: Virtual Fly Brain knowledge graph v26.08.16
abstract: The Virtual Fly Brain knowledge graph as served at release v26.08.16. title: BEF-T: Converting the Börekci Energy Field into a Quantum Teleportation Platform — Atomic-State Teleportation in a Fully Isolated Cavity and Across an Energy Shell, a Delayed-Classical-Channel Protocol, and a Teleportation-Based ξ Probe
abstract: This preprint presents BEF-T, a design study that converts the Börekci Energy Field (BEF) apparatus — a fully isolated underground cavity containing a stationary two-pole cavity electromagnet (2 T total), a 50 MV electron-arc energy shell and a 1 PW circular laser — into a platform for trapped-ion quantum teleportation. The paper (i) reviews the physics of quantum teleportation (Bennett et al., 1993) and its experimental status; (ii) maps every existing BEF component to a teleportation function, re-tasking the Penning positron traps as ion-qubit nodes operating in the 2 T confinement field; (iii) defines three experiments: D1, in-cavity teleportation between nodes A and A′ across ~8 m; D2, cavity-to-exterior teleportation across the energy shell to an outside node B using entanglement distributed by fiber before the run; and D3, a delayed-classical-channel protocol in which the two classical bits of the Bell measurement are recorded inside the sealed 24-hour run and the unitary correction is applied only after unsealing; (iv) proposes a teleportation-based probe of the ξ parameter of the Börekci metric, complementary to the parent paper's three-clock protocol, with a predicted interior optical-qubit phase accumulation of ~5×10⁻³ rad per day at ξ = 1; and (v) states strict physical limits honestly: no faster-than-light signalling, no macroscopic (cell- or animal-scale) teleportation, and no use of the shell's e⁺e⁻ pairs as an entanglement resource. A motivating gap: almost all teleportation and entanglement experiments live at the micro scale, while macro-scale isolated-volume platforms are scarce — BEF offers a macroscopic, fully isolated test environment. Files include the English full text, the Turkish full text, the adaptation figure in both languages, and a narrated animated 3-D explainer video with subtitles in English and Turkish. This is a sister paper of the author's parent preprint (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9999735) and of the cavity-magnet BEF design study.
