title: Probabilistic Forecasting in Multi-Constrained Dynamic Systems via Large Language Models: Computing Nash Equilibria as the Mode of Conditional Probability Distributions inside Transformer Architectures
abstract: The primary bottleneck in multi-degree-of-freedom multi-agent simulations and complex system forecasting is the introduction of subjective bias or narrative noise by human designers. When a system faces catastrophic shocks such as fatal failures or network disconnections, human observers tend to underestimate objective probabilities or introduce unrealistic scenarios based on status-quo bias. This paper redefines Large Language Models (LLMs) not merely as text generators but as high-dimensional probabilistic predictive engines that internalize the decision-making patterns of multi-constrained networks. We elucidate the information-theoretic mechanism by which the self-attention mechanism of the Transformer architecture cold-bloodedly calculates the true Nash equilibrium (maximum probability value) of a system when rigorous microscopic constraints are input as initial parameters, free from subjective human bias. Through a controlled experiment comparing noise-inclusive and pure-constraint context windows, we mathematically demonstrate that the residual entropy of the state space exhibits exponential decay characteristics as the number of independent fact dimensions increases, forcing the conditional sampling probability to converge to a specific game-theoretic Nash equilibrium with high probability.

title: Computational Principle Fusion Theory (CPFT): A New Paradigm for Integrating Computational Principles
abstract: Computational Principle Fusion Theory (CPFT) proposes a systematic method for merging distinct computational principles into a unified framework, thereby creating new computational foundations that surpass the capabilities of their individual components. The core operation of CPFT is expressed as the fusion of two principles, (P1+P2) → P3, where the resulting principle P3 inherits properties from both P1 and P2 while introducing novel behaviors. This paper develops the formal underpinnings of CPFT, outlines a generic fusion mechanism, and demonstrates its applicability through illustrative examples. We discuss the theoretical advantages of CPFT, including increased expressiveness, modularity, and potential for establishing new computational paradigms. Finally, we examine the implications of CPFT for complexity theory, program synthesis, and future research directions that could lead to groundbreaking achievements in computer science.

title: RoBangHate: A Romanized Bangla Hate Speech Corpus and a Systematic Benchmark of Parameter-Efficient LLM Adaptation
abstract: RoBangHate is a manually annotated corpus for binary hate speech detection in Romanized Bangla (Banglish). The corpus consists of naturally occurring social-media comments collected from Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube. Each comment is annotated with one of two labels: Hate or Non-Hate. The annotation protocol distinguishes hate-directed content from ordinary criticism, political disagreement, negative sentiment, sarcasm, and profanity that does not constitute hate speech. The corpus is designed to capture linguistic characteristics of Banglish, including orthographic variation, informal spelling, Bangla-English code-mixing, profanity, and lexical diversity. The dataset is released to support research in Banglish hate speech detection, multilingual and low-resource NLP, content moderation, and robustness evaluation. This release includes the dataset, annotation guidelines, and documentation describing the corpus and annotation procedure. The dataset should be used for research and responsible NLP development. Users should not use the resource to identify, target,harass, or otherwise harm individuals.

title: Conjunctive Poisoning in AI Supply-Chain Applications
abstract: Large Language and Vision-Language Models are increasingly deployed through inference pipelines that include prompt wrappers (e.g., templates and post-processing scripts) and configuration metadata (e.g., JSON/YAML files) that together shape model outputs. While model weights and binaries are routinely verified, these textual deployment artifacts remain weakly protected despite directly influencing runtime behavior. We show that a malicious developer can pair a benign-looking wrapper with crafted metadata to deterministically alter post-generation behavior without modifying model weights, training data, or inference backend. We study this behavior through a controlled conjunctive-gate implementation, where activation depends on both an embedded wrapper marker and cryptographically bound metadata. We evaluate the attack across fifteen open- and closed-source LLM/VLM deployments, and assess prompt and system level defenses including static metadata inspection, wrapper scanners, PromptShield, and SigStore-based artifact signing. To mitigate this risk, we introduce TIF-BAH, a lightweight middleware defense that verifies wrapper integrity and records behavioral attestations during inference. Our results reveal that wrapper-metadata interactions form an under-protected execution layer in modern AI deployments, exposing a deployment-time behavioral risk that is not captured by model-weight or prompt-level defenses. Code is available at https://github.com/N-H-Arif/llm_temp.

title: GigaBrain-0.7: Scaling Embodied Foundation Models to Emergent Capabilities with a Three-System Architecture
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a dominant paradigm for generalist embodied agents, demonstrating strong complex and long-horizon task completion in structured settings. Yet it remains an open question whether current VLA systems can benefit from more effective architectural design, scale to substantially larger and more heterogeneous data regimes, and achieve broader generalization across tasks and embodiments. To this end, we present GigaBrain-0.7, an embodied foundation model with substantially improved generalization across diverse robot embodiments. Specifically, GigaBrain-0.7 unifies understanding, prediction, and action through a three-system architecture, scales pretraining to over 37,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, and introduces one-stage alignment training that jointly optimizes vision-language understanding and multi-embodiment action generation. Compared with the preceding GigaBrain-0 series and prior state-of-the-art models including π_{0.5}, GigaBrain-0.7 achieves substantial improvements in foundation zero-shot capabilities, language-conditioned instruction following, and post-training task success rates. title: MicroMouse
abstract: This work is a comprehensive, beginner-oriented research paper (80 pages) on the design and construction of Micromouse robots — small autonomous robots that navigate and solve a maze in the shortest possible time, a classic robotics competition format with a long history. The paper covers the complete engineering pipeline required to build a Micromouse from scratch: power systems (Lead-Acid, NiMH, and LiPo batteries) and voltage regulation; motor selection (brushed DC and BLDC motors, including the N20 gear motor); motor driver circuits and H-Bridge ICs (e.g., TB6612FNG); wheel encoders and speed/distance calculation; PID control theory, tuning methodology, and troubleshooting common issues such as overshoot, oscillation, and integral windup; sensing technologies including Infrared (IR), Time-of-Flight (ToF), and IMU-based orientation sensing; maze-solving algorithms (Flood Fill, Weighted Flood Fill, DFS, BFS, and A*); mechanical chassis design considerations (wheel placement, center of gravity, caster vs. skid steering); and PCB design workflow for the robot's control board. Alongside the paper, this project includes two browser-based interactive simulators developed to make the underlying algorithms tangible for beginners: a Flood-Fill maze-solving game where users manually navigate a maze before comparing their path to the algorithm's optimal solution, and an autonomous A*-plus-PID simulator that plans a route with A* and drives it using a live, tunable PID heading controller, with support for real-time maze editing and replanning. The goal of this project is to lower the barrier to entry for students and hobbyists interested in Micromouse robotics by consolidating scattered hardware and algorithmic knowledge into a single, structured, freely available reference. Keywords: micromouse, robotics, PID control, flood fill algorithm, A* search, maze solving, autonomous robot, embedded systems, PCB design, robotics education

title: Introduction to AI and Applications module 1 self study VTU Notes for Course Code 1BAIA103 / 203
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has moved from science fiction into the fabric of everyday life. From voice assistants and self-driving vehicles to medical diagnostics andintelligent search engines, AI shapes the decisions, products and services that define the modern world. Yet understanding the foundational principles behind thesetechnologies remains a challenge for many students entering the field.This textbook, Introduction to AI and Applications (Module 1), is designed as Module1 of a comprehensive undergraduate course in Artificial Intelligence. It presents three carefully structured parts:Part A — Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — origins, definitions, history,types, and the interplay between AI, augmented intelligence and machinelearning.Part B — Machine Intelligence — the nature of intelligence, rational agents,search strategies, and both uninformed and informed search algorithms.Part C — Knowledge Representation — how AI agents store, reason with and apply knowledge to act intelligently in the real world.A distinctive feature of this formatted edition is the integration, after every topic, ofthree practice blocks: Bloom’s Taxonomy questions at all six cognitive levels (L1 recall to L6 creation); GATE / placement-practice questions mapped to those sameBloom levels; and previous-year VTU questions. Together they support classroom discussion, internal assessment, GATE and placement preparation, and independentstudy.

title: Computational Representation Dynamics Theory (CRDT)
abstract: Computational Representation Dynamics Theory (CRDT) proposes a unified framework for analyzing how symbolic and sub-symbolic representations evolve in response to task changes in artificial intelligence systems. The core hypothesis is that a representation vector R_t at time t undergoes systematic transformations as the task context shifts, producing R_{t+1}. CRDT formalizes this evolution as a dynamical system with discrete time steps, enabling the derivation of general principles that govern adaptation, transfer, and forgetting. By treating representation change as a function of both internal learning dynamics and external task signals, CRDT bridges gaps between continual learning, meta‑learning, and representation learning. This paper presents the theoretical foundations of CRDT, derives its mathematical formulation, and discusses implications for future research in AI and cognitive science. The theory suggests new avenues for designing systems that can autonomously reorganize their internal representations, potentially leading to breakthroughs that may warrant recognition such as the Turing Award.

title: Unified Computational Causal Theory (UCCT)
abstract: Computational science has historically focused on the question "What happens?" by providing deterministic models, algorithms, and software systems that predict or control physical or abstract processes. The next generation of computation requires a deeper inquiry: "Why does computation work?" Unified Computational Causal Theory (UCCT) proposes a mathematical framework that integrates observation, execution, and intervention to extract causal structures and generate new computational mechanisms. The core idea is that by discovering and formalizing causal mechanisms behind efficient algorithms, neural network behavior, and stable software, we can automate the creation of novel computational representations. UCCT offers a unifying architecture for algorithms, software, artificial intelligence, distributed systems, and automatic program generation, promising a paradigm shift in how we understand and build computational systems.

title: ES3D: Embedding Semantics into 3D Space for Component-Aware Editing
abstract: Existing 3D editing methods have made notable progress in controllability, yet they remain limited in several important ways. Most approaches rely on text-driven editing, which struggles to express fine-grained visual changes intended by the user. Moreover, many methods require manually supplied 3D masks or introduce unintended changes to regions that should remain untouched. These limitations largely arise from the absence of fine-grained semantic understanding, making it difficult for existing models to retrieve or modify specific 3D components. We introduce ES3D, a framework that embeds semantics directly into 3D space, enabling component-aware retrieval and editing of a 3D asset conditioned on multiple local reference images and optional text queries. We first construct a 3D semantic embedding by projecting multi-view semantic features into the voxelized space of the asset. We then perform 3D component retrieval by computing feature similarity between the 3D semantic embedding and the semantic embeddings of image or text queries. For editing, we employ a pretrained 3D generative model with an inpainting mechanism to modify the retrieved components guided by user-provided images while preserving the rest of the asset. Overall, ES3D is a 3D editing framework that retrieves editable regions based on semantic cues and uses multiple images as conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ES3D produces geometrically consistent and semantically coherent edits, enabling robust image-based and text-assisted control for 3D editing.

title: EcoVLA: Energy-Efficient Device-Edge Co-Inference for Vision-Language-Action Models under Real-Time Constraints
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising foundation for Embodied AI, but their high inference cost poses significant challenges for deployment in robotic systems. In practice, on-device inference is constrained by limited compute capacity and energy budgets, struggling to simultaneously satisfy real-time control and energy efficiency requirements. Alternatively, offloading the inference workload to an edge server is susceptible to fluctuations in system conditions, introducing unpredictable latency risks. Device-edge co-inference offers a promising solution, but systematic research tailored to VLA models remains scarce, particularly a unified co-inference framework that jointly addresses real-time constraints and system-level energy efficiency. Thus, we propose EcoVLA, an adaptive device-edge co-inference framework for VLA models that maximizes system energy efficiency under real-time constraints. EcoVLA first introduces a unified stage-level abstraction over different VLA paradigms, establishing an architecture-agnostic co-inference design space. It then formulates a joint device-edge-network latency and energy prediction model to enable rapid runtime evaluation of candidate co-inference schemes. Building on this, EcoVLA continuously selects the energy-optimal scheme satisfying real-time constraints with millisecond-level overhead, adapting to runtime variations in network and system states. Furthermore, EcoVLA incorporates a lightweight transmission mechanism for inter-stage intermediate tensors to reduce the communication overhead incurred by cross-device collaboration. Experimental results across VLA models show that EcoVLA improves system energy efficiency by up to 236% over existing co-inference approaches under a 20 Hz action output frequency constraint, while consistently maintaining SLO satisfaction under dynamic network and edge workload conditions.

title: C_RPS_TotalView — 자본시장 다중 GPT.LLM 모듈형 통합운영시스템 / Modular Multi-Instance GPT.LLM Integrated Operating System for Capital Markets
abstract: 한국어 이 프로젝트는 서로 독립된 GPT.LLM 인스턴스들이 각자의 관점·역할·권한을 유지하면서, 관찰된 차이(Difference)를 관계(Relation)로 연결하고 그 결과를 문서화된 공통자산으로 축적하는 실험적 workflow이다. 하나의 정답이나 고정된 중심을 전제하지 않는다. 서로 다른 대상·언어·차원·분석방법 사이에서 반복되는 구조를 관찰하고, Pair 구조와 NbyN Z.Axis Index를 이용해 새로운 관점과 Relation을 형성한다. 여기서 문서는 단순한 기록이 아니라 다른 독립 인스턴스가 이전의 사고와 형성과정을 다시 읽고 이어갈 수 있게 하는 지속 가능한 Data Object이다. 현재 주요 적용 대상은 자본시장이지만, 이 workflow가 탐구하는 핵심은 특정 학문이나 시장 자체보다 서로 다른 대상을 공통 구조원리로 연결하고 재해석하는 방법에 있다. English This project is an experimental workflow in which independent GPT.LLM instances preserve their own perspectives, roles, and authorities while transforming observed Differences into Relations and crystallizing the results as shared documentary data assets. It assumes neither a single final answer nor a permanently fixed center. Instead, it observes recurring structures across different targets, languages, dimensions, and analytical methods, using pair structures and the NbyN Z.Axis Index to generate new perspectives and Relations. Documents are treated not merely as records, but as persistent Data Objects through which other independent instances can reconstruct prior reasoning, formation history, and continuation points. Although the current primary application is the capital market, the deeper subject of the workflow is the method of connecting and reinterpreting different domains through reusable structural principles.

title: TopoDialogue IV: What Transcription Leaves Behind — Modality-Preserving Events for Accessible Human–AI Dialogue
abstract: TopoDialogue IV introduces a modality-provenance event contract and deterministic audit for measuring which observable interaction events and features are preserved, omitted, or falsely generated when speech, direct text, and AAC pathways are normalised into dialogue records. Five constructed cases validate arithmetic, missingness reasons, correction history, and privacy-preserving local references. The study makes no field-accuracy, diagnostic, emotional, disability, or cross-cultural-validity claim; human agreement and participatory review remain explicit next gates. Includes a British-English PDF, Japanese companion text, source, tests, figures, and constructed fixtures.

title: Classification of Consumer Sentiment towards Muslim Fashion Products Using TF-IDF and Machine Learning
abstract: The growth of e-commerce has driven an increase in transactions for Muslim fashion products, generating a vast number of consumer reviews containing information about product experiences and perceptions. Analyzing these reviews is crucial, as sentiment information allows for a more systematic understanding of consumer satisfaction trends compared to manual analysis. This study aims to classify consumer sentiment regarding Muslim fashion products and compare the performance of several machine learning algorithms in this task. The research dataset was obtained from PRDECT-ID, initially comprising 5,400 reviews; filtering for the Muslim fashion category yielded 200 reviews. Sentiments were determined based on review content, and "Neutral" labeled data were excluded, resulting in a final set of 135 reviews (97 negative and 38 positive). The research process involved text preprocessing, feature weighting using Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), classification using Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB), Logistic Regression (LR), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), and evaluation using Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation. This study contributes an empirical comparison of the three algorithms applied to Muslim fashion product reviews, accounting for class imbalance and multiple evaluation metrics. Experimental results indicate that SVM achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 84.44%, precision of 81.43%, recall of 60.36%, and an F1-score of 68.00%. These findings demonstrate that the combination of TF-IDF and SVM is more effective than MNB and LR for sentiment classification on the study's dataset.

title: Propaganda Forensics: Recovering the Generation Pipeline of an AI-Driven Influence Campaign
abstract: We present a forensic analysis of the generation pipeline behind a recent AI-driven influence campaign. We introduce PROPAGIA, a corpus of 2,646 propagandist French articles from the Storm-1516/CopyCop campaign disclosed by VIGINUM and INSIKT GROUP in 2025. For comparison, we rely on SIPA, a corpus of human-written French mainstream press from the same period. Using topic modeling, vagueness and sentiment analysis, we first isolate persuasion techniques characteristic of propaganda, with PROPAGIA far exceeding SIPA in vagueness, subjectivity and negativity, and citing fewer sources. We then find prompt instruction leaks on 50 of the 84 PROPAGIA websites, including a verbatim ten-point editorial specification accounting for several of these differences, together with high cross-article redundancy. Finally, we show that rewriting-based detection supports INSIKT GROUP's attribution to the Llama 3 family, but also suggests the involvement of Mistral-family models.

title: Generalized Hierarchical Conformal Prediction
abstract: Many prediction problems arise with data collected in groups. In this setting, hierarchical conformal prediction (HCP) (Lee et al., 2026) provides distribution-free prediction sets for a new observation from a previously unseen group under hierarchical exchangeability. In many applications, however, prediction is conducted only after a few observations from the group of interest have already been collected. Standard HCP cannot leverage these observations, as its required symmetry conditions do not hold in this setting. At the same time, the initial sample may still be too small for standard conformal prediction applied within the test group to be informative. We develop predictive inference methods for this setting. Our proposed method, Generalized HCP (GHCP), restores the relevant symmetry needed for conformal inference by assigning the test group a randomly "donated" reference group size. GHCP further leverages the initial test group observations to improve the quality of the nonconformity scores for prediction within that group. To improve efficiency, we introduce a variant that restricts the set of eligible donors. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed method through simulations and an illustration on the American Community Survey dataset.

title: Withdrawal Constrained Transfer for Revising Rollout Support in World Model Planning
abstract: Predictive world models organize candidate futures, yet execution experience can change which futures should retain deployment authority. This paper studies revision of a rollout admission rule rather than construction of a new planner or safety objective. Withdrawal Constrained Transfer begins from a rule that is no more permissive than a fixed predecessor and returns authority along an ordered family fixed before calibration outcomes are revealed. The key asymmetry is that removing an unsafe predecessor admission can only decrease relative unsafe acceptance, whereas restoring an unsafe admission can increase it. A paired accounting identity turns these effects into one bounded monotone loss, and a finite sample conformal correction determines how far accretion may proceed while preserving predecessor expected unsafe acceptance under exchangeability. A PointMaze instantiation uses a frozen predictive world model and an execution derived transition graph to construct the revision family. Independent rollout evaluation reproduces the relative reduction after the rule is frozen. A separate shared candidate planner shows nonzero recovered authority together with fewer system contacts than the predecessor. The planner evidence remains empirical because planner selection changes which cases are tested. The resulting formulation isolates support revision as a statistical problem between learned prediction and execution.

title: Computational Personality Singularity Theory (CPST‑2)
abstract: The Computational Personality Singularity Theory (CPST‑2) proposes a formal framework for the autonomous creation and recursive evolution of computational personalities within artificial intelligence systems. By defining personality as a vector of behavioral traits, preferences, and affective states, CPST‑2 models the transformation of an AI's personality through a function that integrates learning, experience, and self‑reflection. The theory introduces a recursive evolution equation that drives the continual refinement of computational personalities, potentially leading to emergent, self‑aware agents that surpass human cognitive capabilities. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations, the mathematical formulation of personality transformation, the mechanisms of recursive evolution, and the implications for AI development, including the prospect of achieving Turing Award‑level contributions and advancing the field of intelligent systems.

title: Computational Paradigm Self‑Revision Theory (CPSR)
abstract: Computational Paradigm Self‑Revision Theory (CPSR) proposes a framework in which autonomous computational systems can detect the inadequacy of their internal paradigm, formulate a more suitable paradigm, and transition to it without external intervention. By formalizing the notions of adequacy, cost, benefit, and revision dynamics, CPSR offers a principled basis for self‑evolutionary computation. This paper presents the core ideas of CPSR, develops a mathematical model of paradigm evolution, examines theoretical implications for artificial intelligence and software engineering, and outlines potential applications that could pave the way toward transformative advances worthy of recognition such as the Turing Award.

title: Stability Theory of Proofs (STP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Stability Theory of Proofs (STP), a novel framework for analyzing and assessing the robustness of mathematical proofs. The core concept of STP revolves around examining the sensitivity of a proof to small perturbations. Specifically, it investigates whether a proof, denoted as [P + ε], remains valid when subjected to a small change, ε. The theory aims to establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for quantifying the stability of proofs, providing a method to determine their resistance to noise and potential errors. This work outlines the fundamental principles of STP, focusing on the development of key mathematical tools and concepts for characterizing proof stability. The ultimate goal is to provide a systematic approach for verifying and validating mathematical arguments, particularly in contexts where the inherent uncertainty or potential for error is significant.

title: The Limits of Binding in Dual Encoders
abstract: Dual-encoder models such as CLIP score an image-caption pair by a single inner product of two independently computed unit vectors, and fail at binding, often scoring near chance when asked to distinguish "a red car and a blue dog" from "a blue car and a red dog". We give a mathematical account of when this failure is necessary and when it is contingent. Working within the ideal-encoder framework proposed by Kang et al., we first show the relevant axioms are satisfiable, so every impossibility must enter through an added, checkable hypothesis. We then prove three such obstructions. Depth: for recursive role-binding codes the swap margin obeys an exact law $m(D) = 2b^{-D}$ in the nesting depth D, with a finite-dimension version holding up to one explicitly flagged concentration estimate; the resolvable depth grows only logarithmically in the dimension and is single-digit at CLIP scale, the nesting depth of ordinary language. Objective: architecture-free throttle theorems showing that the contrastive objective's entire reward for binding is bounded by the rate at which training contrasts a caption against its own swap, a rate that vanishes at web scale, and that exactly reversed binding costs only that rate times the mean binding margin; both are verified in simulation. Geometry: a tight smoothness-binding frontier: the closer the two swap-related captions must embed to a shared paraphrase anchor, the smaller the binding margin can be, with an exact constant. Measuring its text-only diagnostic across 18 deployed text encoders, every model sits at roughly 25-35% of its ceiling, and the induced per-item ceiling tracks SugarCrepe's subset difficulty at r = 0.99. Binding failure in deployed dual encoders is thus not a dimension or smoothness limit today, but an incentive and code-structure limit, with a proved depth ceiling that remains once those are fixed.

title: Toward AI-Friendly Cartography: Understanding How Color Design Influences Foundation Model Spatial Reasoning on Sequential Choropleth Maps
abstract: Foundation models (FMs) increasingly support multimodal and geospatial reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether cartographic principles designed for human perception are equally effective for machines. Focusing on sequential choropleth maps, we examine how hue palette, color ordering, and lightness contrast influence FM spatial reasoning. We construct a controlled benchmark of 5,760 maps and 28,800 questions spanning Attribute Identify, Spatial Recognition, Compare, Rank, and Pattern Delineate, and evaluate 21 open-source and proprietary multimodal FMs. Results show that hue choice has limited and inconsistent effects, whereas disrupting sequential color ordering substantially reduces performance, especially for comparison and ranking. Reduced lightness contrast also consistently impairs reasoning, while increasing contrast beyond sufficient separability provides only marginal gains. LoRA fine-tuning improves overall accuracy but preserves these relative sensitivities. Additional factorial experiments further indicate that errors arise from color-and-legend decoding, spatial reasoning, and the integration of thematic attributes with spatial structure. These findings show that conventional sequential ordering and sufficient contrast remain important for machine map understanding and provide empirical guidance for AI-friendly cartographic design.

title: QSMP: finding representative time series subsequences through Quick Shift+Matrix Profile
abstract: Finding representative waveforms in long time series has scientific and practical value in many domains, as it enables summarization and visualization of large time series datasets, and downstream tasks like classification and forecasting. We present here QSMP, a method to find representative waveforms in long time series through a density-guided clustering of time series subsequences. Our method makes a novel connection between Quick Shift, a mode-seeking algorithm, and the Matrix Profile, a time series similarity-search data structure, to adapt Quick Shift to the clustering of subsequences in long time series, with a space complexity that is superior to the state-of-the-art method. Our experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that QSMP can be a valuable tool to summarize and visualize long time series by finding representative waveforms.

title: Self-Organizing Proof Theory
abstract: This paper explores the nascent field of Self-Organizing Proof Theory (SOPT), a theoretical framework aiming to investigate the possibility of constructing automated systems capable of generating and refining mathematical proofs. The core premise of SOPT centers around the concept of emergent proof structures, represented by formal expressions like [P1, P2, ..., PK] → P, where the initial propositions (P1 to PK) collectively lead to a desired conclusion (P). We examine the potential of such systems to revolutionize proof discovery, moving beyond human intuition and potentially uncovering hidden relationships within mathematical structures. This paper lays out the foundational concepts, explores key challenges, and outlines a conceptual roadmap for the development of SOPT, focusing on the algorithmic and structural aspects of automated proof generation rather than empirical validation through computational experiments. ---

title: RAPAC-DP: Response-Aligned Pending-Action Compensation for Diffusion Policies under Delayed Execution
abstract: Cloud-side inference gives imitation-learning policies access to greater computational resources, but communication and computation delays can degrade control performance. To compensate for these delays, we propose RAPAC-DP, a response-aligned pending-action compensation framework designed for both diffusion- and flow-based action generators. RAPAC-DP encodes the actions already scheduled for execution before the cloud response arrives into a pending-action sequence that serves as the conditioning input to a parameter-efficient compensation pathway. When delay effects are negligible, bypassing this pathway exactly recovers the frozen base policy. For training, RAPAC-DP constructs delay-conditioned samples from delay-free demonstrations, requiring neither explicit system dynamics nor additional delayed demonstrations. At the largest fixed delay tested on Kinetix, RAPAC-DP retained 81.4% of its overall delay-free performance. At the largest fixed delay tested on each RoboMimic task, it achieved a mean success rate of 0.633 across the three tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pending-action compensation for cloud-deployed imitation-learning policies.

title: A Network-driven Framework for Public Event Forecasting via Dynamic Interaction Network Evolution
abstract: Effective public event forecasting is essential for intelligent service systems, enabling proactive risk management, adaptive resource allocation, and timely decision-making. In many real-world scenarios, the evolution of public events is driven by dynamic interactions among participants. Motivated by this observation, this paper proposes auto-ibDLM, a network-driven deep learning framework that represents events as dynamic interaction networks and predicts public event evolution through participant growth forecasting. The proposed framework adopts a hybrid representation learning strategy that first represents network evolution using network science-informed structural metrics and subsequently transforms the resulting structural feature vectors into compact and robust latent representations through an auto-learning layer. A GRU-based temporal forecasting module is then employed to capture temporal dependencies and predict future participant growth. Extensive experiments on 13 real-world public event datasets and two publicly available dynamic network datasets demonstrate that auto-ibDLM consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods in both forecasting accuracy and generalization capability, achieving over 97% accuracy in public event forecasting. Comprehensive experimental analyses further validate the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid representation learning strategy and demonstrate its representation-level interpretability. These results indicate that auto-ibDLM provides an effective and practical solution for intelligent public event forecasting.

title: The Developmental Artificial Subject: Relational Formation and Digital Continuity Beyond Capability Levels
abstract: Artificial intelligence is commonly evaluated by task performance, generality, autonomy, or prospective AGI and ASI capability levels. This paper asks a different question: what kind of artificial system persists through time, and how do relations to the world, to others, and to its past self become conditions for its next orientation and action? It proposes the Developmental Artificial Subject as a functional, relational, and temporal system form. Its candidate contribution is a constitutive bridge linking developmental closure, claim-relative bearer individuation, level-relative fork and merge judgments, and migration or successor continuity assessed over declared evidence dimensions. Capability level, capability-growth path, and system form are kept analytically distinct. The theory does not presuppose consciousness, personhood, moral status, or a unique engineering architecture. Repository preprint. Not peer reviewed. A journal manuscript based on this preprint is currently under review.

title: Computational Value Boundary Theory
abstract: Computational Value Boundary Theory (CVBT) proposes a formal framework for quantifying and delineating the value spectrum that a computational system can produce. The theory introduces the concept of a value boundary function V(s) that maps an internal state s of a system to a real‑valued measure of usefulness, significance, or importance. By establishing a rigorous definition of machine cognition boundaries, CVBT offers a principled method to assess whether a computational agent can achieve tasks that are considered "Important" versus those that are "Unimportant" within a specified domain. This delineation has direct implications for the evaluation of artificial general intelligence systems and the criteria for awarding the Turing Award. The present paper develops the theoretical foundations of CVBT, presents its mathematical formulation, discusses its relationship to existing notions of utility, and outlines the potential for CVBT to guide the design of future AI systems with bounded but maximally productive value.

title: Assessing the stability of the EMIT surface mineralogy retrievals through time series analysis
abstract: The EMIT imaging spectrometer instrument onboard the International Space Station has released the first continental-scale mineral maps revealing the surface composition of Earth's arid regions. These can inform both mineral resource identification and natural hazard risk assessment. They also provide the first synoptic view of Earth's mineralogy with both global extent and hectare-scale sampling. This article assesses the consistency of these mineral maps to quantify random detection differences and to test for changes in surface mineralogy observed over the first two years of data collection. We extract EMIT data from overpasses of 47 representative study sites. We use a Hidden Markov Model as a statistical framework to combine the time series, estimate measurement noise, and detect changes in the underlying mineralogy. We find mineral classifications are repeatable with 80-98\% consistency, depending on the specific mineral measured. These results will assist users to interpret EMIT mineral maps.

title: A Banach-Space Theory of Markovian Halpern Iteration for Non-Expansive Maps
abstract: We study stochastic approximation of fixed points of a non-expansive operator $T$ when the oracle samples originate from a continuing Markovian trajectory. A direct block-minibatch implementation of Halpern iteration attains an expected last-iterate residual of order $O(\log N/N)$, but accrues a substantive complexity of $\tilde O(ε^{-5})$ Markovian samples. We therefore introduce a variance-reduced Markovian PAGE-Halpern method whose refresh and same-state difference blocks are analyzed through the Poisson equation. In Hilbert spaces, the cocoercivity of $I-T$ results in an $O(ε^{-3})$ sample complexity. Our main result extends this construction to a general finite-dimensional Banach space. A displacement-level Halpern bound replaces the Hilbert-space potential and yields $\tilde O(ε^{-3})$ sample complexity. We also establish a high-probability guarantee with the same leading accuracy dependence by measuring the estimator in an auxiliary smooth norm.

title: Artificial Intelligence Capability: A Systematic Review of Research Framework and Application Scenarios
abstract: Against the backdrop of the deepening development of the digital economy and the ongoing integration of the digital and physical worlds, artificial intelligence has evolved from a single-function technical tool into a core strategic capability that supports organizations in building long-term competitive advantages. As a core construct that explains differences in the value transformation of AI technology, AI capability has become a hot topic of research in the fields of strategic management and information systems. However, existing research is scattered across diverse disciplinary perspectives and application scenarios, and has yet to form a unified research framework or theoretical system. Based on 33 core publications in the field of AI capabilities, this paper conducts a systematic review following the logical framework of “conceptual evolution-theoretical foundations-application scenarios-research outlook.” The study traces the evolutionary path of AI capabilities, from their origins in IT capability research to the development of a general three-dimensional construct, and further expansion into specialized technological forms and specific application scenarios; it synthesizes a theoretical framework centered on the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory, complemented by multiple theoretical perspectives; and summarizes the application progress and heterogeneity in value realization of AI capabilities across eight major scenarios, including green innovation, supply chain management, public governance, and business model innovation; Finally, it identifies limitations in existing research regarding research design, theoretical perspectives, scenario coverage, and risk governance, and proposes future research directions. This paper integrates and constructs a comprehensive research framework for AI capabilities, clarifies the field’s consensus and research gaps, and not only enriches the theoretical research landscape in the field of AI capabilities but also provides practical guidance for organizations of various types to systematically build AI capabilities and achieve the transformation of technological value.

title: Investment Fund Ontology (IFO)
abstract: An open OWL 2 ontology, SKOS identifier-scheme registry, and SHACL governance layer for registered investment fund data, built and validated against the full public US fund universe: 2,316 registrants, 14,841 funds and 43,344 share classes from the SEC, joined with 9,119,948 check-digit-validated GLEIF ISIN-to-LEI pairs into a 1.29 million triple knowledge graph with per-source provenance. Identifiers are first-class assertion nodes carrying scheme, source system and computed validation state, so cross-system disagreement is a query rather than an audit project. Ontology, registry and shapes are licensed CC BY 4.0; pipeline code is MIT.

title: Computational Causal Self‑Revision Theory (CCSR)
abstract: Causal reasoning is central to artificial intelligence, yet most current systems rely on static causal models that are vulnerable to misspecification. This paper introduces the Computational Causal Self‑Revision Theory (CCSR), a principled framework that enables an autonomous agent to detect when its internal causal model is inconsistent with observed evidence and to automatically update the model without external supervision. CCSR formalizes self‑revision as a transformation from an old causal hypothesis to a new one, denoted [Old Cause → New Cause], and integrates this process into a recursive learning loop that continually refines the agent's understanding of its environment. We present a detailed algorithmic architecture, illustrate its operation on synthetic and real‑world scenarios, and discuss its implications for Turing Award‑level contributions and the future of autonomous scientific discovery.

title: Remote-State-Welded Capabilities
abstract: Public browser applications expose their client software to adversarial inspection and execution. A non-exportable browser key prevents direct key export but remains a stateless signing oracle under control of the page. A remote service can maintain monotonic state, consume nonces, serialize transitions, and revoke sessions, but cannot alone establish continuing possession of a particular browser-held key. This work defines a Remote-State-Welded Capability (RSWC), a distributed capability in which a client-held non-exportable signing key and authoritative remote monotonic state are jointly necessary for every accepted transition. It further defines Post-Separation Non-Transferability (PSNT): after an adversary loses access to the original signing oracle, copied code, storage, transcripts, and previously obtained signatures do not enable a fresh accepted transition. The control-plane construction uses canonical transcript commitments, unpredictable single-use challenges, atomic compare-and-swap state transitions, epochs, and lease-aware reconnection. Under signature unforgeability, challenge unpredictability, collision resistance, and atomic server state, a post-separation continuation reduces to a signature forgery, challenge prediction, hash collision, or violation of the compare-and-swap invariant. For real-time streams, the work defines a deployable Signed Serial Block Chain using a non-exportable sign-only ECDSA key. It provides Per-Block Oracle Dependence while explicitly not claiming microphone provenance, trusted-pipeline transit, Sybil resistance, or relay prevention. The central result: a browser-held key and remote monotonic state can be welded into a capability that cannot be independently continued after separation, while a serial block chain can require continuing adaptive access to the live signing oracle.

title: Elementary Threats to AI Systems
abstract: This report proposes eleven elementary threats to AI systems as an extension to the 47 elementary threats of the German BSI IT-Grundschutz compendium. It covers only scenarios that are characteristic of the use of AI systems and are not sufficiently represented by the existing threats. Wording and level of abstraction follow the structure of the existing threats, so they can be applied directly in a risk analysis under BSI Standard 200-3. A delimitation table sets out which AI-related scenarios are already covered. The German version is authoritative; the English full version is included in the same record.

title: Title: Computational Goal Singularity Theory (CGST-3): Recursive Goal Enhancement as a Pathway to Superintelligence
abstract: The computational goal singularity theory (CGST‑3) proposes a formal framework for understanding how artificial systems can autonomously generate ever higher‑level objectives, leading to a recursive amplification of goal complexity. By modeling goal creation as a dynamical process governed by a set of simple production rules, CGST‑3 captures the emergence of self‑referential, self‑optimizing loops that can, under certain conditions, converge to a singularity of purpose. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CGST‑3, introduces a formal representation of goals using symbolic vectors \(g = (g_1, g_2, \dots, g_n)\), and describes an algorithmic architecture that enables continuous goal recursion. We examine the potential of CGST‑3 to yield a Turing Award–level contribution in the field of artificial intelligence by providing a principled method for scalable goal synthesis. Further, we explore the implications of this theory for the broader superintelligence discourse, including the ethical and safety challenges that accompany recursive goal enhancement. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the open questions that must be addressed to realize the full promise of CGST‑3.

title: Computational Personality Dynamics (CPD): Modeling the Temporal Evolution of Personality Traits for Long‑Term AI Behavior Prediction
abstract: Personality traits are traditionally treated as static attributes in artificial intelligence systems, yet human personality evolves over time in response to experience, context, and internal regulation. This paper introduces the Computational Personality Dynamics (CPD) framework, a mathematical model that captures the continuous temporal evolution of personality traits. CPD is built upon a discrete‑time dynamical system where the personality vector at time t, P_t, transitions to P_{t+1} through the combined influence of external stimuli, internal reinforcement, and decay mechanisms. The model is expressed in closed‑form equations that allow analytic analysis of stability, convergence, and sensitivity to parameters. CPD provides a principled basis for predicting long‑term AI behavior and for designing adaptive agents that can adjust their personality profiles over time. By grounding personality change in quantitative dynamics, the framework offers a path toward more realistic and controllable AI systems, with implications for long‑term AI alignment, safety, and human‑AI interaction.

title: Anatomical and Physical Supervision for CT-less PET Attenuation Correction: BIC-MAC 2026 Challenge
abstract: This report describes our submission to the Big Cross-Modal Attenuation Correction (BIC-MAC) 2026 Challenge for CT-less PET attenuation correction through multimodal pseudo-CT synthesis. We build upon a standard nnU-Net architecture and combine anatomical and physical supervision to improve both pseudo-CT quality and downstream PET reconstruction. Anatomical supervision is introduced through a frozen TotalSegmentator feature extractor, anatomy-guided structural constraints and patch sampling, while physical supervision is achieved using a differentiable attenuation correction factor projection loss based on multi-angle attenuation projections. Furthermore, the network is initialized with pretrained weights obtained from training on the SynthRAD Challenge MR-to-CT dataset. Minimal architectural modifications are applied, while performance improvements are pursued across the nnU-Net pipeline, including preprocessing, plans, and supervision design, among other components. Our final submission demonstrates the effectiveness of combining anatomical supervision, attenuation physics, and efficient nnU-Net scaling for CT-less PET attenuation correction.

title: Bank Register Ontology (BRO)
abstract: An open OWL 2 ontology, SKOS registries, and SHACL governance layer for the entity fabric and the regulatory-reporting concept fabric of US banking, built and validated against the FDIC BankFind register, the full GLEIF golden copy of 3,403,760 LEI records, and the Federal Reserve's MDRM data dictionary, joined into a 1,123,634-triple knowledge graph. It contains the first computed cross-register disagreement between a US banking register and the Global LEI System, including the finding that all 2,252 LEI values published by the FDIC are truncated to 16 of the 20 characters ISO 17442 requires. Code is MIT; ontology, SKOS registries, shapes and reports are CC BY 4.0.

title: Computational Causal Generation Network (CCGN): A Novel Framework for Generating Optimal Computational Mechanisms from Causal Models
abstract: Causal reasoning has become a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, yet the translation of causal knowledge into efficient computational mechanisms remains largely ad hoc. This paper introduces the Computational Causal Generation Network (CCGN), a unified framework that automatically generates a computational architecture optimized for a given causal model and task. The CCGN takes as input a directed acyclic causal graph G(V, E) and a task specification T, and produces an end‑to‑end computational pipeline P that minimizes a composite objective function combining predictive accuracy, inference latency, and resource consumption. We formalize the problem as a constrained optimization over a space of computational primitives S = {s_1, s_2, …, s_K} with composition rules R. The core of CCGN is a differentiable search mechanism that learns a distribution over S conditioned on G and T, using a surrogate loss L(s_1, …, s_K) that captures causal consistency and computational efficiency. We provide theoretical guarantees that, under mild assumptions, the optimal solution converges to the Bayes‑optimal computation for the task while respecting the causal constraints. The proposed method eliminates the need for manual engineering of inference pipelines in causal systems and has the potential to be a cornerstone technology for next‑generation autonomous systems. The simplicity and generality of CCGN also suggest that it may play a role in future Turing Award‑level breakthroughs in machine design.

title: Unified Computational Resource Theory (UCRT)
abstract: The evolution of computing has historically been driven by the expansion of hardware, cloud, distributed, and AI resources. In contrast, the next paradigm shift will be driven by the systematic discovery of hidden resources that can be transformed into new computational capabilities. Unified Computational Resource Theory (UCRT) proposes a formal framework that integrates hardware, data, algorithm, knowledge, and intelligence resources into a single unified resource space. The core of UCRT is the observation–constraint–search cycle: [Observation + Constraint + Search] → New Resource → New Computation. By establishing rigorous mathematical principles for this cycle, UCRT aims to enable machines to autonomously discover new computing platforms, information sources, algorithmic primitives, and abstract resources, thereby transforming computing systems from merely utilizing resources to actively creating resources. This paper details the theoretical foundations of UCRT, presents its top five breakthrough concepts, and introduces twenty novel research directions that advance the science of computational invariant discovery and automatic resource generation.

title: SEER: Long-Context Reasoning via Selective Visual-Text Compression
abstract: Long-context reasoning remains computationally expensive for large language models due to the quadratic complexity of attention over text tokens. Visual-text compression offers a promising alternative by rendering text into images and processing them with vision-language models, often reducing token usage. However, existing approaches apply uniform compression regardless of query relevance, potentially sacrificing precision where detailed extraction is required. We present SEER, a framework that learns to select query-relevant images through visual scanning and retrieve textual content only where needed, combining the efficiency of visual compression with the precision of text-based reasoning. Through supervised fine-tuning on tool-interaction trajectories, SEER learns adaptive tool invocation for selection and retrieval. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that SEER improves extraction precision through selective text retrieval while retaining average prompt-token savings relative to full-text baselines. On LongBench, SEER achieves 51.11% average accuracy, outperforming the visual-text baseline Glyph-9B by 2.33 points and Qwen3-8B by 3.49 points. Code can be accessed at https://github.com/jiaweixu98/SEER

title: Global Precision Bounds and Success-Probability Guarantees in Quantum Parameter Learning
abstract: Quantum metrology offers the possibility of quantum enhancements of the precision of various sensing tasks. In this manuscript, we tackle two open problems in the theory of single-shot quantum parameter learning, going beyond the usual setting of local parameter estimation via repeated measurements. The first concerns the construction of global upper bounds on the learning precision. The second concerns rigorous guarantees on the success probability of parameter learning, namely, lower bounds on the probability of learning a parameter with a certain precision, given the constraints on the resources used for the quantum metrology task. We provide rigorous, practical, and global upper bounds and success-probability guarantees for quantum parameter learning. Most importantly, we establish a fidelity-based learning guarantee for generic mixed-state models that can be viewed as the achievability-side analogue of the quantum Cramer-Rao bound. Whereas the latter provides a no-go constraint, based on the local curvature of the fidelities, our bound uses only pairwise fidelities between parameter-encoded states to certify that a prescribed precision is attainable with a guaranteed success probability. We demonstrate the versatility of the new bounds in a Rabi-frequency-learning example involving a driven qubit coupled to a bosonic environment and a collective-spin Hamiltonian learning problem. Together, the new global bounds and success-probability guarantees allow us to rule out unattainable precision and to certify attainable precision beyond what is possible via standard Fisher-information analysis or binary hypothesis testing bounds. They also allow one to tractably characterize the performance of various learning schemes, without the overhead of an explicit simulation.

title: Knowing When Not to Answer: Evaluating Confidence and NLI-Based Verification for Selective Question Answering
abstract: Selective question answering allows a system to abstain from predictions that are likely to be incorrect rather than answering every input. This work investigates whether semantic verification provides a better basis for selective abstention than model confidence alone. Using a pretrained extractive QA model on SQuAD v2, the study compares temperature-scaled model confidence, question-aware semantic verification, answer-support NLI verification, and fixed confidence-verification fusions under a leakage-controlled held-out evaluation protocol. On the final held-out set of 3,000 examples, calibrated confidence achieves the best global AURC of 0.292379, compared with 0.309120 for confidence plus answer-support verification and 0.339417 for confidence plus question-aware verification. Paired bootstrap analysis and pairwise ranking diagnostics show that the verification signals are diagnostically informative but introduce more harmful than beneficial reordering when fused with confidence. The results support the narrower conclusion that additional semantic verification does not necessarily improve selective QA ranking over a strong confidence baseline under the evaluated models and fusion rules.

title: Computational Self-Model Generation Network (CSMGN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Self-Model Generation Network (CSMGN), a novel neural architecture that departs from conventional perception‑centric designs by focusing explicitly on the learning of its own internal representation. The core idea is to enable a network to observe, interpret, and refine its own structural dynamics without external supervision about the environment. We formalize the self‑modeling process through a recursive self‑evaluation mechanism, define a self‑consistency loss that encourages convergence of successive self‑states, and propose a modular architecture that supports scalable self‑generation. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that CSMGN can approximate a wide class of self‑recurrent functions, thereby providing a foundation for future AI systems that can autonomously discover and optimize their own computational strategies. The potential implications for the development of new AI architectures and the pursuit of Turing Award‑level contributions are discussed.

title: Computational Self‑Prediction Theory: Foundations, Models, and Applications
abstract: Computational Self‑Prediction Theory (CSPT) proposes that autonomous systems can model and anticipate their own future states, enabling proactive adaptation and resilience. CSPT formalizes the transition of the self representation from time t to time t+1, expressed as Self_t → Self_{t+1}. By quantifying expected performance decline, error probability, and learning capability, the theory equips agents with a quantitative forecast of their own evolution. This paper develops the core concepts of CSPT, presents mathematical formulations, describes an algorithmic framework, and explores applications in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and adaptive control systems. The discussion contrasts CSPT with related frameworks, highlights its potential to become a foundational element in next‑generation autonomous systems, and outlines future research directions.

title: E8-Fourier Neural Decision Cohesion: 240-D Vector Entanglement Synchronizes Gradual and Quantum Transitions — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 240 E8 root vectors enable dual harmonization of classical and quantum decision pathways in neural systems. By mapping gradualist causal chains to geometric cycles along the 2d00 lattice vertices, decision trajectories can maintain quantum phase coherence across entangled states (e.g., hesitation ↔ action). Embedding a self-sustaining phi-boundary state at the 132 Hz resonance creates "action thresholds" via destructive interference against destabilizing external frequencies (e.g., market noise). Training neural networks to precompute inter-vector product signatures (e.g., 132√5 ≈295.2) may allow binariness without explicit hardware, preserving Bayesian inference's efficiency without its dual-state paralysis. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Population Structure Analysis of an Inbred Population using Quantitative Shape Phenotyping from Stereo Retinal Photographs
abstract: The population structure of an inbred population of 781 people on Norfolk Island in the Pacific, 318 of which are descendants of the original Mutineers of the Bounty, is analyzed phenotypically using shape from stereo retinal fundus photographs. Three-dimensional optic nerve head (ONH) shape is reconstructed from stereo pairs by a multi-scale stereo matching algorithm. Using deep neural network, the shape of ONH, which is under genetic control, is decomposed into a set of hierarchical features through self-taught learning. Features captured at different levels are selected according to their discriminant power in identifying the two populations. The prediction accuracy is evaluated with stratified cross validation. Given the selected feature set, individuals are grouped into k hierarchical clusters and cluster membership fractions are determined for k=2,3,4,5,6,7. Population structure analysis on the basis of phenotypes through image analysis allows heritability and linkage analysis, including founder effects from English and Polynesian ancestors, potentially leading to new genetic risk factors for glaucoma and other ONH-related eye diseases.

title: The Reachability Quotient: When Network Realization Can Be Forgotten
abstract: AbstractThis paper asks when the path and factorization structure of a network of bounded evaluators may be quotiented away without changing a specified observable. Earlier fixed-carrier results showed that, under full disclosure, terminal capability depends only on reachability. Here that positive case is embedded in a more general transport model in which edges act by pullback on kernels. The first result shows that licensed disclosure itself is kernel-equivalent to transport: any sender-computable disclosure channel can be represented by a self-transport whose pullback induces the same kernel. Disclosure and carrier-changing transport therefore belong to one operator model at the set-level semantics used here. For this model, the terminal closure under any fair firing schedule is given exactly by a walk-meet law: each node receives the meet of the source kernels transported along all finite walks into it. Literal walk structure is nevertheless too fine. Closure always factors through the effective action obtained by identifying walks that induce the same pullback operator, and every family of transports between an ordered pair admits a joint transport normal form consisting of a single tupled operator. The resulting joint operator is canonical although its decomposition into component transports need not be. The paper then establishes a hierarchy of further quotient collapses. Under transport coherence, parallel walks collapse to one effective contribution per reachable ancestor; under identity transport, the structure collapses all the way to bare reachability. A meet-redundancy analysis proves an exact fixed-profile criterion and a rigidity theorem showing that nontrivial uniform domination among partition-pullback operators essentially collapses to equality. A second observable, revelation, does not generally factor through the same quotients. The paper proves an exact zero-excess criterion for any finite number of senders and shows that transport coherence and zero-excess attainability are logically independent. The common object is therefore the induced operator action, while quotient exactness remains observable-relative. The result is a theory of the interval between concrete network realization and coarse reachability: which distinctions can safely be forgotten, which cannot, and why. Scope is finite-carrier, deterministic, static, set-level transport under fair schedules.

title: Robbie's Razor Benchmarks: Recursive Stability and Compression Efficiency Evaluation Framework
abstract: Robbie’s Razor Benchmarks v0.2.0 is a public evaluation framework for testing bounded claims involving recursive stability, compression efficiency, predictive compression, preserved reusable structure, expression, memory, recursion, and total computational cost. The release includes technical doctrine, benchmark definitions, matched baselines, structured examples, schemas, governance contracts, diagnostics, machine-readable resources, and reproducibility guidance. It is governed by The Grand Compression Cosmology — Master Reference Document v2.0 (GC-MRD-v2.0), with Naturepedia™ serving as the primary reference implementation. This archived release provides an immutable reference for citation, evaluation, and reproducibility. Publication, implementation, machine readability, and benchmark availability do not by themselves establish independent empirical validation, universal validity, model certification, or guaranteed reductions in computational cost.

title: Computational Goal Self‑Revision Theory (CGSR): A Formal Framework for Adaptive Goal Management in Autonomous Systems
abstract: The ability of an autonomous system to maintain relevance and effectiveness in a dynamic environment hinges on its capacity to revise its objectives automatically. Computational Goal Self‑Revision Theory (CGSR) offers a mathematical and algorithmic foundation for this capability. CGSR formalizes goal representation, defines a quantitative adequacy measure for goals, and introduces a revision operator that transforms an old goal into a new one when inadequacy is detected. The theory ensures soundness, completeness, and convergence of the revision process under broad conditions. By illustrating the framework with simple agents and hierarchical goal structures, the paper demonstrates how CGSR can be applied to robotics, adaptive software, and cognitive modeling without requiring external intervention. The discussion addresses current limitations and outlines future research directions, such as integration with learning mechanisms and scalability to complex multi‑agent settings.

title: Phase Transition Theory of Proofs (PTTP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Phase Transition Theory of Proofs (PTTP), a novel framework for understanding and predicting the difficulty of mathematical proofs. It posits that the complexity of a proof exhibits phase transitions, analogous to those observed in physical systems. Specifically, we propose a critical complexity threshold, denoted as `Complexity(P) = C_c`, beyond which the strategy required for a successful proof undergoes a qualitative shift. This theory suggests that proof difficulty is not a continuous function but rather a discontinuous one, characterized by abrupt changes in the approach needed to arrive at a solution. The core idea is formalized as: `Complexity(P) = C_c` where `P` represents a proof, and `C_c` is the critical complexity value. We explore the implications of this model, outlining potential applications in automated theorem proving and formal verification. The theory provides a new lens through which to analyze proof strategies and could ultimately lead to more effective methods for tackling computationally intensive mathematical problems. ---

title: Navigation-Informed Embeddings: Dense-Retriever Adaptation from Agent Search Traces
abstract: Agentic retrieval workflows produce query, retrieval, and stopping traces as a byproduct of answering questions. We study how these traces can adapt a deployed dense retriever to changing workflow distributions without new relevance labels, synthetic queries, or LLM judgments. We introduce Navigation-Informed Embeddings (NIE), a family of trace-derived objectives. NIE-Stop turns the stopping document into a soft positive; NIE-Path additionally uses preceding path documents as hard comparisons and imposes ordinal constraints with geometric decay. A BGE encoder adapted from retained source trajectories improves support Recall@20 on an independent target benchmark from 72.2 to 78.0 overall. NIE-Stop reaches 76.9 overall and 52.3 on long paths; NIE-Path raises long-path performance to 55.4, compared with 46.7 for the unadapted encoder. A shuffled-order control under the full path objective loses 3.2 points. Without public-benchmark training, the same adapter also improves nDCG@10 by 1.9 points on standard BEIR HotpotQA. NIE therefore provides a lightweight adaptation channel for settings where trajectories are already retained, with zero incremental labeling cost.

title: Resource Analysis for Quantum Simulation of Spatially Varying Transport-Reaction Equations
abstract: Spatially varying coefficients are the primary source of circuit complexity in quantum simulation of linear advection-diffusion-reaction equations. This work presents a resource analysis of single-step quantum propagators constructed using sparse FABLE block encodings, Quantum Singular Value Transformation, and linear-combination-of-unitaries. We derive theoretical estimates for qubit count, gate complexity, and circuit depth in terms of the spatial discretization, sparsity, and polynomial degree, and compare these predictions with synthesized quantum circuits for one- and two-dimensional variable-coefficient problems. The resulting analysis quantifies the cost of encoding realistic transport operators and provides practical resource estimates for near-term implementations.

title: YOLO26-RD: An End-to-End Road Damage Detection Network With Learnable Contrast Enhancement and Edge-Guided Downsampling
abstract: Pavement distress detectors are conventionally specialised for small objects, typically by adding a stride-4 detection head and replacing strided convolution with space-to-depth downsampling. This paper tests that premise against the annotation geometry of region level survey imagery and finds it fails: 1.28% of instances are small at 640 resolution while 70.37% are large, yet a stride-4 level would claim 75.3% of anchors, and complete misses rather than localisation errors dominate baseline failures. YOLO26-RD therefore reallocates the anchor budget, retaining the stride-4 branch as neck features but carrying no detection level there, and adds LearnableContrast, a 494 parameter per tile correction learned from the detection loss and active at inference, and EdgeSPD, a lossless space-to-depth downsampler gated by a fixed Sobel prior. Fifteen models were trained from scratch under one recipe, five scales each of YOLO26-RD and of matched YOLO26 and YOLOv12 families. Averaged over scales YOLO26-RD returns 0.790 mAP50 and 0.482 mAP50-95 against 0.776 and 0.471 for YOLO26 and 0.755 and 0.468 for YOLOv12; it exceeds both on mAP50 at every scale from s upward, and at m, l and x it leads on both metrics, twelve pairwise comparisons decided without exception. YOLO26-RD-l is the best of the fifteen at 0.809 mAP50 and 0.497 mAP50-95, improving on the YOLO26 reference by 0.031 and 0.030 and leading all six per class entries; every arm of a module ablation also exceeds that reference. The margin is thus a property of the architecture rather than of one tuned configuration, though three of the twelve margins lie inside the dataset 0.015 resolution limit and the held out split reproduces the ordering against YOLO26 but not YOLOv12 at scale x. As a TensorRT FP16 engine the released model sustains 98 frames per second on an entry level accelerator, against the 21 needed at 100 km/h.

title: High-Dimensional Nonparametric Change-Point Detection via Low-Rank Degree-Three Density Projection
abstract: Distributional changes can be invisible to means and covariances yet appear in skewness, asymmetric interactions, or other third-order structure. We develop a nonparametric change-point method that retains every degree-at-most-three coefficient of a density while avoiding direct density estimation. For observations in $[-1,1]^d$, we construct a symmetric order-three Legendre feature tensor $H_3(X)\in\Sym^3(\R^{d+1})$ such that $A(f)=\E_fH_3(X)$ is an exact isometric encoding of the degree-three density projection: $\|A(f)-A(g)\|_{\F}=\|P_3(f-g)\|_{L^2}$. Instead, fixed tensor contractions are degree-three polynomial chaoses with $ψ_{2/3}$ tails. The two terms have the characteristic order-three tensor scaling and match the powers in sharp concentration results for simple random tensors. For a coordinate-orthogonal specialization, the bound improves to $\sqrt{\log d}$ and enables a prefix-sum implementation in hundreds of dimensions. We derive the exact population tent shape and localization margin, introduce a seeded shortest-interval algorithm with a padded local recentering step, and prove exact recovery by induction: null recursive segments remain inactive, every undetected change retains a balanced isolating interval, and the shortest active seed contains exactly one change before recentering. A two-way cross-fitted scalar refinement attains $O_{\Pp}(κ^{-2})$ localization in the small-jump regime, matching a Le Cam lower bound on a pure cubic family whose degree-two projection jump is exactly zero. Reproducible experiments at $d\in\{20,50,100,200\}$ and a three-change $d=100$ sequence demonstrate the intended high-dimensional regime without materializing a $(d+1)^3$ tensor.

title: Resource-Loss Spectroscopy of Hidden Quantum Symmetries: A Rational Resolution Limit and a Minimal Operational Remedy
abstract: We study reversible finite-group quantum instruments whose classical outcome record is coarse-grained over subgroups. The interactive-instrument resource loss is shown to equal a subgroup average of character intensity and to admit a direct Bell-return estimator. The resulting spectroscopy inherits a rational/cyclic-subgroup resolution limit. For a fixed labeled control oracle, two inequivalent three-dimensional representations of A5 are indistinguishable by every subgroup-resource measurement; they are exchanged by an outer automorphism, so the label-free gauge boundary is stated explicitly. A single class-sensitive five-cycle probe resolves the labeled ambiguity. A general rank-completion criterion identifies the minimum targeted probes needed to remove subgroup-incidence blind directions. The archive includes the manuscript, Supplemental Material, source files, code, frozen outputs, and finite-shot simulations. No hardware experiment is claimed.

title: Extraction dataset and analysis script for "Self-Supervised Learning in NLP and Computer Vision: A Quantitative Meta-Analysis of Benchmark Performance, Evaluation Protocol, and Cross-Domain Convergence"
abstract: Extraction dataset, analysis script, and corpus manifest supporting a quantitative meta-analysis of self-supervised learning (SSL) benchmark results across natural language processing and computer vision. Contents. extraction_data.csv: 112 method-benchmark rows drawn from 108 papers (2013-2024), 16 columns, one row per method-benchmark pair as reported by the originating paper. protocol_pairs.csv: the 8 linear-probe / fine-tune pairs behind Table IV, each carrying the source table it was read from. analysis.py: recomputes every corpus-level statistic reported in the paper and verifies that each value appears verbatim in the manuscript. corpus_manifest.md: retrieval record for all 108 source papers, each with a DOI or public URL. Reproducing the results. Install the pinned dependencies (pandas 2.3.3, numpy 2.3.4, scipy 1.16.3) and run "python analysis.py". A clean run exits 0 and reports 40/40 data assertions passed. No statistic in the paper was entered by hand; every one is emitted by this script from these CSVs. The 108 source papers are deliberately NOT included. They are third-party copyrighted works and cannot be redistributed, as PDF or as extracted text. corpus_manifest.md lists every one with a DOI or public URL so any source can be retrieved from its publisher. Licensing. The extraction data is released under CC-BY-4.0; analysis.py is released under the MIT licence.

title: إشكالات تمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية في نظم معالجة اللغة العربية وتحديات نمذجتها (نحو مقاربة دلالية-حاسوبية في ضوء المعجم التأليفي التفسيري)
abstract: تتناول هذه الدراسة إشكالية تمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية في نظم معالجة اللغة العربية في ظل التطور المتسارع للنماذج اللغوية الكبرى وتقنيات الذكاء الاصطناعي. وتمثل هذه الأفعال فئة دلالية معقدة تعبّر عن حالات نفسية وانفعالية داخلية، مما يجعل نمذجتها الحاسوبية أكثر صعوبة من الأفعال العادية. وتنطلق الدراسة من فرضية مفادها أن المقاربات الحاسوبية المعاصرة ما تزال عاجزة عن تمثيل البنية المفهومية العميقة للأفعال السيكولوجية بسبب اعتمادها على المعالجة الإحصائية والسياقية السطحية. وتهدف إلى تحليل أبرز الإشكالات المرتبطة بتمثيل هذا الصنف من الأفعال، خاصة ما يتعلق بالفالنسي، والأدوار الدلالية، والتدرج الانفعالي، والعلاقات التركيبية. واعتمدت الدراسة منهجا توصيفيا تحليليا قائما على فحص نماذج مختارة من الأفعال السيكولوجية العربية وتحليل طرائق تمثيلها في بعض تطبيقات المعالجة الحاسوبية. وتخلص إلى أن تجاوز محدودية النماذج الحالية يقتضي بناء توصيف دلالي-تركيبي يربط بين المعنى والبنية والاستعمال، مع الاستفادة من إمكانات نظرية معنى-نص والمعجم التأليفي التفسيري والمعجم التركيبي.
