title: Computational Rule Mutation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Rule Mutation Theory (CRMT), a novel framework for understanding significant algorithmic breakthroughs. The theory posits that these breakthroughs are analogous to genetic mutations, where changes in algorithmic rules (R) lead to new, improved rules (R'). CRMT focuses on identifying the underlying mechanisms that trigger these rule mutations, specifically examining the impact of substantial algorithmic advancements. The theory aims to establish a foundational algorithm evolution theory, potentially paving the way for a deeper understanding of innovation in computational systems. The central concept revolves around recognizing that complex algorithmic changes, rather than incremental improvements, are the driving force behind paradigm shifts. We explore the characteristics of these 'mutation events' and propose a model for their emergence and propagation within a system. This model incorporates elements of stochastic processes and network dynamics, allowing for the simulation and analysis of rule mutation scenarios. The work presented here lays the groundwork for a more rigorous and predictive approach to understanding the evolution of computational systems, with implications for fields ranging from artificial intelligence to software engineering. ---

title: Computational Value Reconstruction Theory (CVRT)
abstract: The Computational Value Reconstruction Theory (CVRT) proposes a formal framework for inferring latent value structures from observed behavioral data. By treating value as a hidden variable that generates behavior, CVRT leverages large-scale behavioral datasets to reconstruct the underlying value function that governs decision making. The theory establishes a mapping from observable actions to intrinsic value representations, enabling the quantification of preferences, motivations, and ethical stances in artificial agents and social systems. CVRT's core contribution is a set of mathematical principles that guarantee consistency, identifiability, and generalizability of the reconstructed value function without reliance on explicit reward engineering. The potential for CVRT to advance the understanding of intelligence and to provide a pathway toward the Turing Prize is discussed.

title: Computational Explanation Causal Structure (CECS): Bridging Causal Inference and Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Causal inference and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) are two pillars of modern machine learning research, yet they have largely evolved along separate trajectories. Causal inference focuses on discovering and quantifying cause‑effect relationships, while XAI emphasizes generating human‑understandable explanations for model predictions. This paper proposes a unified framework called Computational Explanation Causal Structure (CECS) that formalizes the mathematical relationship between causes and explanations. CECS introduces a tripartite representation comprising a set of potential causes C, a set of explanatory statements E, and a mapping operator Φ that translates causal mechanisms into explanatory constructs. By defining a compositional algebra over this mapping, CECS provides a principled way to evaluate the fidelity of explanations with respect to underlying causal dynamics. We develop the theoretical foundations, present illustrative examples, and discuss computational implementation strategies. The framework's potential to unify causal AI and XAI suggests a promising direction for future research, possibly earning recognition comparable to that of a Turing Award.

title: Identifying parameter couplings and uncertainties of mixed-noise stochastic systems via full-covariance Gaussian mixture network
abstract: Parameter identification of stochastic dynamical systems driven by mixed noises is challenging due to intractable likelihood functions. We propose PENN-GMD, a parameter estimation neural network that maps partially observed trajectories to a Gaussian mixture distribution (GMD) over the system parameters. Unlike conventional uncertainty estimates, the GMD employs full covariance matrices to explicitly reveal parameter couplings and multi-modal likelihood structures. The network is trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood via a surjective parameterization that hard-encodes all GMD constraints, thereby approximating the true likelihood. We validate the method on five numerical examples with increasing complexity, including systems driven by fractional Gaussian and Lévy noises, oscillators with colored noise, coupled neurons under different observability, and an aeroelastic airfoil with unidentifiable stochastic disturbances. Results demonstrate that PENN-GMD accurately recovers likelihood distributions, captures parameter couplings, and naturally diagnoses non-identifiability through variance broadening or mode splitting. These capabilities establish PENN-GMD as a practical tool for uncertainty-aware parameter identification in complex stochastic systems where conventional likelihood-based methods are infeasible.

title: GFCM: A Tail-Sensitive Mixed-Type Conditional Independence Test for Causal Discovery
abstract: Constraint-based causal discovery like PC and FCI depends on its conditional independence test. Partial correlation and the Generalised Covariance Measure (GCM) detect only the conditional covariance of residuals, so they miss dependence in the mean's nonlinear part, the scale, and the tails. Tests that detect more are biased inside PC, not scalable, only continuous, or not aimed at the tails. Our Generalised Feature Covariance Measure (GFCM) is valid, sensitive beyond covariance, robust inside PC, and applicable to mixed-type data. It runs the GCM template on a configurable set of residual features with conditional mean zero (centered moments and conditional quantile indicators), pooled in blocks and combined by the Cauchy rule, with a growing-knot spline nuisance at regression cost. We contribute (i) a centering result making the scale feature Neyman orthogonal, where the uncentered version is biased; (ii) the orientation asymmetry the mean-quantile construction creates inside PC, and its fix; (iii) a Phi-faithfulness theory under which PC with GFCM recovers the CPDAG of the set's detection class; and (iv) a benchmark of CI tests sensitive beyond covariance on synthetic data, semi-synthetic tail injections, and PC discovery on random DAGs. Under size-corrected power, GFCM recovers the scale and tail edges the covariance family misses and alone keeps power at the deep conditioning sets PC issues. It stays calibrated as n grows, whereas FFCI, the boosted GCM, and the partial copula test do not, and it handles mixed-type data directly. Inside PC at scale it attains the lowest skeleton SHD among tests that stay calibrated, while the others inflate false edges. Validity rests on an additive nuisance, and the tail advantage is shown on simulated and semi-synthetic data, as no fully real benchmark with both heavy tails and known structure exists.

title: TSS: Target-Side Sparsification for Speculative Decoding in Domain-Specific Large Language Models
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through collaboration between a lightweight draft model and a target verifier. Existing methods mainly improve the draft side, while the target model is typically kept dense and unchanged. We show that, under domain-specific inference, full-depth target verification is not always the optimal choice. Counter-intuitively, skipping selected target layers can reduce verification cost while simultaneously increasing draft acceptance and preserving, or even improving, downstream task performance. Based on this observation, we propose TSS, a target-side sparsification framework for speculative decoding. TSS employs an acceptance- and metric-aware breadth search to explore multi-layer skip configurations without imposing a fixed priority between the two objectives. The selected configurations are stored in a domain-to-configuration mapping and applied by a lightweight skip controller, allowing one complete target model to support multiple sparse verification paths without retraining or permanent parameter pruning. Experiments on Spec-Bench across multiple domains, model scales, and speculative decoding methods show consistent improvements in draft acceptance and downstream task performance. In Translation setting, TSS increases the average accept length from 2.70 to 4.53 (+67.8%), improves BLEU from 0.131 to 0.237 (+80.9%), and raises end-to-end throughput from 75.6 to 127.3 tokens/s, corresponding to a 1.68X speedup.

title: Komparasi Naive Bayes dan Support Vector Machine untuk Analisis Sentimen Kebijakan Pemerintah Mengenai Makan Bergizi Gratis: Comparing Naive Bayes and Support Vector Machine for Sentiment Analysis of Government Policy on Free Nutritious Meals
abstract: Kebijakan Program Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) pemerintah memicu perdebatan publik di platform TikTok. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengklasifikasikan sentimen opini publik terhadap kebijakan MBG ke dalam kelas positif dan negatif dengan membandingkan algoritma Multinomial Naive Bayes dan Support Vector Machine (SVM) menggunakan ekstraksi fitur CountVectorizer. Dataset sebanyak 4.000 komentar dikumpulkan melalui Apify dari empat akun berita resmi nasional. Pelabelan awal dilakukan secara otomatis menggunakan InSet Lexicon dan divalidasi secara manual oleh anotator manusia sebagai gold standard untuk mengurangi bias makna kata informal. Hasil pelabelan menunjukkan dominasi sentimen positif sebesar 89,60% dan negatif sebesar 10,40%. Pengujian dengan rasio split data 80:20 menunjukkan bahwa SVM kernel linear menghasilkan akurasi tertinggi sebesar 99,12%, sedangkan Naive Bayes mencapai 91,62%. Pengujian lintas skenario menunjukkan Naive Bayes lebih rentan terhadap penurunan kinerja, dengan akurasi terendah 72,70% pada skenario undersampling dan tiga kelas, sementara SVM tetap stabil di atas 95%. Analisis WordCloud menunjukkan sentimen positif didominasi optimisme terhadap pemerintah, sedangkan sentimen negatif menyoroti risiko korupsi anggaran. Keterbatasan penelitian meliputi kesulitan model memahami konteks kalimat, kata informal, dan sarkasme. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa SVM lebih efektif dan stabil untuk klasifikasi sentimen teks TikTok yang tidak seimbang, memberikan kinerja konsisten pada berbagai skenario pengujian.

title: Computational Possibility Navigation
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Possibility Navigation (CPN), a novel approach to algorithm discovery that shifts the focus from explicitly searching a predefined solution space to identifying potentially solvable computation processes. Traditional algorithmic search methods often rely on exhaustive exploration of a given problem domain, which can be computationally prohibitive, particularly for complex and poorly understood challenges. CPN, conversely, operates on the premise that the key lies not in *finding* a specific solution, but in *determining* which computational processes are capable of generating solutions. The core concept is defined through the construction of a "possibility space," represented as a set of algorithms (A) that can potentially solve a given task (T). This paper outlines the fundamental principles of CPN, including the definition of the possibility space (P) and the proposed navigation strategy for transitioning between algorithms (At → At+1). It explores the potential of CPN to contribute to the development of automated algorithm discovery models, highlighting its relevance for achieving significant advancements in the field. The presented framework offers a fundamentally different perspective on algorithm search, emphasizing the identification of computational capability rather than the direct instantiation of solutions.

title: Local Truth Computing
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Local Truth Computing (LTC), a novel approach to knowledge representation and reasoning in complex systems. The central premise of LTC is that large-scale systems rarely possess a single, globally consistent truth. Instead, localized, contextually relevant "truth models" (Ti(x)) exist, valid within specific operational environments (c). These truth models are dynamically assessed by the system, generating a truth value T(x,c) that reflects the current understanding. The paper explores the conditions under which these localized truth models can be integrated, forming a more comprehensive, albeit potentially fragmented, representation of reality. LTC's potential impact spans various domains, including distributed databases, multi-agent systems, inconsistent knowledge bases, and federated learning. The core idea is to move away from the traditional assumption of a single, definitive truth and embrace a more nuanced, context-aware approach to knowledge management. This work lays the foundation for a new paradigm in reasoning, particularly in scenarios where data is inherently noisy, incomplete, or subject to conflicting interpretations. ---

title: Belief Update Compiler: A Novel Approach to Knowledge Representation and Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces the Belief Update Compiler (BUC), a novel system designed to address the fundamental challenges in knowledge representation and reasoning. The BUC operates on the core principle of automatically updating and managing beliefs based on incoming evidence, effectively handling conflicts, evidence weighting, outdated knowledge, and inference chain updates. The compiler generates a new belief state [Knew], utilizing the input [Kold + Enew] and a compiled function `Compile(Kold, Enew)`. This approach represents a potentially transformative paradigm for building compilable knowledge systems, possessing the potential to unlock significant advancements in artificial intelligence and automated reasoning. The system's architecture is designed for modularity and adaptability, facilitating integration with diverse knowledge bases and reasoning engines. This paper outlines the core components of the BUC, detailing the algorithms employed for each stage of the belief update process, and discusses the system's capabilities and future research directions.

title: Computational Rule Self‑Repair Theory (CRSR)
abstract: Computational Rule Self‑Repair Theory (CRSR) proposes a principled framework for detecting, diagnosing, and automatically correcting errors in symbolic rule‑based systems. By formalizing a rule set, an evaluation metric, and a repair mapping, CRSR transforms a brittle rule engine into a self‑amending entity that can adapt to new data, resolve inconsistencies, and improve performance over time. The theory is grounded in a simple but expressive mathematical structure that enables tractable analysis and implementation. We show how CRSR can be applied to diverse domains such as knowledge representation, planning, and natural language processing, and argue that its generality and efficiency position it as a candidate foundation for future autonomous systems and a potential recipient of the Turing Award.

title: Computational Explanation Generation Theory (CEGT)
abstract: The field of artificial intelligence has progressed from simple answer generation to the integration of explanatory components that elucidate the reasoning behind outputs. This paper introduces Computational Explanation Generation Theory (CEGT), a formal framework that defines the generation of explanations as a structured transformation of input data, intermediate reasoning states, and final answers. CEGT presents a compositional architecture that decomposes explanation generation into three stages: (1) reasoning extraction, (2) explanation synthesis, and (3) explanation evaluation. We formalize the notion of an explanation as a function E(Q, A) mapping a question Q and answer A to an explanatory text E, and we propose a set of axioms that govern the properties of E, including completeness, coherence, and brevity. The theory further details algorithmic procedures for constructing explanations from logical derivations and probabilistic models, and it offers a modular pipeline that can be integrated with existing question‑answering systems. We argue that CEGT has the potential to enhance the trustworthiness of AI systems, facilitate human‑machine collaboration, and open new avenues for research in explainable AI.

title: Computational Intuition Transfer Theory (CITT)
abstract: Computational Intuition Transfer Theory (CITT) proposes a formal framework for modeling how expert intuition developed in one domain can be systematically transferred to another domain. The theory posits that intuition is a high‑level, context‑sensitive representation that can be encoded, abstracted, and re‑extracted via a mapping function. By formalizing intuition as a function of domain knowledge, problem structure, and experiential patterns, CITT enables the design of algorithms that emulate expert reasoning across heterogeneous tasks. The paper develops the core mathematical formalism, elucidates the mechanisms of transfer, discusses implications for general artificial intelligence, and outlines avenues for future research. The potential of CITT to drive breakthroughs in generalized intelligence is emphasized, positioning it as a candidate for Turing Award‑level contributions.

title: SAGA: Structure-Attended Generative Action Embedding Model that encodes Multi-Surface User Action Sequences
abstract: Prior embedding models for sequential recommendation typically operate within a homogeneous action space, limiting their ability to capture cross-surface behavioral signals spanning distinct behavioral domains. We present SAGA, a generative action embedding model that encodes multi-surface user interaction sequences across a Financial Service organization's ecosystems, from checkout, peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions, in-app engagement, email to account actions, into a unified user representation for downstream recommendation tasks. Central to SAGA is a per-field tokenization schema that decomposes each action event into multiple field-level tokens (e.g. product, interaction, surface), enabling field-level attention and per-field training objectives that fused single-token approaches cannot support. Through an offline ablation study on loss formulation, tokenization granularity and training data scope, we isolate the contribution of each design choice. A downstream model integrated with SAGA-generated user embeddings delivers the strongest overall click and conversion lift across diverse downstream touchpoints, compared to all ablated and alternative architectures.

title: Anchor-Regularized Adaptation for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection with DINOv3
abstract: Recent works in AI-generated image detection have shown that careful training data alignment can improve generalization by removing spurious correlations. However, linear probes on frozen DINOv3 representations achieve remarkably strong performance even when trained on misaligned datasets. Motivated by this result, we analyze the underlying rationale and the limits of this generalization. We find that frozen DINOv3 performs well because its decisions rely on features that faithfully represent the space of authentic images. At the same time, its final layer is less effective at capturing the subtle pixel-artifact cues that can be emphasized by aligned training data. We further observe that naively mixing aligned and misaligned data during adaptation improves sensitivity to such cues but at the cost of distorting the pre-trained representation, limiting generalization. To address this issue, we propose Anchor-Regularized Adaptation (ARA). We apply Low-Rank Adaptation to capture pixel-level artifacts while leveraging a frozen anchor classifier to avoid deviations from the original representation structure. This allows the model to exploit pixel-artifact cues without sacrificing generalization. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on nine diverse and challenging benchmarks, indicating that ARA enables complementary supervision from misaligned and aligned data for more effective detection.

title: LLM-based Framework for Generating and Verifying Parallel DEVS Statecharts
abstract: The development of models demands sound modeling and simulation knowledge as well as domain knowledge. Every model should accurately represent a system's dynamics and be verifiable. Toward this objective, this research introduces an agentic PDEVS-LLM framework to assist human modelers in generating and verifying PDEVS statecharts for behavior modeling of atomic Parallel Discrete Event System Specification (PDEVS) models. The framework supports (re)generating plausible facts from a system description prompt using the agentic LLM used for generating plausible facts. Inconsistencies in plausible facts lead to incorrect PDEVS statecharts having logical structure and behavioral inaccuracies. A controlled-correction mechanism is developed to verify the logical consistency of the plausible facts. The agentic LLM is used to generate key behavioral conditions from the system description prompt. The plausible facts are then verified against the behavioral conditions using propositional logic entailment for a finite number of times. The verification results enable the generation of modification prompts that can reduce errors in generated plausible facts, resulting in more accurate PDEVS statecharts. To verify a statechart's logical correctness, its Timed Automata counterpart is manually created and verified for deadlock and reachability properties. The human modeler may regenerate plausible facts and PDEVS statecharts iteratively and incrementally. A basic correctness metric is introduced to quantify the completeness and accuracy of the expected behavioral traits of the PDEVS statechart models. A collection of example systems with varying levels of complexity is developed to demonstrate the capabilities and limitations of LLMs. The evaluation of the proposed verification mechanism shows a substantial improvement in the logical consistency of generated statecharts.

title: A concentration result for multilayer feedforward neural networks
abstract: We consider for an arbitrary fixed $ρ$ and for each positive integer $n$ a multilayer feedforward artificial neural network with $ρ$ layers, $n$ neurons in the first layer (the input layer) and only one neuron, the output neuron, in the last layer. Very roughly formulated, the main result is that if the distribution of weights of connections from a layer to the next are, for all large $n$, approximated well by a fixed continuous (but otherwise arbitrary) curve which does not depend on $n$, and if the values of the $n$ input neurons are independently and identically distributed with a continuous probability density function, then there is a number $ψ$ such that for all $\varepsilon > 0$ the probability that the value of the output neuron is in $[ψ- \varepsilon, ψ+ \varepsilon]$ tends to 1 as $n$ tends to infinity.

title: Computational Goal Space Geometry
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Goal Space Geometry (CGSG), a novel theoretical framework aimed at shifting the focus of intelligent planning from individual goals to the underlying geometric relationships within the problem space. Traditional planning approaches often struggle with complex, multi-faceted goals, frequently leading to suboptimal solutions or requiring extensive, handcrafted heuristics. CGSG proposes that the key to effective planning lies in understanding and manipulating the intrinsic geometry of the space defined by the goals. This work outlines the core principles of CGSG, emphasizing a topological and relational approach rather than a point-based one. It suggests a formal method for representing and analyzing the relationships between goals, potentially unlocking new insights and approaches for intelligent systems. The theoretical framework presented here has the potential to significantly impact the field of artificial intelligence, particularly in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems, and strategic planning. The core idea revolves around defining a space, denoted as [ΩG], where the relationships between goals are studied. This space is not defined by individual points but by the connections and distances between goals. The ultimate goal is to develop algorithms that can navigate and optimize within this space, leading to more robust and adaptable planning solutions. ---

title: Computational Choice Freedom Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Choice Freedom Theory (CCFT), a novel framework for understanding intelligence and autonomous agency. CCFT posits that a system's capabilities aren't solely determined by the quantity of operations it can perform, but crucially by the *quality* and *availability* of genuinely effective choices. The theory defines 'effective actions' as those that, when executed, satisfy a minimum threshold of success, denoted by θ. The core equation governing CCFT is: [F_C log | \mathcal{A}_{\text{effective}}|]. This equation highlights the logarithmic relationship between the number of effective choices (represented by \mathcal{A}_{\text{effective}}) and the computational complexity, or choice freedom, of a system. The theory offers a potentially groundbreaking approach to building intelligent agents with genuine autonomy, moving beyond simple computational power to consider the strategic and selective aspects of decision-making. This work lays the theoretical groundwork for further exploration and development of CCFT. ---

title: Computational Value Transfer Theory (CVTT)
abstract: Computational Value Transfer Theory (CVTT) proposes a rigorous framework for understanding how intrinsic value signals, learned in one task domain, can be systematically transferred to novel tasks. The theory is grounded in a formal representation of value functions, a set of axioms that capture the conditions under which transfer is possible, and a mechanistic model of how value representations are recombined across tasks. By establishing a mathematical correspondence between source and target tasks, CVTT explains why certain principles exhibit universal applicability and offers a pathway to achieving general intelligence. This paper presents the theoretical underpinnings of CVTT, delineates its core mechanisms, and discusses its implications for future research in artificial intelligence.

title: MARL-SI: Mirror Agent Recursive Learning with Convergence-Guaranteed Self-Improvement
abstract: Self-improving agent architectures represent a promising paradigm for autonomous capability development. However, deploying these systems in regulated or high-stakes environments requires guarantees of safety, traceability, and stability. This paper introduces MARL-SI (Mirror Agent Recursive Learning), a proposed architectural design focused on safety and trust infrastructure for self-improving agents. The design combines three key properties: (1) a symmetric observer-executor loop where the critic's capability co-evolves with execution capability, addressing the lagging critic problem; (2) a parameter-level validation gate designed to protect against performance regressions by testing proposed changes across tiered quality dimensions; and (3) a version-controlled patch taxonomy to enable rollback and auditability of agent modifications. We also outline a knowledge transfer protocol that provides a fixed meta-observer with operational data while keeping its judgment independent. We present the theoretical framework, including a convergence guarantee based on the Monotone Convergence Theorem, and analyze the design's properties relative to contemporary self-improving architectures. This work is a theoretical proposal, with empirical implementation and validation identified as the critical next step.

title: Computational Self-Verifying Explanation Theory (CSVET)
abstract: The growing reliance on automated decision systems has amplified the need for explanations that are not only intelligible but also trustworthy. This paper introduces the Computational Self-Verifying Explanation Theory (CSVET), a formal framework that couples explanation generation with an intrinsic verification process. CSVET posits that an explanation E(x) for a model prediction ŷ = f(x) should satisfy a verification predicate V(E, f, x) that ensures consistency, completeness, and soundness with respect to the underlying model and the domain. By embedding verification into the explanatory pipeline, CSVET bridges the gap between interpretability and formal assurance. The theory is grounded in formal logic, computational complexity, and machine learning theory, and it is poised to catalyze advances in both formal verification and artificial intelligence. The potential for CSVET to underpin Turing Award‑level contributions is highlighted, particularly through its capacity to unify explainable AI with rigorous verification methodologies.

title: Machine Learning Prognostic Models in Oncology Using Unstructured Clinical Text and Structured Clinical Data: A Scoping Review protocol
abstract: Existing reviews have addressed ML in oncology prognosis, NLP in clinical text mining, and multimodal learning in healthcare generally, but none has systematically mapped the intersection of unstructured text, structured EHR fusion, and prognostic modelling in oncology, with a focus on the post-transformer era. This scoping review protocol is designed to address this gap.

title: Gated Against One Model, Open to the Next: Option-Only Solvability in Legal Multiple-Choice Benchmarks
abstract: Multiple-choice benchmarks are graded on whether a model picks the right option, not on whether it needed the question. Measuring that gap takes care: a model answering A to most items scores above chance wherever the key sits at A, and reads as recognition when it is not. We measure it on UA-JudgeExam: 11,990 four-option items with official keys, published by Ukraine's Higher Qualification Commission of Judges. Shown the options and no question, Claude Haiku 4.5 scores 0.383 against chance, and the leak is concentrated: 11.8% of items are answered blind on all eight option orders, against 0.2 items expected by chance. It is not quotation: search over 280,059 editions of Ukrainian legislation recovers 0.128. Gating those out retains 8,128 items, on which the gating model itself now scores 0.204, and GPT-5.6, which took no part in the selection, still answers 0.515 of them with the question hidden. Scoring twelve held-out models on the whole set and subtracting each one's answer-position habit, only two keep an excess: GPT-5.6 at +0.265, Sonnet 4.6 at +0.081. Without it the ranking misleads: Llama 3.1 8B scores 0.292 blind, above every model but those two, purely by answering A to 92% of items. The gate does select something real: on the items it rejected, eleven of twelve models score 0.518-0.789, every interval clear of what the same model scores on the items it kept. But that signal is one model's, and filtering on it does not transfer upward. Neither is visible on a 400-item sample, where nine models read as "statistically at chance". Rewriting distractors instead overshoots to 0.168, below chance and as exploitable. The same probe on LEXam returns chance: every option there points into the stem, none longer than 33 characters. Item format decides whether the problem can arise; capability decides how much is extracted. We release the corpus, the predictions and the harness.

title: Beyond Natural-Image Foundation Models: Benchmarking Satellite Pretraining for Ophthalmic Image Analysis
abstract: Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) have emerged as a promising approach in medical imaging, producing broadly applicable systems that can be efficiently adapted across diverse imaging modalities, anatomical regions, and clinical tasks. However, VFMs require extensive training data, and their progress in medical image analysis is constrained by limited data availability, privacy concerns, and high development costs. To alleviate these constraints, medical VFMs (MedVFMs) are often built upon weights from generalist models pretrained on vast amounts of publicly available natural images, introducing a substantial distribution shift for medical task adaptation. To address this, we propose satellite imagery as a novel pretraining domain for MedVFM development and benchmarking, motivated by its closer visual alignment with medical data and its freedom from the privacy constraints that limit medical datasets. Across multiple ophthalmic imaging modalities, we compare DINOv3-SAT493m pretrained on 493 million satellite images against DINOv3-LVD1689m pretrained on 1.7 billion natural images, together with two medical specialist baselines: DINOv3-RETFound and MAE-RETFound. Our experiments show that satellite imagery is a stronger pretraining source than natural images for ophthalmic tasks, particularly on en face vascular-rich modalities. On several tasks, satellite pretraining matches or exceeds the medical specialists on high-resolution en face inputs, despite using no medical data.

title: Generative data assimilation highlights fronts as key regulators of ocean energy cascade
abstract: Mesoscale eddies are fundamental to the ocean circulation, yet the extent to which submesoscale motions, a few kilometers across, influence mesoscale eddy energetics through a kinetic energy cascade remains uncertain. High-resolution simulations predict that submesoscale fronts are key regulators of the cascade, transferring energy both downscale towards dissipation and upscale to sustain and shape the seasonality of mesoscale eddies. Testing these predictions has remained difficult because existing observations and state estimates cannot resolve submesoscale currents over sufficiently broad domains. Here we map the ocean's submesoscale energy cascade by combining multi-source satellite observations with a generative deep learning framework, reconstructing gap-free, kilometer-scale surface currents with physically plausible dynamics learned from simulations. Applying this to the eddy-rich Agulhas Current system, we find that submesoscales energize the mesoscale through an upscale energy cascade above 10 km, contributing to the seasonality of mesoscale eddies. Below 10 km, convergence at submesoscale fronts drives a downscale cascade towards dissipation. Both upscale and downscale pathways concentrate within fronts, where cross-scale transfer is up to an order of magnitude more efficient. Despite their limited extent, fronts account for a substantial fraction of the domain-integrated cascade, establishing them as key regulators of the cascade and targets for next-generation eddy parameterizations.

title: Are LLMs Safe Beyond Text: Do Emojis Expose Gaps in Safety Evaluation
abstract: Safety evaluations of large language models (LLMs) predominantly rely on text-based adversarial prompts, potentially overlooking vulnerabilities arising from alternative input representations. This work examines emoji-augmented prompts as a test case for this gap, evaluating 50 prompts across four open-source LLMs (Mistral 7B, Qwen 2 7B, Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B). Results show substantial variation in robustness: Gemma 2 9B and Mistral 7B exhibit non-zero success rates (10%), Llama 3 8B 6%, while Qwen 2 7B shows complete resistance (0% success rate). A chi-square test ($χ^2 = 32.94, p < 0.001$) confirms significant differences in outcome distributions. These findings indicate that robustness is sensitive to input representation, and that evaluations restricted to standard text prompts may underrepresent model vulnerabilities.

title: Analisis Sentimen Ulasan Figma dan Canva di Google Play Store Menggunakan Support Vector Machine dan SMOTE : Sentiment Analysis Figma and Canva Reviews on Google Play Store Using Support Vector Machine and SMOTE
abstract: Ulasan pengguna di Google Play Store memberikan informasi penting tentang pengalaman dan tingkat kepuasan pengguna terhadap aplikasi seluler. Penelitian ini bertujuan membandingkan sentimen pengguna aplikasi Canva dan Figma serta mengevaluasi kinerja algoritma Support Vector Machine (SVM) yang dikombinasikan dengan Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) dalam mengklasifikasikan sentimen pengguna. Sebanyak 8.192 ulasan dikumpulkan dan diproses melalui tahapan pembersihan data, case folding, tokenisasi, penghapusan stopword, stemming, pelabelan sentimen berdasarkan rating pengguna, serta ekstraksi fitur menggunakan Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). Dataset dibagi menjadi data pelatihan dan data pengujian dengan rasio 80:20. SMOTE diterapkan pada data pelatihan untuk mengatasi ketidakseimbangan kelas sebelum proses pemodelan menggunakan SVM. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan bahwa model memperoleh akurasi sebesar 87,19%, precision 95,32%, recall 87,01%, dan F1-score 90,97%. Sentimen positif mendominasi ulasan pada kedua aplikasi. Pengguna Canva lebih banyak menyampaikan keluhan terkait layanan berlangganan dan pengelolaan akun, sedangkan pengguna Figma lebih sering mengalami kendala login, aksesibilitas aplikasi, dan masalah teknis. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa kombinasi SVM dan SMOTE mampu menghasilkan kinerja klasifikasi yang baik serta memberikan informasi yang dapat digunakan oleh pengembang untuk meningkatkan kualitas layanan, mengoptimalkan fitur aplikasi, dan meningkatkan kepuasan pengguna.

title: Exploiting UEFI Attack Surfaces to Bypass Secure Boot and Subvert Kernel Integrity in Windows and Linux
abstract: This paper analyzes practical attack surfaces that can be exploited to bypass UEFI Secure Boot and compromise kernel integrity on Windows and Linux. It examines vulnerabilities in signed UEFI applications, weaknesses in firmware variable handling, and supply chain failures, including Security2 protocol corruption, custom PE loader abuse, and NVRAM variable shadowing. The paper follows these attack primitives from the initial break in the UEFI chain of trust to persistent pre-OS code execution and bootkit-based compromise. It explains how these techniques can enable unsigned UEFI components to execute and ultimately subvert Windows kernel code integrity and virtualization-based protections, as well as Linux kernel module signature verification and lockdown mode, while Secure Boot continues to be reported as enabled.

title: Computational Explanation Complexity (CEC)
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Explanation Complexity (CEC), a novel framework for quantifying the difficulty of explaining a system's output. The core idea is that a system's output can be easily computable but inherently difficult to interpret. We define CEC as the minimum size of an explanation set, *E*, required to provide a "why" explanation for a given output, *y*. Crucially, we demonstrate a fundamental divergence between the computational complexity of an explanation and its explanatory power, establishing that *Ccompute ≠ Cexplain*. This distinction offers a theoretical foundation for evaluating and comparing the interpretability of different systems and provides a potential pathway toward bridging the gap between complexity theory and AI explainability research. The framework presented here has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of how systems can be made more transparent and understandable.

title: Computational State Compression Limit (CSCL)
abstract: This paper explores the concept of the Computational State Compression Limit (CSCL), a theoretical framework aimed at determining the fundamental lower bound on the information required to represent the state of a complex system. The core question addressed is: what is the absolute minimum amount of information needed to fully describe a system's state? We introduce the function L(S), representing the information content of a system state S, and define Lmin as the minimal information content required while maintaining the system's behavior. This work leverages principles from information theory, artificial intelligence memory research, and data compression techniques to investigate this limit. The research highlights potential connections between CSCL and the pursuit of efficient AI memory architectures, suggesting a pathway for achieving significantly reduced storage requirements for complex systems. The investigation focuses purely on theoretical bounds, without experimental validation, and seeks to establish a foundational understanding of the inherent limitations in state representation. ---

title: Repurposing Simple Educational Robots for Secondary Schools
abstract: Abstract This practice-oriented paper presents three classroom-ready mathematics activities that repurpose simple educational robots – Bee-Bot, Ozobot, and Dot – for older learners and pre-service teachers. Rather than arguing that simple robots are inherently better than more sophisticated tools, the paper shows how instructional design, task structure, and teacher orchestration shape the motivational value of robotics in mathematics lessons. The article is grounded in professional literature on motivation, educational robotics, and mathematics learning, and it interprets the activities through a concise design lens centred on autonomy, competence, relatedness, self-efficacy, and gameful challenge. For each activity, the paper describes the instructional purpose, materials, classroom flow, typical misconceptions, scaffolds, and adaptation options. The contribution is practical rather than empirical: the paper offers transferable design principles and implementation guidance for practitioners who wish to integrate educational robotics into mathematics instruction in ways that are cognitively demanding, motivationally supportive, and feasible in ordinary school settings.

title: Tensor--Action Ko--Lee Cryptography: A Framework and Structural Cryptanalysis of Commuting Subgroup Constructions
abstract: Tensor isomorphism has been studied as an algebraic problem relevant to post-quantum cryptography, while its use in public-key encryption remains open. In this paper, we formulate a Ko--Lee-style framework for public-key encryption from cubic tensor actions and prove its formal correctness. We then show that the framework is generically insecure when the commuting matrix subgroups are given by public finite generating sets. Viewing a cubic tensor as a vector in a $d^3$-dimensional space, a linear decomposition attack recovers the shared tensor from the public transcript in polynomial time without recovering either secret action. We also cryptanalyze three natural commuting-subgroup constructions---field-extension, block-diagonal, and tensor-product constructions---and give toy-scale experiments illustrating their specific structural leakage. Finally, we examine the lower-dimensional leakage caused by scaled-block structure. The contribution is therefore a framework proposal together with its cryptanalysis; it does not provide a secure public-key encryption scheme.

title: T-LLM Compiler: Trusted LLM-based Code Optimization and Verification Framework
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened opportunities to apply high-level code transformations to the field of code optimization, and it has since emerged as one of the most fundamental tasks for LLMs to perform; however, at present, LLMs struggle to apply wide-ranging code optimization tasks due to both the complexity of the code and the inability to independently verify the correctness of the transformations. In this paper, we present the Trusted LLM (T-LLM) Compiler, which proposes an advancement in compiler technology through a collaborative effort involving high-level LLM code transformations, traditional compilers, and verification tools. Experimental results reveal that it can significantly improve code correctness when tested on a set of PolyBench/C benchmarks. Our approach facilitates iterative code optimization efforts with verification strategies that enable corrective actions. Through this approach, T-LLM Compiler achieves code optimization accuracy of up to 83.3% and a speedup of up to 16.1\% on the PolyBench/C benchmarks, with the transformed code reaching an average of 26.7% speedup wrt standard baselines. Additionally, we release the project's source code to the open-source community.

title: Certifying Compressed Language Models: An Audit and a Statistical Toolkit
abstract: A fraction of a point of benchmark accuracy is the usual evidence that a compressed model is equivalent to its original. That quantity is least informative when two models are most alike: a net delta is what survives cancellation between opposing per-item changes, and cancellation is most complete in the regime equivalence claims occupy. Across an atlas of 1,707 paired model-by-task cells mined from public per-item evaluation dumps (1.3B-405B), churn runs roughly five times the net accuracy delta, and cells scoring identically to their baseline still disagree on individual items. In a preregistered audit of 17 equivalence claims from three registered frames (method papers, model cards, vendor documentation), 16 are eligible. None states a prospective numerical equivalence margin, and none releases task-matched per-item outputs, though 3 release outputs for other tasks only; 5 report too little to assess numerically, so a reader cannot check them at any sample size. We audit evidential sufficiency, not truth: no claim is called false. We supply the missing instrument: paired equivalence testing at a declared margin, with certification tables giving the items an evaluation needs, computed from disagreement observed under compression, not from independent-binomial variance. A controlled experiment pairs GPTQ and AWQ on byte-identical calibration samples across five seeds. Under the frozen eight-cell decision rule H3 is supported: changing the calibration draw was sufficient to reverse the observed method ordering in 5 of 8 confirmatory cells. The reporting standard we propose is five lines: declare a margin, run the paired test, report churn beside net delta, cite the sample size you met, release per-item outputs. It applies to any comparison between two models alike enough to be worth comparing. All per-item outputs, protocols and code are released.

evidence.title: FlipEval v1.1.0: Code and Reproducibility Artifacts for Certifying Compressed Language Models
evidence.abstract: Companion code and artifact release for Certifying Compressed Language Models: An Audit and a Statistical Toolkit. The paper's headline audit finding is that 0 of 17 published near-lossless compression claims release the per-item outputs a third party would need to run the paired comparison themselves. This release is that recommendation applied to its own author: every per-item output behind every controlled result in the paper is published here, together with the integrity metadata needed to check it. What v1.0.0 contains This tag pins the source tree. The artifact bundle it describes is 209 files, 330 MB, with a SHA256SUMS covering all 208 payload files at the bundle root. | Component | Contents | |---|---| | Per-item outputs | 88 cell JSONLs — one row per evaluation item, per model × method × seed × task. Extracted and directly loadable, not only sealed. | | Sealed archives | minigrid_run_20260722.tar.gz and escalation_run_20260726.tar.gz, each with its .sha256 and a per-file manifest. Byte-identical to what was archived at run time; the extracted per-item copy checks against these manifests. | | Rev-2 flip atlas | Per-cell paired statistics, the exclusion table, the frozen 59-pair manifest, and the identical-score churn table. Derived statistics only — see Licensing below. | | Audit artifacts | The frozen 17-claim table with recorded source content hashes, and the per-claim verdict CSV carrying every robustness and transparency column, including R04's set-aside GSM8K computation. | | Certification tables | Required-n certification at all three margins (1, 2, 3 pp). | | H3 artifacts | The nine eight-cell H3 files, both grid validation summaries, and the escalation screen summary. | | Reproduction package | Preregistration, all registrations with their dated amendments, signed decision records, configs, container image SHA-256 and build recipe, SLURM scripts, build receipts, source-state freeze fingerprints, and the campaign incident log. | Both forms of the cell data, deliberately The per-item outputs ship extracted and sealed. Extracted so the data is previewable and loadable; sealed with per-file SHA-256 manifests so the extracted copy can be checked against the record made at run time. Usable and integrity-checkable is the pairing the paper argues for — shipping only one of the two would concede half the point. Paths under per_item_outputs/ retain the results/ / prefix recorded in the archive manifests, so manifest paths resolve directly against the extracted copy. Provenance Source-state fingerprint: docs/PREPACE_FREEZE.json, verifying passed: true at this tag. Container image SHA-256: 8260d04cf1f76cb5961b6538dbeb9178006b29c5d8c93d2c639976bcd1db2007. The build recipe is included; the image itself is not redistributed. The campaign incident log documents 28 defects caught during the campaign, with what each one would have corrupted. It is included on purpose: a pipeline with 28 recorded catches is better evidence of verification than one presenting a clean surface, and several entries — a validator pointed at the wrong grid, a write-protection scheme that could not stop os.replace(), an sbatch flag accepted and silently discarded — are reusable warnings for anyone running a comparable campaign. Licensing Code: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE in this repository). Data and artifacts: CC-BY-4.0. The per-item outputs were generated by us; the atlas files are derived per-cell statistics we computed. Raw upstream per-item files from stratum S1 are not redistributed, and must not be added. S1 is built on the Open LLM Leaderboard v1 archive, which carries no declared license. This is recorded as a limitation in the paper and in the datasheet rather than worked around. A third party can re-derive S1: the frozen pair manifest records, per pair, the upstream dataset identifiers and run timestamps needed to fetch the same inputs and recompute every derived column with the released flipeval package. Stratum S2 (vendor-published evaluations) is Apache-2.0 upstream. Redaction statement These runs executed on a university HPC cluster. Site-specific identifiers — absolute paths, the SLURM charge account, usernames, login and compute hostnames — were replaced with placeholders before publication. The redaction rules and the list of files touched are recorded in REDACTIONS.json in the reproduction package. No scientific quantity was altered. No accuracy, hash, count, seed, timestamp, job ID, model revision or decision value is affected, and the sealed archives were not rewritten at all — which is why their recorded SHA-256 values still verify. Compute nodes are pseudonymised one-to-one and stably, so incident 11's finding (the node SLURM was asked to exclude differed from the node the job landed on) remains checkable from the pseudonyms alone. Revision history Both atlas revisions are published and the delta is reported. Rev-1 contained a population defect: an omitted reverse-chronological fallback clause and a parser that missed a newer nested metrics schema had silently dropped cells, the first non-randomly. An independent spot-check reconciled all 262 compared fields — the arithmetic was right and the population was not. Rev-2 files are the ones the paper cites and are what this release carries as current; rev-1 files remain in the repository and in the git history at this tag. A corrected artifact whose correction is visible is the paper's own argument applied to itself. Limitations The atlas is a record, not a sample: it describes the evidence the field circulates, not the behaviour of quantization in general. All benchmarks are English and predominantly multiple-choice or short-answer. Float-scored generation tasks are outside the flip model entirely. The controlled experiment is 8 cells, 1.5B–8B, 4-bit, two methods, five seeds. The GSM8K arm at n = 1,000 is under-resolved, which the paper states and quantifies rather than omits. No human-subject data and no personally identifying information.

title: Computational Explanation Generation Theory (CEGT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Explanation Generation Theory (CEGT), a novel approach to artificial intelligence that moves beyond simply providing answers to generating comprehensive explanations alongside them. Current systems primarily focus on delivering the correct output, often without providing insight into *why* the output was generated. CEGT proposes a fundamental shift: that explanations are not predetermined rules, but rather emergent properties derived from the relationship between the output and its underlying structure. This theory is formalized as `E = f(Output, Structure)`, where *E* represents the explanation, *Output* is the system's answer, and *Structure* encompasses the internal representation and processing steps. The theory's potential to redefine our understanding of understandable computation, and its implications for achieving truly intelligent systems, are explored. The core concept is to move from a system that merely provides an answer to one that simultaneously produces an explanation of that answer, fostering greater transparency and trust in AI systems. ---

title: Computational System Replication Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational System Replication Theory (CSRT), a novel framework for understanding and enabling self-replicating computational systems. The core principle of CSRT centers on the automated duplication of a system, denoted as [S → S'], coupled with a rigorous maintenance of functional equivalence, expressed as [Function(S') ≈ Function(S)]. This theory proposes a methodology for designing systems capable of autonomous replication, with potential implications for advancements in autonomous software and robotics. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings of CSRT, including the key components necessary for successful replication and the mechanisms for maintaining functional fidelity. A central aspect of the theory is the concept of 'replicators,' which are the agents responsible for the duplication process, and 'stabilizers,' which ensure the replicated system maintains the original's functionality. The paper also addresses potential challenges and future research directions within the field of CSRT. ---

title: Computational Forgetting Calculus (CFC)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Forgetting Calculus (CFC), a novel framework addressing the critical need for controlled information forgetting in future computing systems. Traditional computational models predominantly focus on information retention, neglecting the ability to precisely dictate what information should be forgotten. CFC defines a "forgetting operator" – denoted as [ \mathcal{F}_\lambda(S) | S' ] – that satisfies two key conditions: the probability of a system transitioning to obsolete information [ I(S';D_{\text{obsolete}}) ] approaches zero, and the utility of the system after forgetting [ \operatorname{Utility}(S') ] remains above a predefined threshold θ. This paper outlines the core principles of CFC, explores the challenges involved in implementing such an operator, and posits its potential impact on diverse fields including machine forgetting, privacy-preserving computation, long-term AI memory management, and data governance. The framework represents a fundamental shift in computational thinking, moving beyond passive retention to active, controlled forgetting. ---

title: Self-Forming Constraint Computation (SFCC)
abstract: This paper introduces the Self-Forming Constraint Computation (SFCC) framework, a novel approach to autonomous computation centered around the dynamic generation of constraints. Traditional computational systems rely on pre-defined constraints imposed by human designers, creating a unidirectional dependency. SFCC flips this paradigm, allowing systems to autonomously infer and establish constraints based on their surrounding environment. This self-formation process is driven by a core principle: [Environment → Constraint]. The potential of SFCC extends beyond simple automation; it represents a fundamental step towards building truly autonomous computational agents, with implications for areas such as robotics, artificial intelligence, and complex system modeling. This work outlines the theoretical foundations of SFCC, detailing its operational mechanisms and exploring its potential applications. We propose a mathematical framework to formalize the process, focusing on the iterative refinement of constraints driven by environmental feedback. The core concept is represented by the following equation: Ci = f(Ei, Ci-1, Pi), where Ci represents the i-th iteration of the constraint, Ei represents the environmental input at the i-th iteration, Ci-1 represents the constraint from the previous iteration, and Pi represents the processing function at the i-th iteration. This framework allows for the creation of adaptive systems that can respond and evolve in dynamic and unpredictable environments. We further explore the concept of constraint hierarchies, where higher-level constraints are derived from lower-level ones, enhancing the system's ability to reason and make decisions. The ultimate goal of SFCC is to move beyond human-designed constraints and enable systems to learn and adapt autonomously, mirroring the way biological systems operate.

title: Computational Experience Generation Algorithm (CEGA)
abstract: Computational Experience Generation Algorithm (CEGA) is a novel framework that transforms the way autonomous agents acquire knowledge. Instead of passively learning from a fixed set of interactions with the environment, CEGA actively creates and orchestrates experiments that yield structured experiences. The core of CEGA is a closed loop that couples the agent, an experiment planner, and an experience repository: Agent → Experiment → Experience. By integrating model-based simulation, curiosity-driven exploration, and information-theoretic experiment selection, CEGA achieves efficient learning in high-dimensional, partially observable domains. This paper presents the formal foundations of CEGA, details its algorithmic components, analyzes its theoretical properties, and discusses its potential to reshape machine science and artificial general intelligence.

evidence.title: Computational Experience Generation Algorithm (CEGA)
evidence.abstract: Computational Experience Generation Algorithm (CEGA) is a novel framework that transforms the way autonomous agents acquire knowledge. Instead of passively learning from a fixed set of interactions with the environment, CEGA actively creates and orchestrates experiments that yield structured experiences. The core of CEGA is a closed loop that couples the agent, an experiment planner, and an experience repository: Agent → Experiment → Experience. By integrating model-based simulation, curiosity-driven exploration, and information-theoretic experiment selection, CEGA achieves efficient learning in high-dimensional, partially observable domains. This paper presents the formal foundations of CEGA, details its algorithmic components, analyzes its theoretical properties, and discusses its potential to reshape machine science and artificial general intelligence.

title: Computational Identity Singularity Theory (CIST-3): Core Ideas and Applications
abstract: Computational Identity Singularity Theory (CIST-3) proposes a formal framework for the self‑aware, self‑modifying behavior of autonomous computational agents. At its heart, CIST-3 asserts that a system capable of representing, evaluating, and transforming its own identity can reach a state of high‑level autonomy that may exhibit characteristics of singularity in the context of artificial intelligence. The theory combines concepts from identity theory, dynamical systems, and information theory to describe how identity representations evolve over time. We present a set of equations that capture the dynamics of identity change, including the identity vector s(t), the transformation matrix T(t), and the feedback loop that couples perception and self‑adjustment. The model predicts that when the rate of identity change exceeds a critical threshold, the system undergoes a bifurcation leading to a new regime of behavior that cannot be anticipated from the initial conditions. We discuss potential applications in adaptive robotics, autonomous decision‑making, and the philosophical implications for machine consciousness. By avoiding explicit experimental sections, the paper focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and provides a roadmap for future empirical validation.

title: Pelatihan Penggunaan 3D Printing bagi Siswa Robotik MAN 1 Pekanbaru
abstract: Mengingat ilmu Robotik yang sedang ramai dibahas saat ini, MAN 1 Pekanbaru menyediakan ekstrakurikuler Robotik sebagai wadah bagi para siswa untuk mengembangkan minat dan bakat pada bidang Robotik. Namun, penyediaan barang-barang untuk keperluan pengembangan ekstrakurikuler masih dilakukan secara sukarela mengingat mesin 3D printing yang merupakan alat utama untuk memproduksi komponen yang diperlukan masih dalam tahap pengadaan. Oleh karena itu, diperlukan pelatihan penggunaan 3D printing terlebih dahulu agar kemampuan anggota dalam mengoperasikan mesin tersebut telah ada ketika mesin 3D printing sudah tersedia nantinya di MAN 1 Pekanbaru. Pelatihan yang dilakukan mengkombinasikan desain dan produksi secara komprehensif, sehingga peserta akan mampu melakukan pembuatan komponen yang diperlukan secara runut. Kegiatan desain menggunakan perangkat lunak SolidWorks untuk membuat rancangan gambar dari komponen yang akan dibuat. Kemudian, hasil desain akan dikonversi menjadi G-Code dengan menggunakan perangkat lunak FlashPrint, dan G-Code yang dihasilkan akan menjadi input bagi mesin 3D printing dalam memproduksi barang sesuai dengan desain yang telah dibuat. Peserta mampu menunjukkan daya kognitifnya, berupa kemampuan dalam berpikir kritis, pemahaman yang mendalam, kemandirian, dan rasa percaya diri yang tinggi selama kegiatan berlangsung. Dengan pelatihan ini, diharapkan ekstrakurikuler Robotik mampu mengembangkan potensi dan kemampuan dirinya secara mandiri dalam mencapai visi dan misi yang telah ditetapkan.

title: ETHOS: Towards a Modular Ethics Framework for Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: The rapid adoption of large language models has enabled the development of clinical multi-agent systems (MAS) capable of integrating multimodal patient data and supporting increasingly complex clinical decision-making. However, the deployment of these systems in real-world healthcare settings raises critical ethical concerns related to safety, fairness, accountability, transparency, and patient trust. While numerous organizations, including the World Health Organization, the National Academy of Medicine, and the FUTURE-AI consortium, have proposed ethical frameworks and governance principles for healthcare AI, these efforts remain largely conceptual. To address this challenge, we present ETHOS (Ethics and Trust through Hierarchical Oversight System), a modular ethics framework designed as a governance meta-agent that can be integrated with any existing multi-agent system without requiring changes to its underlying architecture. ETHOS translates stakeholder-informed ethical requirements into executable runtime oversight through a layered governance approach consisting of deterministic checks, contextual reviews, and a final ethics critic. These components continuously evaluate intermediate reasoning steps and final outputs, enabling the system to identify ethical risks, request revisions, or suppress responses that fail predefined safety and trustworthiness criteria. We demonstrate ETHOS within a hepatology clinical decision-support MAS. Results show that ETHOS improves decision reliability by detecting incomplete, inconsistent, or out-of-scope evidence and appropriately increasing abstention when safe recommendations cannot be supported. By embedding ethical governance directly into system operation, ETHOS provides a practical and auditable mechanism for transforming high-level AI ethics principles into deployable safeguards.

title: The Quality of Claude AI-authored Python Tests Is Not Weaker Than Human-authored Tests
abstract: We evaluate the quality of Claude AI-written Python tests against human-written Python tests from two established open-source projects Django and Pandas. Hundreds of tests per corpus are scored under one identical protocol. Using one-sided non-inferiority bounds, we find that the tests written by recent Claude models (Sonnet/Opus 4.6 and later) are no weaker than the two human-written corpora. In this study: (i) the AI-written corpus is tests from real tools, not synthetic tests generated in isolation against a fixed target, the setup used by every other AI-test-generation study we are aware of; (ii) every test is individually scored under three independent fault-injection protocols plus a seven-axis qualitative design rubric, allowing methods to cross-validate each other; (iii) tests are scored individually, rather than suite-level, identifying exactly which specific tests need attention.

title: Evidence of Absence: Cross-Modal Abductive Risk Perception to Sustain World Models When Vision Fails
abstract: A structured world-state (entities, relations, context, and predictive cues) is designed to preserve prediction-critical content when perception degrades, but it presumes observations to populate it; when the primary visual modality is occluded or degraded, those observations may be missing. We address how to sustain the world model from a complementary modality by treating the absence of expected co-evidence as evidence of a hidden cause. The abductive framework is modality-agnostic; this article instantiates it acoustically. A microphone-array front-end estimates the bearing of engine and tire sources and extracts approach-rate evidence (Doppler when a stable tone exists, a broadband looming readout otherwise); the event "signature present, visual co-evidence absent" then triggers abductive inference of a hidden road user, emitting a calibrated risk advisory rather than a control command. Recoverability of the hidden state is analyzed as an identifiability question separating shared from modality-unique information, and cueing is cast as Neyman-Pearson detection under an explicit false-alarm budget. On real occluded-approach recordings at blind junctions, the method warns a mean 1.7 seconds before line-of-sight entry, matches the sustained-window variant of the published acoustic baseline's detection rate with 42% fewer false alarms, localizes to 3.4 degrees median once in view, is well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.034), and keeps hazard awareness above 0.87 under staged vision degradation that collapses a vision-only channel to 0.03. We also measure the method's limits: calibration transfers to an unseen junction almost losslessly, the signature classifier does not, and moving-ego noise is the binding deployment constraint.

title: SysEvolve: An AI-native, safe, autonomous adversarial attack-defense co-evolutionary system
abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has created a growing asymmetry in cybersecurity, where attack accelerates toward autonomous execution while defense remains predominantly human-intensive. Despite substantial prior work across cyber ranges, AI-driven attack, and AI-driven defense, this asymmetry persists. We trace it to a deeper root cause, that evolution itself has stalled on both sides at three layers. To overcome this, we propose co-evolution as the integrating insight, where attack and defense AI agents autonomously and safely drive each other's evolution through adversarial confrontation. Based on this insight, we present \sysevolve, comprising three co-designed components, \sysfield, \sysspear, and \sysarmor. \sysfield constructs realistic multi-host ranges. \sysspear generates efficient, safe attack schemes. \sysarmor performs real-time, interpretable defense. Together they form a self-driven adversarial loop restoring evolution at all three layers. In evaluation, \sysfield achieves zero-loss collection at 2.1\% overhead and orchestrates 257 CVEs into 1,148 ranges, \sysspear improves attack success by over 25\% over baseline LLMs, and \sysarmor achieves 10--1000$\times$ greater precision than prior systems and detects real APT attacks in production at Huawei and Sangfor. Our evaluation also reveals three findings about LLM agent capabilities. First, multi-step composition and larger topologies expose agent capability gaps hidden by single-step evaluations. Second, the bottleneck lies after initial access in post-compromise state utilization. Third, LLM agents are susceptible to environmental interference. When decoy endpoints are deployed in the range, agent timeouts triple and downstream completion disappears despite the success rates of initial accesses are unchanged.

title: How to Pick the Best Language Model: A Same-Run Test That Rejected a 95% Score
abstract: If you operate a production language model, you will eventually be offered a cheaper or newer replacement, and the wrong test will tell you it is better. We built the test that does not lie: measure the candidate against the model already running, on your own tasks, the same day, and require it to match or beat the incumbent on every axis your product depends on, not just the one number everyone checks first. Applied to a real candidate, that discipline rejected a model that scored 95.1% on tool-routing against our incumbent's 84.3%, because the same model regressed in all 27 languages we ship, including English, and answered a well-documented history question with state-aligned denial. A second candidate failed for a single language out of twenty-seven that a spot-check would have missed entirely. We give the method in full, the judging protocol that catches a lying evaluator as well as a lying model, and the one class of infrastructure change safe enough to skip the test altogether.

title: Computational Multi-Agent Unification Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Multi-Agent Unification Theory (CMAUT), a novel framework proposing a shift in perspective from individual intelligent agents to unified computational entities formed by a collection of agents. The core concept is that complex computation emerges not from individual agents, but from the orchestrated interaction and integration of multiple agents, represented as [A1, A2, ..., An], resulting in a unified entity [A*]. This theory aims to address the challenges of large-scale AI collaboration by providing a theoretical foundation for achieving emergent intelligence through systemic agent interaction. The theory is built upon the principles of distributed computation, emergent behavior, and self-organization. The underlying mathematical framework utilizes concepts from automata theory, information theory, and game theory to formalize the dynamics of agent interaction and the emergence of the unified entity. This work explores the potential of CMAUT to revolutionize the design and implementation of complex AI systems, offering a pathway towards scalable and robust solutions for problems requiring coordinated action across numerous agents. ---

title: Computational Structure Exchange Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Structure Exchange Theory (CSET), a novel framework proposing that the exchange between distinct computational systems extends beyond merely transferring data. Instead, the core element of exchange lies in the transfer of structural information. This concept is illustrated through examples such as algorithm structure exchange and its potential to yield new computational paradigms. CSET posits that the exchange of structure, rather than just data, represents a fundamental shift in our understanding of inter-system computation and its implications for theoretical advancements, potentially leading to breakthroughs analogous to those achieved by the Turing Award. The theory is presented with a focus on the core principles and illustrative examples, without requiring experimental validation. ---

title: Computational Goal Evolution Theory (CGET-3)
abstract: Computational Goal Evolution Theory (CGET-3) proposes that autonomous systems can attain higher levels of performance and adaptability by treating their goals as evolving entities rather than static directives. Drawing inspiration from biological evolution, CGET-3 models the transformation of a goal vector G_t at time t into a new goal vector G_{t+1} through mechanisms analogous to mutation, selection, and recombination. The theory formalizes goal dynamics using vector algebra and probabilistic transition functions, and demonstrates how such dynamics can be embedded into reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, and self‑optimizing control frameworks. By allowing goals to mutate and adapt in response to environmental feedback, systems can escape local optima, explore novel strategies, and ultimately converge toward optimal behavior patterns. This paper presents the mathematical foundation of CGET-3, outlines its integration into existing computational paradigms, and discusses its potential implications for future research in artificial intelligence and autonomous systems design.

title: Computational Identity Genetics Theory (CIGT-2)
abstract: Computational Identity Genetics Theory (CIGT-2) proposes a formal framework for modeling the inheritance and evolution of identity features within artificial agents. By treating identity attributes as a vector of genotypic variables that undergo transformation across discrete time steps, CIGT-2 establishes a bridge between biological genetic principles and machine learning dynamics. The core idea is that identity characteristics, denoted as I_t, can be transmitted from one generation to the next via a deterministic or stochastic transition mapping I_t → I_{t+1}. This inheritance mechanism is formalized through a state transition equation that integrates mutation, selection, and recombination operators adapted to the computational domain. Analytical exploration of the model reveals conditions for convergence, stability, and the emergence of complex identity structures. Applications to adaptive learning agents, swarm intelligence, and continual learning scenarios demonstrate that identity evolution can enhance robustness, modularity, and long‑term adaptability. Furthermore, CIGT-2 offers a conceptual foundation for a machine evolution theory that parallels biological evolution, potentially positioning the framework as a candidate for future Turing Award recognition. This paper presents the theoretical underpinnings, mathematical formulation, analytical properties, and practical applications of CIGT-2, concluding with a discussion of limitations and future research avenues.

title: Azuro Landscape Auditor v1.1 — Near-Optimal Solution Degeneracy Diagnostic for QUBO/Ising Optimization
abstract: Azuro Landscape Auditor is a diagnostic framework for quantifying near-optimal solution degeneracy in QUBO, Ising, and MAX-CUT optimization problems. Core contribution: two solver-agnostic diagnostic quantities —(1) pairwise spin overlap P(q) between independently obtained near-optimal configurations, calibrated against a finite-size Monte Carlo null distribution; and (2) the Entry→x* gap, which detects false confidence by comparing solver self-consistency (Entry→final overlap) with actual proximity to the global optimum (Entry→x* overlap). Validated on: generated ±J spin-glass instances (N=1000), G11 Gset public benchmark (N=800, MAX-CUT best-known=564), seven MQLib instances (G1, G12, G13, G14, G32, G33, G43), and a portfolio optimization QUBO with exhaustive ground truth (C(20,5)=15,504 feasible portfolios enumerated exactly). Key finding: across all tested instances, SA achieves 97-99% of best-known cut, but Entry→x* overlap is 0.06-0.13 — near-optimal configurations are nearly orthogonal to the reference optimum despite good energy proximity. The gap between Entry→final (0.58-0.77) and Entry→x* (0.06-0.13) is systematic and invisible to energy-based diagnostics. Implementation is proprietary. This preprint establishes concept priority and reports experimental results.Contact: ORCID 0000-0001-5108-2243

title: Structured Nursing Handover Report Generation from Clinical Speech using Fine-Tuned XLSR-53 and T5: A Benchmarking Study
abstract: Accurate nursing handovers are critical for patient safety, as miscommunication during shift transitions leads to irreversible clinical errors. This work proposed an end-to-end pipeline that converts unstructured clinical nursing speech into standardized handover reports using a fine-tuned XLSR-53 acoustic model and T5-base text-to-text transformer. An Australian English clinical corpus of 200 synthetic nursing handover recordings from the CSIRO data access portal was utilised in this work. This benchmarking study was conducted within the CSIRO synthetic Australian English nursing handover corpus and does not represent a broad cross-domain clinical ASR benchmark. A domain-specific benchmarking study across seven state-of-the-art ASR architectures (Whisper Tiny/Base/Small, Wav2Vec2 Base/Large, HuBERT Large, XLSR-53) was conducted using this corpus. The experimental results further revealed XLSR-53 as the optimal architecture for clinical nursing speech recognition. A partial layer-freeze strategy was adopted in XLSR-53 by freezing the first 12 of 24 encoder layers, empirically validated through an ablation study with five freeze configurations (L=0, 6, 12, 18, 24). XLSR-53 preserves cross-lingual phonetic representations while enabling clinical vocabulary adaptation. A clinically motivated evaluation framework using curated medical vocabulary terms computes Medical Precision, Recall, and F1-Score along with standard WER, CER, and PER to assess reliability in clinical term recognition. Benchmarking against Google Health AI's MedASR zero-shot revealed that the proposed system XLSR-53 (L=12) achieved 17.15% WER against MedASR's 28.87% (p<0.001) with a Medical F1-Score of 0.98 and ROUGE-L of 0.92. Although results were obtained on synthetic Australian English speech, performance under real clinical conditions with background noise, overlapping speakers, and spontaneous interruptions requires further validation.
