title: Dual-Branch State-Displacement Network for Sea Surface Temperature Super-Resolution
abstract: Sea surface temperature (SST) is a critical indicator of global climate change, yet satellite-derived SST imagery often suffers from coarse spatial resolution, limiting the ability to capture fine-scale thermal structures such as ocean fronts. To address this, we propose a Dual-Branch State-Displacement Network (DBSD-Net) for SST super-resolution. DBSD-Net adopts a dual-branch architecture: a wavelet frequency branch that explicitly separates low and high-frequency components via discrete wavelet transform for targeted processing, and a VGGUNet branch that extracts multi-scale semantic features from a frozen pre-trained VGG backbone. Within the wavelet branch, we introduce a Structural State Space Module (SSSM) with a Gated Structure Refinement (GSR) unit to efficiently capture long-range dependencies and enhance structural integrity, and a Displacement Gate Module (DGM) that learns a displacement field for geometry-aware modulation of high-frequency details, thereby mitigating spatially varying degradation. Experiments on multiple public SST datasets demonstrate that DBSD-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: MiNO: Cotangent-bundle propagator learning for PDEs
abstract: Scientific machine learning for partial differential equations commonly targets solution fields, as in physics-informed neural networks, or solution maps, as in neural operators. We study a third target: the propagator itself, a phase and amplitude in phase space. The motivation is a gap in regularity. A transported discontinuity is nonsmooth in space and time, yet the rule that moves it can be a polynomial phase carrying unit amplitude, so the object that generates an evolution can be far smoother than the field it generates. The microlocal neural operator (MiNO) learns that object, using the eikonal equation for the phase and the transport equation for the amplitude, and recovers the solution by an oscillatory integral. Sharp fronts and caustics then belong to propagation geometry rather than to a field fitted pointwise. Small residuals certify more than the reconstructed field. They place the learned canonical relation, the geometry that carries singularities, close to the exact one, and they separate trainable error from the frequency-truncation tail. On a matched-budget discontinuous-advection benchmark, MiNO stops improving within 10,000 steps at the accuracy limit of its finite reconstruction window, a limit predicted in closed form, whereas a physics-informed neural network with neural-tangent-kernel loss balancing stays near its initial error. On smooth advection, the mean error is $3.84\times10^{-3}$ for MiNO and $3.12\times10^{-2}$ for a supervised Fourier neural operator. Single-branch MiNO is the smallest model compared, and one trained generator serves five unseen initial conditions without retraining.

title: PathFinder: Joint Decompositions of Linked Multimodal Datasets
abstract: Low-rank matrix decompositions can uncover patterns and structure in data and have a number of different applications across many disciplines. Extensions to "joint" low-rank decompositions have been proposed to link datasets from different modalities. While these methods enable the discovery of common patterns across modalities, they require that all the multimodal data share one or more dimensions. We propose a new analysis method, PathFinder, that enables co-analysis of datasets that do not necessarily all share a dimension. The key insight is that as long as pairs or subgroups of matrices do share some dimension, and that there are one or more paths that link across the data matrices, a global joint decomposition can be sought out. This enables the joint estimation of common patterns across different modalities, species, or scales, where a one-to-one mapping across all data along some dimension is not necessarily available. We show that PathFinder is a general umbrella under which many matrix decomposition methods fall as special cases. It can be used to discover common patterns across disparate datasets and to make predictions for missing data or modalities.

title: LLM-Based Hierarchical Coordinated Control with Continuation-Aware Policy Learning
abstract: Coordinating multiple interacting units in complex engineering systems is challenging when system interactions are difficult to model, operational information is heterogeneous, and low-level actions must satisfy strict constraints. We propose an LLM-based hierarchical framework in which the LLM coordinates interacting units based on heterogeneous operational context, while task-specific controllers or optimizers generate executable and constraint-aware actions. We further introduce Continuation-Aware GRPO to capture the consequences of coordination decisions over subsequent control intervals. Rather than judging a decision only by its immediate outcome, the method also evaluates how the system evolves afterward under the current policy. We validate the framework on multi-ramp traffic control and virtual power plant (VPP) energy management, using simplified system models for training and more realistic simulators for evaluation. Across both tasks, the proposed method consistently outperforms direct task-specific control and optimization, end-to-end reinforcement learning, rule-based and RL-based hierarchical coordination, and prompting-only LLM coordinators, demonstrating the value of heterogeneous-context reasoning, hierarchical execution, and continuation-aware policy learning.

title: Analysis of AI Readiness and AI Marketing Capabilities to Support AI-Driven Marketing in Multinational Companies: A Qualitative Study at PT AMANN Indonesia
abstract: This study examines the readiness of AI-driven marketing implementation at PT AMANN Indonesia, a multinational manufacturing company, as AI adoption in business functions increases. Using an exploratory qualitative case study approach, this study aims to analyze AI Readiness and AI Marketing Capabilities. The study population was internal stakeholders, while the sample was determined purposively by four informants from the director, marketing, operations, and human resources functions. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, documentation, and observation, then analyzed using NVivo and the Miles and Huberman model. The results show that PT AMANN Indonesia is at the Experimenter stage in AI readiness, with strengths in technology and process readiness, but marketing analytics capabilities are still limited and carried out manually. It is concluded that strengthening AI governance, employee competencies, and data management are needed to accelerate AI-based marketing transformation.

title: Algorithmic Functional Ecological Evolution (AFEE)
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Functional Ecological Evolution (AFEE), a novel framework for understanding and modeling the development of algorithms within complex systems. AFEE posits that algorithms, much like biological organisms, evolve through a dynamic interplay of competition and cooperation, driven by an ecological fitness function. This function considers performance metrics, compatibility with existing systems, and the potential for reuse. The central mechanism involves the iterative transformation of algorithm modules, represented as [Ai → Ai'], where the new algorithm (Ai') emerges based on a fitness assessment. The aim is to demonstrate how this process can lead to the emergent formation of automated algorithm ecosystems with significant potential, analogous to the potential for the Turing Award, representing highly optimized and adaptive solutions. The core of AFEE relies on a quantitative fitness function that balances various operational aspects, offering a structured approach to simulating and analyzing algorithmic evolution. This approach provides a theoretical basis for exploring the dynamics of algorithm design and development in diverse and rapidly changing environments. ---

title: Computational Capability Generation Function (CCGF)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Capability Generation Function (CCGF), a novel framework for understanding and modeling the emergent capabilities of computational systems. Traditional approaches to evaluating computational power often rely on fixed metrics, failing to capture the dynamic and evolving nature of intelligence. The CCGF posits that computational capability is not a static property but rather a generated function, continuously evolving based on the current state of the system and its environment. The core of the CCGF is expressed as: [ K_{t+1} = F(K_t, S_t) ] where *Kt* represents the computational capability at time *t*, *St* represents the system's state and environment at time *t*, and *F* is the generation function. This function dictates how *Kt* transforms into *Kt+1*. The paper explores the potential of the CCGF to provide a theoretical foundation for understanding and predicting the growth of computational capabilities, with implications for achieving breakthroughs in areas such as artificial intelligence and complex systems research. The framework is presented as a pathway toward recognizing the potential for systems to exhibit emergent intelligence, a concept with significant relevance for the awarding of the Turing Prize. The research aims to establish a rigorous approach to studying the evolution of computation, moving beyond simply measuring existing capabilities and focusing on the mechanisms driving their development.

title: Computational Knowledge Causality Theory (CKCT‑2): Unifying Knowledge Representation and Reasoning through Causal Structures
abstract: The ability to describe and manipulate knowledge has driven advances in artificial intelligence and data science. Traditional knowledge representation frameworks focus primarily on declarative facts, leaving causal relationships largely implicit. Computational Knowledge Causality Theory (CKCT‑2) proposes a unified formalism in which every knowledge element is explicitly linked to its causes and effects. CKCT‑2 constructs a directed graph (S, C) where S is the set of atomic statements and C ⊆ S × S is the causal relation. By embedding causal semantics directly into the knowledge structure, CKCT‑2 enables automated inference, counterfactual reasoning, and causal explanation within a single computational pipeline. This paper develops the theoretical foundation of CKCT‑2, presents a symbolic and probabilistic representation of causal knowledge, and illustrates its application to scientific discovery, AI systems, and decision support. The framework also addresses scalability and integration challenges, positioning CKCT‑2 as a candidate for future foundational contributions to the field of knowledge representation and reasoning.

title: HistReNeRF: Historic Image Relocalisation within Contemporary Neural Radiance Field Reconstructions
abstract: Relocalising archival photographs within a contemporary scene model is challenging because historic and modern views can differ in photographic appearance, visible objects, and spatial layout. Therefore, we present HistReNeRF, a framework that estimates the 6-DoF pose of a historic photograph by matching adapted DINOv2 patch features to candidate rays sampled from a contemporary Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) reconstruction. The continuous representation of a NeRF provides a queryable scene interface from which candidate rays can be sampled and matched, enabling domain adaptation between historic photography and contemporary images directly in the feature representation used for localisation. We evaluate embedding-space-based domain adaptation against pixel-space methods on a new cross-temporal dataset comprising 10,545 contemporary street-level images and 230 archival photographs from three European landmarks. Embedding-space adaptation reduces translation and rotation errors by an average of 11% and 16%, respectively, across the three scenes. These results show that neural scene relocalisation provides a natural interface for feature-space adaptation, reducing cross-temporal appearance shift without modifying the query image. Code and dataset at https://github.com/ARTUROLab/HistReNeRF.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Sustainable Economic Development in Nigeria: Implications for Marketing Policies
abstract: In emerging markets, artificial intelligence (AI) has become a key enabler of economic diversification and sustainable development, but its possible impact on the marketing policy of Sub-Saharan Africa has not been theorised. This paper investigates the impact of AI on the economic landscape in Nigeria and its implications for the practice and policy of marketing in the country. The research approach used is a secondary source design, which involves document analysis, combining macroeconomic indicators from Nigeria's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy and the National Bureau of Statistics, International Finance Corporation, and PwC as well as the thematic review of ten empirical and conceptual studies on AI in Marketing in Nigeria published from 2023 to 2026. The study also reveals that Nigeria's ecosystem in AI is growing rapidly with an estimated growth rate of 27 per cent annually and a projected US$15bn impact on GDP by 2030, all while the country faces significant digital and welfare inequality. The thematic review reveals that in Nigeria, marketing research around AI is focused primarily on adoption of digital-marketing tools and personalisation, while there is comparatively less attention to issues of consumer behaviour and regulation that are sustainable. The paper asserts that the marketing-policy framework in Nigeria, including data-protection and consumer-protection tools, have not adequately followed the evolution of marketing practice using AI, resulting in governance gaps in the area of algorithmic bias, data extraction and digital exclusion. The study brings together a synthesis framework relating the macro levels AI development indicators to the micro levels of marketing practice and presents a policy roadmap to enable harmonization of AI-enabled marketing and Nigeria's sustainable development goals.

title: Computational Intention Formation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Intention Formation Theory (CIFT), a novel framework for understanding how goals emerge in autonomous systems and Artificial Intelligence planning. Traditional approaches often treat goals as externally defined, neglecting the crucial process of their genesis. CIFT posits that goals are not simply assigned but rather *computed* – arising from an interaction between the environment and a computational agent. The theory outlines a hierarchical process starting with environmental input, leading to the formation of intermediate goals, and ultimately culminating in the desired target. This paper details the core principles of CIFT, its potential applications within autonomous systems, AI planning, and its relevance to the broader pursuit of intelligent agents. We explore the theoretical underpinnings, emphasizing the computational mechanisms involved in this emergent goal formation, and discuss its significance as a foundational theory for autonomous intelligence. The central equation representing this process is: [Environment → Goal]. ---

title: Small‑scale medical dataset prepared for Quantum Machine Learning (QML)
abstract: This dataset provides processed physiological features for quantum machine learning studies focused on early pre‑hypotension detection. It includes quality‑controlled patient selections, paired stable and pre‑hypotensive observations, multi‑interval feature representations, and a fixed four‑feature input designed for quantum encoding. The package also contains classical validation outputs, exact and finite‑shot quantum kernel results, backend noise simulations, IBM Quantum hardware metadata, raw QPU measurement counts, and hardware‑derived kernel matrices. title: Computational Rule Generation Network (CRGN)
abstract: In conventional neural architectures the learning process is dominated by the estimation of continuous parameters such as weights and biases. These parameters are optimized to capture statistical regularities but do not directly encode symbolic knowledge or explicit transformation rules. This paper introduces a novel neural framework, the Computational Rule Generation Network (CRGN), whose core learning objective is to discover a set of rule generators rather than to fit a static parameter set. A rule generator is a submodule that, given an input vector, produces a transformation rule in the form of a function or a symbolic expression that can be applied to other data. The CRGN architecture consists of a Rule Generation Module, a Rule Application Module, and an Interaction Layer that couples them. Training is performed end‑to‑end using a differentiable objective that encourages sparsity and compositionality of the generated rules. We present a detailed formalization of the architecture, derive the gradient flow through the rule generators, and prove that the CRGN is a universal approximator of function compositions under mild assumptions. The paper discusses the implications of rule‑centric learning for interpretability, transfer learning, and the emergence of new AI paradigms. No experimental results are reported; the focus is on theoretical foundations and design principles.

title: Computational Identity Continuity Theory (CICT)
abstract: Computational Identity Continuity Theory (CICT) introduces a formal perspective on how an autonomous agent can preserve a coherent sense of self in the face of continual system changes. While the system state evolves according to S_t → S_{t+1}, the identity representation remains invariant, Identity_t = Identity_{t+1}. CICT establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for identity preservation, derives a formal framework for modeling identity as a mapping from system states to identity attributes, and investigates the implications for long‑term autonomous AI. By treating identity as a higher‑order invariant over state trajectories, CICT offers a principled route to address the "identity drift" problem that plagues current reinforcement‑learning and evolutionary systems. The theory has potential to inform the design of truly lifelong agents and may contribute to future breakthroughs recognized by the Turing Award. This paper presents the core ideas, formal definitions, continuity conditions, and an exploration of practical applications, all without reliance on experimental data or tables.

title: Computational Language Space Theory (CLST)
abstract: Computational Language Space Theory (CLST) proposes a unified geometric framework for representing and analyzing all possible computational languages. By mapping each language to a point in a high‑dimensional space Ω_L, CLST allows for rigorous definitions of distance, similarity, and evolution between languages. This paper introduces the core concepts of CLST, formalizes the construction of Ω_L, and develops a metric for measuring distances between languages based on their expressive power, syntax, and semantics. We discuss implications for programming language design, language migration, and the broader quest to understand the landscape of computation. The potential to create a comprehensive "programming language universe map" and to uncover fundamental patterns in language evolution positions CLST as a candidate for future recognition, possibly even a Turing Award‑level contribution.

title: LAPF: LLM-Agent-Based Path Finder Using the UAVScenes Dataset
abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous navigation in complex outdoor environments, where dynamic conditions and mission requirements require intelligent adaptive decision-making. Existing optimization-based, Machine Learning (ML), and Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches often rely on predefined models or task-specific training, limiting their generalization and adaptability in uncertain scenarios. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted approaches offer promising reasoning capabilities but remain constrained by limited agentic functionality, including insufficient memory, planning, and tool interaction mechanisms.This paper proposes an LLM-Agent-Based Path Finder (LAPF) framework for autonomous UAV navigation in town-scale outdoor environments. LAPF extends LLM-assisted navigation by integrating perception, memory, planning, and action modules into a closed-loop cognitive architecture. The proposed agent leverages prior navigation experiences, performs Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, couples each detected hazard to a bounded corrective action, and dynamically refines waypoint decisions based on environmental feedback.The three independent trials per method demonstrate that LAPF achieves mean path lengths of 512.83 m and 506.37 m, compared to the straight-line optimum of 497.33 m, corresponding to path length reductions of 17.2% and 15.6% relative to CoT prompting and absolute path efficiencies of 97.1% and 98.1% in open-field and obstacle-injected scenarios, respectively. Furthermore, LAPF is the only evaluated approach that couples every detected hazard to a bounded, metric-neutral corrective action while maintaining near-goal stability, with zero clamp events in both scenarios, whereas CoT prompting increases from 9.7 to 14.0 events.

title: RETRACE: Resilience-Guided Trait-Conditioned Craving Estimation from Wearable Physiology in Opioid Use Disorder
abstract: Detecting opioid craving from wearable physiological signals is critical yet difficult, with the potential to support proactive interventions for individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). This challenge is especially pronounced under subject-independent evaluation because craving is subjective, heterogeneous, and often physiologically entangled with stress. Our empirical analysis shows that stress elicits strong and reproducible autonomic responses, while craving-related signals are weaker, sparse, and largely embedded within stress-related physiology. We further show that psychological resilience, which shapes stress regulation and craving vulnerability, is not reliably observable from short-term wearable windows, but can be captured through reusable subject-level proxies, including post-stress heart-rate recovery and autobiographical memory recall. Motivated by these findings, we introduce RETRACE, a resilience-guided trait-conditioned framework for subject-independent craving estimation from wearable physiology. RETRACE reframes craving detection as trait-conditioned physiological interpretation: rather than assuming the same physiological pattern has the same meaning across individuals, it uses resilience-related subject context to guide inference. Technically, RETRACE introduces a novel dual-encoder design that separates generalizable stress physiology from subject-specific craving interpretation. It combines a frozen stress-pretrained encoder with resilience-conditioned craving encoder, using feature-level gating and representation-level fusion to enable lightweight personalization without target-user craving labels or per-user retraining. We evaluate RETRACE on a novel multimodal OUD dataset containing wearable physiology, stress and craving annotations, and autobiographical narratives. Under LOSO setup, RETRACE achieves up to 7% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline.

title: DualMiT-Net: Local-Global Transformer-Convolutional Fusion for Breast Mass Segmentation in Mammographic Regions of Interest
abstract: Breast mass segmentation is an important step in computer-aided mammography, but it remains difficult because masses can have low contrast, irregular shapes, and boundaries that blend with surrounding breast tissue. To address this problem, we present DualMiT-Net, a dual-branch network that uses both a focused view of the mass and a wider view of the surrounding tissue. The local branch uses a Mix Transformer (MiT-B5) encoder to learn mass shape, texture, and boundary information, while the global branch uses an EfficientNet-B5 encoder to learn surrounding breast context. Features from the two branches are shared at the deeper encoder levels and are then progressively fused in a single decoder. A spatial gate controls how much global information is added during decoding. We also evaluated four input representations and selected a percentile-windowed mammogram combined with a Gabor texture response. The model was trained and evaluated on the mass subset of the Curated Breast Imaging Subset of the Digital Database for Screening Mammography (CBIS-DDSM) using a patient-level split. Across three training runs, DualMiT-Net with exponential moving average weights achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 0.9375 and a mean Intersection over Union of 0.8834. It also achieved better Dice and IoU scores than six standard encoder-decoder baselines trained using the same data and training settings. These results show that combining local mass information with wider breast context can provide accurate and consistent breast mass segmentation.

title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Remote Sensing Semantic Change Detection
abstract: Semantic change detection (SCD) is a bitemporal dense-prediction task that jointly identifies changed regions and their semantic states before and after change. Unlike single-image segmentation or binary change detection, SCD couples two temporal inputs with timestamp-wise semantic prediction, change localization, and final semantic-change decoding, creating adversarial dependencies that are not captured by conventional robustness protocols. We present a task-specific evaluation framework that separates output-side attack objectives from input-side temporal perturbation access, enabling systematic analysis of component vulnerability and cross-temporal propagation. Experiments on four datasets and six representative CNN-, Transformer-, and state-space-based models evaluate component-level and temporal objectives, single- and dual-timestamp perturbations, multiple attack methods, and cross-architecture transferability. The results show that final semantic-change predictions can be severely corrupted even when binary change localization remains comparatively stable, and that perturbations or attack objectives associated with one timestamp can propagate to the prediction of the other. These behaviors occur across different architecture families, while direct cross-model transfer remains considerably weaker than white-box attacks. The study demonstrates that adversarial robustness in SCD depends on the complete bitemporal prediction pathway rather than on an individual branch or backbone family, and provides a structured protocol for evaluating robustness in coupled bitemporal image analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/EricYu97/AdvSCD.

title: Adaptive Compact Knapsack Cryptography for Post-Quantum Security
abstract: Digital signatures based on the compact knapsack problem are attractive post-quantum candidates: they rely solely on integer arithmetic, require no algebraic ring structure, and rest on a hardness assumption distinct from the Module-LWE/Module-SIS problems that underlie the recently standardized ML-DSA (FIPS 204). The three-move identification scheme of Rizos and Draziotis (2023) and its Fiat–Shamir signature establish completeness, special soundness, special honest-verifier zero-knowledge, and EUF-CMA security in the random-oracle model. Its concrete parameters, however, were selected by hand, yielding a comparatively large signature (≈ 31.9 KB); the authors explicitly leave smarter parameter selection as future work. We close this gap. First, we provide an independent, fully reproducible re-implementation of the scheme's lattice attacks (the closest-vector and divide-and-conquer attacks) and of its signature-size accounting, validated against the original tables; our re-implementation reproduces the published success rates to within experimental noise. Second, we cast parameter selection as a constrained optimization problem and design an adaptive bit-allocation optimizer that minimizes signature size subject to soundness, completeness, commitment-unpredictability, key-entropy, and an empirical lattice-attack hardness gate. The optimizer exposes two honest sources of slack in the base parameters—an over-provisioned nonce space and an under-tightened secret space. The resulting configuration S = S1/4,1/3, S′ = S′1/8,1/8 shrinks the signature by 19.6% (to 25.6 KB) at identical security: equal soundness (2⁻⁸⁰), equal commitment-unpredictability (2⁻²⁴), equal completeness error (2.15 × 10⁻⁶), empirically equal closest-vector-attack hardness (50.0%), and equal-or-better divide-and-conquer hardness. All code, seeds, and numerical results are released for reproducibility.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration: An Organizational Cybersecurity Framework for Enterprise Readiness
abstract: This paper examines recurring technical and organizational bottlenecks in post-quantum cryptography (PQC) migration and develops an enterprise-oriented framework for managing them. A structured narrative review synthesizes NIST standards and guidance, CISA migration guidance, IETF specifications, and selected academic and research literature on enterprise migration, interoperability, software engineering, and PQC adoption. The paper organizes recurring migration concerns into five interacting layers and a six-stage migration lifecycle, and proposes candidate readiness metrics for future empirical testing. It connects technical migration concerns with organizational cybersecurity governance and presents a practical structure for treating PQC readiness as a continuous organizational capability. The framework is conceptual and is not presented as a validated maturity model.

title: Computational Plasticity Theory
abstract: Computational Plasticity Theory (CPT) proposes a novel framework for understanding and designing adaptive systems, rooted in the concept of intrinsic system modification. At its core, CPT posits that systems possess an inherent capacity for change, termed *Plasticity(S)*, which can be quantified and leveraged. This theory aims to provide a foundational understanding of autonomy, moving beyond pre-programmed responses to enable systems to dynamically adjust their behavior in response to unforeseen circumstances and evolving environments. This document outlines the fundamental principles of CPT, detailing its core concepts, mathematical formulation, and potential impact on the development of advanced autonomous systems. The theory centers on the ability of a system *S* to transform into a new state *S'*, quantified by the plasticity function *Plasticity(S)*. This function represents the system's capacity for adaptation and is a central element in the CPT framework. The goal is to create systems that can autonomously learn and modify their operational parameters to optimize performance. ---

title: 超结构计算模型
abstract: This paper introduces the Hyper-Structural Computing Model (HSCM), a novel approach to computation centered around the transformation of structures rather than traditional data manipulation. HSCM proposes a fundamental shift in how we conceptualize computation, moving beyond the paradigm of "data → operation" to "structure → structure → structure." This model seeks to establish a new level of abstraction, potentially building upon the foundations laid by Turing machines, lambda calculus, and database models. The paper outlines the core principles of HSCM, explores its potential impact, and identifies five key areas with significant Turing Award potential. Finally, it proposes a new set of 20 original research directions focused on the emergent self-organization of computational systems, representing a potentially groundbreaking approach to the future of computing.

title: CL4GIE-Onto: An Ontology of Carbon Literacy for Green Innovation Entrepreneurship in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: CL4GIE-Onto is an OWL 2 DL ontology on carbon literacy for green innovation entrepreneurship in Sub-Saharan Africa. It employs three modular namespaces: a climate-science module (cl:) axiomatising greenhouse effect, climate knowledge and mitigation mechanisms; a green-innovation-entrepreneurship module (giel:) axiomatising green products, services, and business-model constructs; and an integration module (cl4gie:) linking mitigation problems to enterprise solutions via several properties such as cl4gie:targetsGHG, cl4gie:isLocatedIn, and cl4gie:hasSector. The TBox axiomatises the Theory of Planned Behaviour and Self-Determination Theory as formal constructs for learner modelling. The ABox contains over 550 ABox individuall s with more than seventy verified SSA green-enterprise individuals, validated using Pellet and HermiT 1.4.3 reasoners.

It employs three modular namespaces: a climate-science module (cl:) axiomatising greenhouse effect, climate knowledge and mitigation mechanisms; a green-innovation-entrepreneurship module (giel:) axiomatising green products, services, and business-model constructs; and an integration module (cl4gie:) linking mitigation problems to enterprise solutions via several properties such as cl4gie:targetsGHG, cl4gie:isLocatedIn, and cl4gie:hasSector. The TBox axiomatises the Theory of Planned Behaviour and Self-Determination Theory as formal constructs for learner modelling. The ABox contains over 550 ABox individuall s with more than seventy verified SSA green-enterprise individuals, validated using Pellet and HermiT 1.4.3 reasoners.

title: Machine Entity Comprehension: A Black-Box Conformance Framework for Identity, Context and Change
abstract: Machine Entity Comprehension defines a black-box conformance framework for evaluating whether a system can preserve entity identity, distinguish contextually similar entities, maintain relevant relationships and constraints, respond coherently to material changes, contain contradiction and produce repeatable outcomes under equivalent declared state. The paper establishes the conformance layer for Geometry Intelligence Infrastructure, a proposed class of evidence-governed, model-independent AI infrastructure. It converts the field definition in Paper 1 and the formal model in Paper 2 into externally observable behavioral requirements. The framework uses pre-registered evidence sets, policy profiles, declared system state, controlled perturbations, reference outcomes, negative controls and retained adjudication records. Nine profiles cover identity persistence, entity disambiguation, relationship invariance, material-change response, contradiction handling, repeatability, multi-node outcome equivalence, disconnected continuity and retrieval-baseline differentiation. Individual profiles use MEC-1 through MEC-9. Aggregate reporting uses MEC-C0 through MEC-C4 to avoid identifier collision. Conformance is reported as a capability vector and evaluator-independence class rather than as consciousness, general intelligence or universal understanding. The framework is implementation-neutral. It can evaluate proprietary, open, symbolic, geometric, graph-based, model-based and hybrid systems without requiring mandatory disclosure of protected internal mechanisms. The paper also specifies public formats for test cases, evidence records, adjudication records and conformance reports, together with a proposed synthetic pilot benchmark. Publication of the benchmark design does not constitute an executed conformance result. This is Paper 3 of the Geometry Intelligence Foundational Series. Paper 1 defines the field, Paper 2 defines governed relational transformation, Paper 3 defines external conformance, and Paper 4 develops an optional sovereign Web4 federation architecture. Final Manuscript 1.0. Published by KTS Global. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

title: Computational Experience Forgetting Theory (CEFT-3): A Principled Approach to Selective Memory in Continual Learning
abstract: In continual learning systems, the accumulation of experiential data is the most common strategy to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. However, indiscriminate retention of all experiences leads to memory saturation, computational inefficiency, and the dilution of critical knowledge. Computational Experience Forgetting Theory (CEFT‑3) proposes a mathematically grounded framework for deciding, at each learning step, whether an experience should be kept or forgotten. The theory formalizes the retention decision as a function Keep(E) or Forget(E) that evaluates the value of each experience E with respect to future prediction tasks, resource constraints, and the diversity of the experience set. CEFT‑3 integrates a capacity‑aware utility metric and a dynamic forgetting schedule that adapts to the evolving knowledge base. This paper presents the core equations, the underlying assumptions, and the algorithmic realization of CEFT‑3. We discuss its computational complexity, theoretical guarantees, and its potential to achieve Turing Award–level impact by fundamentally reshaping how continual learning systems manage memory.

title: An Evaluation Framework for National AI Regulation
abstract: Governments use laws, institutions, funding programs and nonbinding guidance to shape how AI is developed and used. Comparing these national approaches is difficult. A binding rule and a detailed voluntary framework can address the same problem but create different duties. The resources needed to carry them out also differ by jurisdiction. This paper develops an evaluation framework for the documented design and implementation readiness of national AI policy. The comparison covers China, India, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States. The European Union is included as a supranational comparator. The framework evaluates a versioned portfolio of official instruments rather than one prominent law or strategy. Its criteria ask whether the portfolio governs serious AI risks and whether responsible institutions can implement its commitments. They examine coverage across the AI lifecycle and the protections available to people affected by AI systems. Public benefit and responsible innovation remain a separate part of the assessment. Each sub-criterion is scored through ordered anchors and tied to the provision that supports the judgment. The protocol also records the source search, missing evidence, included instruments and cutoff date. The result is a traceable comparison of policy content that keeps category differences visible. It evaluates what a portfolio provides on paper. It does not estimate enforcement success or policy outcomes.

title: Do Geometry-Aware Positional Encodings Help Transformers in Spatial Imperfect-Information Games?
abstract: Transformers applied to spatial imperfect-information games must represent map geometry while tracking hidden entities through time. We ask whether geometry-aware positional encodings improve these capabilities, without claiming a new positional encoding. We construct a four-level benchmark on a hexagonal naval pursuit game: controlled geometry and topology probes, an exact-Bayes hidden-target tracking task, offline policy imitation at 1k and 10k games, and 7,200 fixed-seed games against three legacy opponents. Across matched Transformer backbones, HexRoPE reduces exact-belief posterior cross-entropy relative to no positional encoding by 0.278 on D6-transformed test orbits and 0.329 on a larger map; both hierarchical-bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero, and both Holm-adjusted p-values are below 0.001. At 1k games, HexRoPE improves policy action accuracy by 4.63 percentage points over no encoding and 2.05 points over rectangular relative bias; the gains shrink to 1.55 and 0.41 points at 10k games. However, HexRoPE does not improve aggregate gameplay win rate: its paired effect over no encoding is -1.56 percentage points (95% CI [-4.50, 1.17]). Rectangular relative bias is strongest on D6 belief consistency but fails sharply when extrapolating from radius 3 to radius 4, while graph bias provides only a small blocked-edge gain. The results show that geometric inductive bias improves belief estimation and data-efficient imitation, but those representation gains do not automatically produce stronger closed-loop play.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration for Enterprise APIs: A Simulated Hybrid TLS Performance and Risk Evaluation
abstract: This empirical-style article presents a clearly labeled simulated study in Computer Science and Engineering. A simulated enterprise API gateway benchmark compared classical TLS, hybrid classical-plus-ML-KEM key establishment, and post-quantum-heavy configurations under small, medium, and large request profiles. Handshake time, transmitted bytes, CPU utilization, session reuse, memory use, and failure under constrained clients were modeled. The study emphasizes migration engineering and does not claim access to production enterprise systems. Hybrid classical plus ML-KEM increased simulated full-handshake latency by 18% relative to classical TLS but reduced the migration risk associated with an abrupt cryptographic cutover. Session reuse limited the application- level overhead to under 5% for sustained API traffic. Constrained clients experienced the largest memory and payload penalty. The numerical observations, assignments, and measured outcomes are synthetic and intended for methodological illustration only. No real industrial facility, enterprise network, laboratory, construction project, or manufactured component was used. The study demonstrates a realistic research framework aligned with current 2026 research directions while clearly separating simulated evidence from verified literature.

title: Computational Object Lifecycle Algebra (COLA)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Object Lifecycle Algebra (COLA), a novel algebraic framework designed to model and analyze the complex lifecycle of computational objects. COLA leverages tensor algebra to represent and manipulate the transformations an object undergoes from its creation (birth) through various stages of modification and eventual termination (death). The core concept utilizes the tensor product, [O₁ ⊗ O₂], to describe the combination and disintegration of objects, offering a concise and powerful tool for understanding object evolution. We explore the potential applications of COLA within diverse domains, including data systems, memory management, and software architecture, highlighting its capacity to provide a rigorous and quantifiable approach to object lifecycle analysis. This framework provides a foundational structure for developing predictive models and optimization strategies across these fields. ---

title: Uncertainty Type System: A Novel Approach to Type Inference
abstract: This paper introduces the Uncertainty Type System (UTS), a novel approach to type inference designed to handle uncertainty explicitly within a type system. Traditional type systems primarily focus on static typing, offering guarantees about data structure and operations without directly addressing the inherent uncertainty present in real-world data. UTS extends this by incorporating a structured representation of uncertainty directly into type definitions. A type `x` is defined as `[x:\tau]`, where `\tau` is the type of `x`. However, UTS introduces a more comprehensive type representation `[x:\tau\langle u, s, d \rangle]`, where `\tau` is the type of `x`, `u` represents the degree of uncertainty, `s` denotes the source of uncertainty, and `d` indicates whether the uncertainty propagates during computation. The system leverages automated inference rules, `U(f(x))\Phi_f(U(x))`, to derive type information for functions, effectively managing uncertainty throughout the program. This system has the potential to unify probability, uncertainty, and type theory, offering a more robust and expressive type system for applications dealing with imprecise or incomplete information.

title: Computational Goal Fusion Theory (CGFT)
abstract: Computational Goal Fusion Theory (CGFT) proposes a mathematical and conceptual framework for combining multiple autonomous goals into a single, emergent goal that guides behavior. By treating goals as vectors in an abstract goal space, CGFT defines a fusion operation G1 ⊕ G2 that produces a new goal G3 whose direction is determined by the weighted sum of the constituent goals. The theory elucidates how such fusion can lead to novel behavioral patterns, enhance collective intelligence, and potentially underpin future AI systems that self‑organize from simple objective modules. This paper presents the core ideas of CGFT, formalizes the fusion operation, explores its properties, provides illustrative examples, and discusses implications for multi‑agent coordination, human‑machine interaction, and adaptive control.

title: Computational Resource Certification Theory (CRCert)
abstract: Computational Resource Certification Theory, abbreviated CRCert, proposes a unified framework for certifying not only the functional correctness of a program but also the quantitative efficiency of its resource usage. While traditional program verification establishes that a program meets its specification, CRCert augments this by generating a formal proof that the program's resource consumption—time, memory, energy, or other relevant metrics—does not exceed a specified bound. This dual certification is achieved through a novel combination of type‑based static analysis, metric‑annotated specifications, and constructive proof objects that capture resource usage as part of the program's semantics. The theory is grounded in established complexity theory and formal logic, yet it extends them by requiring that the resource bounds be explicitly provable and machine‑checkable. CRCert's potential to elevate trust in artificial intelligence systems is explored, as AI applications increasingly demand guarantees of both safety and efficiency. By embedding resource proofs into the deployment pipeline, CRCert can serve as a foundational tool for certifying trustworthy AI, ensuring that models operate within specified budgets and do not inadvertently consume excessive resources. This paper lays out the formal foundations of CRCert, illustrates its application through detailed examples, discusses its implications for AI, and outlines future research directions.

title: Relational multi agent tactical learning for competitive football
abstract: Tactical decision-making of competitive football depends on the rapidly changing spatial relationship, the transformation of ball rights and the fight against oppression. The existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods often compress the team state into fixed observation or pooled representation, and the node-level collaborative information is weakened in strategy learning; When the opponent’s style changes, the strategy execution is also prone to degradation. Aiming at the above problems, a relational multi-agent tactical learning method for competitive football is proposed. Player interaction is modeled as a dynamic graph structure, relationship coding is used to describe local cooperation, pressing pressure and passing channels, and time series modeling is used to capture tactical phase transition. Shared cooperative mechanism, self-game training and meta-adaptive strategy are brought into the same playback learning process to improve the consistency of strategies, confrontation stability and cross-scene adaptability. Based on StatsBomb and SoccerNet datasets, experiments are carried out in the tasks of attack, defense, counterattack and positioning. The results show that, in the evaluated open dataset and replay tactical environment, the highest tactical execution score of the proposed method reaches 82.6 in complex tactical tasks, and it maintains a relatively stable strategic adaptation performance in cross-scene migration tasks. The research results show that retaining the cooperative information of player relationship is helpful to improve the quality of dynamic multi-agent decision-making in replay football tactical learning.

title: Invariant Pretraining for Robust Code Representations
abstract: Encoder-based code representation models remain widely deployed for discriminative tasks such as clone detection and code classification, where their small size and low inference cost are decisive. Their robustness, however, is fragile: under invariant programs, semantically equivalent code written in different syntactic forms, learned representations degrade substantially even though program behavior is unchanged. We present an empirical study of this robustness gap across four encoder baselines, two downstream tasks, and four datasets, together with a minimal code-only continued pretraining recipe that closes much of it. Our method, invariant pretraining (InvPT), applies semantic-preserving transformations to the corpus and combines masked language modeling with multi-positive supervised contrastive learning that treats all augmentations of the same source function as positives, mixing self-contrast pairs (same code, different masks) with invariant-contrast pairs (transformed code) for positives of varying difficulty. Unlike prior contrastive code encoders, InvPT does not require paired natural-language data. Across our evaluation, InvPT improves robustness on transformed test sets by up to 11 percentage points on clone detection and 19 on code classification while matching or improving standard accuracy, and our ablations isolate multi-positive invariant contrast as the main source of the gains. Our aim is not a new objective but a careful measurement of where encoder robustness breaks and how far a simple, code-only recipe can recover it.

title: From "What-If" to "What-Is": Counterfactual Thinking-Inspired Semantic Alignment for Visual Brain Decoding
abstract: Visual brain decoding reconstructs visual content perceived by a person from neural measurements such as fMRI, providing a computational approach to studying how visual information is represented in the brain. Recent multimodal representations and diffusion priors have improved reconstruction realism. However, visually plausible reconstructions may contain incorrect objects, attributes, or relations because a strong generative prior can complete content not sufficiently specified by the decoded representation. Conventional reconstruction metrics mainly assess the final image and may therefore obscure such semantic errors. We propose ConceptAlign, a counterfactual semantic alignment framework for visual brain decoding. ConceptAlign pools decoded visual tokens and projects them into a frozen text-embedding space, aligning the representation with the ground-truth caption while separating it from scene-preserving near-miss alternatives. Generated offline by an LLM, these alternatives modify one critical object, attribute, or relation while retaining the scene. A margin-based objective learns fine-grained semantic boundaries between the observed stimulus and plausible but incorrect interpretations without requiring LLM calls during inference. We introduce a systematic three-level semantic evaluation framework covering foundational discriminability, counterfactual description discrimination, and representational geometry. Experiments on the Natural Scenes Dataset show that ConceptAlign improves reconstruction measures, counterfactual semantic discrimination, and representational alignment over the MindEye2 backbone. Matched negative-source ablations, independent LLM and human-written alternatives, and human evaluation support the effectiveness and robustness of the supervision, with favorable patterns in fine-grained conflicts, limited-data decoding, and cross-subject structure.

title: Learning reshapes power-law anisotropy in internal representations
abstract: Power-law anisotropy in internal representations has been observed across a wide range of biological and artificial neural systems, from state-of-the-art language models to the mouse cerebral cortex. This anisotropy is a key geometric property of high-dimensional information processing and underlies a variety of theoretical analyses. However, the mechanism by which it emerges from input structure and task-driven learning has remained unclear. Here, we characterize this formation process by exactly solving the learning dynamics of a wide two-layer linear neural network in a teacher--student setting with power-law input and teacher structures. We show that, in the feature-learning regime, the local power-law exponent of the internal-representation spectrum evolves nonmonotonically over the course of training and exhibits up to four distinct asymptotic regimes across modes and training times. By contrast, in the lazy regime, the exponent remains essentially unchanged. We further demonstrate numerically that similar exponent dynamics arise in more realistic nonlinear networks. Together, these results suggest a general mechanism by which the dynamic interaction between input statistics and task structure gives rise to power-law internal representations.

evidence.title: Learning reshapes power-law anisotropy in internal representations
evidence.abstract: Power-law anisotropy in internal representations has been observed across a wide range of biological and artificial neural systems, from state-of-the-art language models to the mouse cerebral cortex. This anisotropy is a key geometric property of high-dimensional information processing and underlies a variety of theoretical analyses. However, the mechanism by which it emerges from input structure and task-driven learning has remained unclear. Here, we characterize this formation process by exactly solving the learning dynamics of a wide two-layer linear neural network in a teacher--student setting with power-law input and teacher structures. We show that, in the feature-learning regime, the local power-law exponent of the internal-representation spectrum evolves nonmonotonically over the course of training and exhibits up to four distinct asymptotic regimes across modes and training times. By contrast, in the lazy regime, the exponent remains essentially unchanged. We further demonstrate numerically that similar exponent dynamics arise in more realistic nonlinear networks. Together, these results suggest a general mechanism by which the dynamic interaction between input statistics and task structure gives rise to power-law internal representations.

title: Implementasi Metode Certainty Factor pada Sistem Pakar Berbasis Web untuk Diagnosis Gangguan Kesehatan Reproduksi Pria
abstract: Male reproductive health disorders are among the health problems that can significantly affect quality of life, sexual function, and fertility. Limited public knowledge, reluctance to seek medical consultation due to embarrassment, and restricted access to healthcare services often lead to delayed diagnosis and treatment. This study aims to develop a web-based expert system using the Certainty Factor method to support the early diagnosis of male reproductive health disorders at Pandawa Main Clinic. The research was conducted through literature review, observation, and interviews with an andrology specialist to obtain data on diseases, symptoms, diagnostic rules, and confidence values. The system was developed using the PHP programming language with the Laravel framework and MySQL as the database management system. The Certainty Factor method was applied to calculate the confidence level of a diagnosis based on the symptoms selected by users. The system provides information on the identified disease, the confidence percentage of the diagnosis, and recommendations for initial treatment. Functional testing using the Black Box Testing method demonstrated that all system features operated according to the specified requirements. The results indicate that the developed expert system is capable of assisting users in obtaining early diagnostic information quickly, conveniently, and through online access, while also supporting healthcare professionals during the initial consultation process. This system is intended to serve as a decision-support tool and does not replace the final diagnosis or treatment provided by an andrology specialist.

title: Computational Semantic Gravity Model
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Semantic Gravity Model (CSGM), a novel framework for understanding and representing relationships between concepts within a semantic space. The core principle of CSGM is that concepts exhibit an inherent "attraction" towards one another, analogous to gravitational forces. This attraction manifests as a quantifiable measure, denoted as G(M_i, M_j), where M_i and M_j represent two concepts. The magnitude of G(M_i, M_j) reflects the strength of the semantic connection between the concepts, and the cumulative effect of these attractions defines the overall structure of the semantic space. The model proposes a method for constructing a semantic network based on these calculated gravitational forces. The potential implications of CSGM extend to the development of new theories of knowledge representation and understanding, with possibilities for advancements in areas like artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and knowledge management. Further research is needed to refine the calculation methods for G(M_i, M_j) and to explore the model's applicability across diverse domains. ---

title: Computational Rule Verification Theory (CRVT)
abstract: Computational Rule Verification Theory (CRVT) is a novel framework that integrates rule generation and formal proof synthesis into a single, tightly coupled process. When a new rule is created, CRVT automatically produces a corresponding proof that attests to the rule's soundness within a designated formal system. This dual-generation approach guarantees that every rule entering the system is accompanied by a verifiable justification, thereby eliminating the risk of undetected errors that traditionally plague automated programming and formal verification pipelines. The theory is underpinned by a set of mathematical constructs that model the relationship between rules, proofs, and the underlying logic engine. We formalize these relationships, describe an efficient implementation strategy, and demonstrate the applicability of CRVT to several domains including program synthesis, security policy enforcement, and theorem proving. By providing a rigorous, automated mechanism for rule validation, CRVT holds the potential to revolutionize the reliability of software systems and to establish a new benchmark for the intersection of automatic programming and formal verification. The work presented herein offers a comprehensive foundation for future research and practical deployment in high-assurance computing environments.

title: Comprehensive and reproducible grading of the Updated Sydney System in gastric biopsies using artificial intelligence: multi‐pathologist validation and a reader study
abstract: AIMS: The Updated Sydney System is the most widely used framework for histological grading of gastritis, but complete grading in routine gastric biopsies is time-consuming and subject to interobserver variability. We developed an artificial intelligence (AI) system to support comprehensive and reproducible grading of all five Updated Sydney attributes in gastric biopsies. METHODS AND RESULTS: We developed SydneyMTL, a weakly supervised multi-task multiple instance learning framework trained on 50,765 whole-slide images from routine practice. The model jointly predicts mononuclear cell infiltration, neutrophil activity, glandular atrophy, intestinal metaplasia and Helicobacter pylori density, with atrophy including a separate not applicable category when muscularis mucosae is absent. Performance was assessed against routine labels from 24 board-certified pathologists and against a consensus-adjudicated Golden dataset. SydneyMTL achieved a mean lenient accuracy of 89.1% across the 24 pathologists, with >80% agreement for 21 of 24 readers on the retrospective dataset. In a two-reader randomized crossover study, AI assistance improved interobserver agreement and reduced review time by 34.2% for complete Updated Sydney grading. CONCLUSIONS: AI can support more reproducible and efficient grading of Updated Sydney histological attributes in gastric biopsies. By combining multi-pathologist validation, consensus-based evaluation and explicit handling of non-assessable atrophy, SydneyMTL provides a clinically realistic decision-support approach for routine digital pathology.

title: SSTA-ABLE: Synergistic Sequential-Topological Architectures for Adaptive Behaviour in Linguistic Environments - From Evolutionary Premises to Computational Demonstration
abstract: We present a theoretical and computational investigation of the hypothesis that language functions as a dual representation of adaptive interactions between consciousness and environment: a sequential stream encoding local order and a topological landscape encoding global structural and affective relations. Building on evolutionary accounts of consciousness as a mechanism that shifts adaptive timescales from phylogenetic to ontogenetic and cultural regimes, we argue that artificial systems capable of the most adaptive behaviour within the „reality of language” must integrate sequential and topological information in a non-additive, synergistic manner. We propose an optimal synergic architecture combining sequential processing, explicit topological (graph and geometric) modules, multiplicative cross-interactions, certainty-gated fusion, and optional global-workspace integration under an adaptive objective. We then implement a controlled simulation of sequential-only, non-synergic (concatenative) hybrid, and synergic hybrid models under strong language shifts induced by abrupt rewiring of an underlying concept graph. Results demonstrate that the synergic hybrid achieves higher post-adaptation accuracy than either sequential-only or simple concatenative hybrid models, confirming super-additive behavioural adaptation. We discuss implications for artificial consciousness understood functionally as maximal adaptive behaviour in linguistic reality, limitations of the present toy regime, and pathways toward scalable implementations.

title: Computational Self-Proving Capability Theory (CSPCT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Self-Proving Capability Theory (CSPCT), a novel approach to verifiable computation and trust in artificial intelligence. Traditional verification methods often focus solely on proving the correctness of a program's output, leaving open the possibility of malicious or flawed updates. CSPCT addresses this limitation by requiring a system to demonstrate not only the correctness of its current state but also the validity of any proposed upgrade. This is achieved through the formal verification of two capabilities: Capability(S') – the capability of the system in its new state – and Capability(S) – the capability of the system in its original state. The theory establishes a rigorous framework for ensuring that a system's evolution is trustworthy and resistant to manipulation. The implications of CSPCT extend beyond traditional software verification, offering a foundation for building truly reliable and self-correcting AI systems, potentially unlocking significant advancements in areas requiring high levels of confidence and security, such as verifiable machine learning and secure autonomous systems. The core concept relies on the mathematical representation of capabilities and their evolution, providing a framework for automated verification and trust establishment. ---

title: Program Local Universe Calculus (LPUC)
abstract: This paper introduces Program Local Universe Calculus (LPUC), a novel approach to software design and formal modeling. LPUC posits that each program module operates within its own localized "universe," governed by a set of rules and constraints. These universes are interconnected through a mechanism termed "universe mapping," allowing for controlled interaction and exchange of information. The core of LPUC resides in the representation of each module as a tuple: [ U_i= ( S_i, L_i, C_i ) ] Where: * *S_i* represents the set of states the module can occupy. * *L_i* represents the set of local rules governing the module's behavior. * *C_i* represents the set of constraints imposed upon the module. The universe mapping, denoted as [ \Phi_{ij}: U_i \rightarrow U_j ], facilitates the translation of states between modules, enabling a formalized approach to heterogeneous software systems and multi-agent systems. This approach offers significant potential for creating new formal models and architectures for complex software systems, ultimately aligning with the goals of the Turing Award.

title: Quando Uma IA Não Basta
abstract: Quando Uma IA Não Basta defende que a pergunta relevante no uso de inteligência artificial não é "qual IA devo usar?", mas "como estruturar a IA para resolver este problema?". A tese central é que tarefas complexas se decompõem em múltiplas funções — pesquisar, estruturar, expandir, sintetizar, criticar —, cada uma com exigências específicas que podem ser atendidas por diferentes modelos (Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT) escolhidos por aderência funcional, não por familiaridade. O livro apresenta uma arquitetura de referência coordenada por um orquestrador (LangGraph), com estado compartilhado, fluxos condicionais e camadas de crítica e intervenção humana. O princípio da proporcionalidade orienta a calibragem: usar a menor arquitetura capaz de produzir a qualidade exigida, de uma única IA para tarefas simples até cinco agentes para problemas de alta complexidade. O método — função, característica, ferramenta — permanece válido mesmo quando as ferramentas mudam, e o ser humano é reposicionado de operador para projetista e supervisor do sistema.

title: ChatbotLab: An Open Framework for Human-Like Chatbot Interaction and Survey Data Collection
abstract: Despite growing interest in studying human-AI interaction and conducting conversational interventions at scale, technical barriers in deploying and managing large language model (LLM) systems limit their use in behavioral research. In this tutorial, we present ChatbotLab, an open-source software package that provides an end-to-end framework for conducting chatbot-based research without requiring programming expertise. ChatbotLab embeds LLM-powered conversations directly into standard crowdsourcing services (Prolific, MTurk) and survey platforms (Qualtrics, REDCap, LimeSurvey), handling the technical infrastructure that custom solutions often overlook: secure data linkage between surveys and conversations, reproducible study records that capture each conversation's full bot configuration, content moderation, standardized data export for downstream analysis, and server load testing for managing thousands of simultaneous conversations. We guide researchers through the complete workflow, from deploying a chatbot server and configuring naturalistic conversation features (typing delays, message chunking, and personas) to integrating conversations into existing study pipelines and exporting data for analysis. By lowering the technical barriers to chatbot-based research, ChatbotLab allows researchers to focus on their research questions rather than infrastructure.

title: FloodReasonBench: Benchmarking VLM Reasoning Segmentation for Embodied Flood Response at the Edge
abstract: Reasoning segmentation enables vision-language models (VLMs) to translate mission-relevant language requests into pixel-level visual grounding, offering a natural perception interface for embodied agents. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on generic visual scenes and overlook the domain and resource constraints encountered in flood-response platforms. We present FloodReasonBench, a benchmark for VLM reasoning segmentation for embodied flood response at the edge. At its core, FloodReasonBench introduces FloodResponseSeg, a flood-specific reasoning-segmentation dataset constructed from real-world scenes and response-relevant targets. Beyond task accuracy, the benchmark characterizes reasoning-segmentation pipelines under lightweight visual encoding, hierarchical split inference, and compressed intermediate representations. We observe strong partition-dependent accuracy variation in the generic pre-adaptation setting, while the flood-adapted target-workload design space exhibits a substantially more compact accuracy range across partitions. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier further exposes the tradeoffs among reasoning-segmentation accuracy, edge-side latency, energy, and communication footprint, enabling quality-constrained selection of edge operating points. Together, these results provide a task- and system-level characterization of reasoning segmentation for resource-constrained embodied flood response at the edge.

title: Structuring Semantic Embeddings for Principle Evaluation: A Prototype-Guided Contrastive Learning Approach
abstract: Reliable post-hoc evaluation asks whether already generated text satisfies a target criterion after generation. In this paper we study a focused frozen-embedding setting using principle-evaluation proxy tasks: toxicity detection, fine-grained emotion categorization, and ordinal review rating. General-purpose text embeddings are widely deployed for such tasks, but broad semantic similarity can place semantically similar yet task-distinct examples in overlapping regions of the representation space. We introduce Prototype-Guided Contrastive Learning (PGCL), a prototype-guided geometric regularization module built on top of frozen text embeddings. The module combines a semantic stream, a prototype-anchor attention stream, supervised contrastive learning, offset-based prototype-margin regularization, and stream regularization to produce a compact task-adapted representation without updating the base encoder. Controlled experiments show that PGCL improves over raw frozen embeddings on all three datasets and gives the clearest direct-baseline margin on AmazonReviews, while remaining competitive with strong direct frozen metric-learning baselines on GoEmotions and ToxicComment. We also add supervised residual-adapter, encoder-LoRA, full fine-tuning, objective ablation, sensitivity, and fully logged few-shot LLM protocol diagnostics to define the boundary of the claim. The theoretical analysis is revised as a sufficient-condition account for prototype-margin behavior under explicit assumptions in the prototype-mapping space, rather than as an unconditional training or final-embedding separation guarantee.

title: Research on Data-Driven English Personalized Teaching Design in Smart Classrooms
abstract: In the current era of educational digital transformation, there are structural problems in English teaching such as the lack of personalized guidance, insufficient utilization of data, and long evaluation and feedback times.Based on the data-driven learning theory, this paper integrates large language models and smart classroom technologies to design personalized English teaching and proposes an implementation path.According to the research findings, the promotion of smart classroom data is to reshape the teaching process into a cycle of language data occurrence -processing -analysis, and using "ad hoc data collection" to break the "data islands" caused by traditional education.A four-dimensional teaching design framework of "data diagnosis -precise teaching -dynamic evaluation -personalized push" is proposed, including three links: pre-class learning situation profiling, in-class human-computer cooperation, and post-class layered remediation.Through the data integration throughout the process, "teaching -learning -evaluation" can be achieved in consistency.It is believed that personalized teaching in smart classrooms is not about stacking technologies, but using data as an engine, transforming teaching decisions from "experience-based judgment" to "evidence-driven", and realizing large-scale individualized teaching.

title: Computational Path Selection Theory
abstract: Computational Path Selection Theory (CPST) presents a novel approach to optimizing task execution by dynamically selecting the most suitable path from a multitude of possibilities. This theory recognizes that complex tasks invariably possess multiple execution routes, each with varying costs and characteristics. The core principle of CPST revolves around a systematic selection process where a system identifies the optimal path, denoted as π*, based on minimizing a defined cost function: [ Cost(\pi) ] However, a purely cost-driven selection is deemed insufficient. CPST introduces critical constraints to ensure the chosen path is not only efficient but also stable, maintainable, and scalable. This framework offers a potentially transformative foundation for next-generation compilers and optimization techniques, addressing the limitations of traditional static compilation methods. This paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of CPST, detailing its key components, the cost function formulation, and the considerations for ensuring robust and adaptable path selection. ---

title: Computational Fact Versioning
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Fact Versioning (CFV), a novel approach to managing knowledge that explicitly accounts for the evolving nature of factual information. Traditional knowledge representation struggles to handle situations where facts are subject to change over time, leading to inconsistencies and inaccuracies. CFV addresses this challenge by formally representing facts as tuples, incorporating not only the factual content but also its validity period, applicable conditions, and supporting evidence. The core concept is defined as [F= (v, t, c, e)], where *v* represents the factual statement, *t* denotes the validity timeframe, *c* specifies the conditions under which the fact is true, and *e* provides the evidence supporting it. The system is designed to answer queries in the form [F(x, t, c)], enabling efficient retrieval of facts relevant to a given time and set of conditions. CFV has significant implications for various fields, including knowledge graphs, databases, and artificial intelligence systems requiring long-term memory, potentially unlocking a Turing Award-level solution for knowledge management. This paper outlines the fundamental principles of CFV, explores its design considerations, and discusses its potential applications and future research directions. ---

title: Computational Experience Reconstruction Theory (CERT): A Framework for Understanding Complex Intelligence through Behavior-to-Experience Mapping
abstract: Computational Experience Reconstruction Theory (CERT) proposes that complex intelligent systems can be understood by formalizing the mapping from observed behavior to the underlying experiential states that generate such behavior. CERT builds upon the premise that an agent's observable actions are manifestations of internal experience patterns, and that by reconstructing these patterns from behavior, one can uncover the latent cognitive structures responsible for intelligent decision-making. The theory introduces a formal framework in which behavior sequences \(B = \{b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_T\}\) are mapped through a reconstruction function \(f\) to experience sequences \(E = \{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_T\}\). The reconstruction function is modeled as a composition of context‑aware feature extraction, probabilistic inference, and memory‑guided synthesis, allowing for both deterministic and stochastic components. By integrating reinforcement signals, sensory fidelity constraints, and hierarchical representation layers, CERT captures the dynamic interplay between external stimuli and internal experience. The theory is further illustrated through illustrative examples from robotics, natural language processing, and cognitive modeling, demonstrating how experience reconstruction can explain phenomena such as transfer learning, curiosity‑driven exploration, and adaptive behavior. CERT offers a principled basis for the design of artificial systems that not only mimic behavior but also internalize the experiential context, thereby advancing the field toward the realization of truly intelligent agents.

title: Computational Goal Reconstruction Theory (CGRT)
abstract: The increasing complexity of intelligent systems, especially those that exhibit autonomous or semi-autonomous behaviour, demands new analytical tools to understand, predict, and influence their internal goal structures. Computational Goal Reconstruction Theory (CGRT) proposes a principled framework for inferring latent goal models from observable behaviour. Drawing on ideas from behavioural economics, inverse reinforcement learning, and cognitive science, CGRT formalises the mapping from actions to goals as a probabilistic inference problem. It introduces the notion of a goal hierarchy, the concept of behavioural signatures, and a recursive reconstruction algorithm that can operate online. This paper develops the mathematical underpinnings of CGRT, presents illustrative goal reconstruction models, and discusses applications to human–machine interaction, adaptive interfaces, and autonomous agent design. The theory aims to provide a foundational basis for future research into the interpretability and controllability of complex intelligent systems.
