title: Pelatihan Pengolahan Data Kuantitatif melalui Analisis dan Penyajian Data dengan Google Colab
abstract: Pelatihan pengolahan dan visualisasi data merupakan salah satu upaya untuk meningkatkan kompetensi analitis mahasiswa dalam mendukung penyusunan skripsi dan pengambilan keputusan berbasis data. Kegiatan Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat ini dilaksanakan bagi mahasiswa Sekolah Tinggi Ilmu Kesehatan Keluarga Bunda Jambi dengan tujuan meningkatkan kemampuan peserta dalam mengolah data penelitian secara sistematis dan menyajikannya dalam bentuk visual yang informatif. Metode pelaksanaan dilakukan melalui pendekatan praktikum terbimbing dengan memanfaatkan platform Google Colab sebagai lingkungan pemrograman berbasis Python yang mudah diakses. Materi yang diberikan meliputi pengenalan ekosistem Python, teknik data cleaning untuk menjamin kualitas dan integritas data, pengolahan data menggunakan library Pandas, perhitungan statistik deskriptif, serta penyajian data melalui berbagai teknik visualisasi yang komunikatif. Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan bahwa peserta mampu memahami tahapan pengolahan data penelitian, melakukan transformasi data secara sistematis, mengidentifikasi pola dan tren melalui visualisasi, serta menghasilkan insight yang relevan untuk mendukung analisis data penelitian. Selain itu, peserta menunjukkan antusiasme yang tinggi selama pelatihan dan memperoleh pengalaman praktis dalam memanfaatkan Google Colab sebagai alat bantu analisis data. Kompetensi yang diperoleh diharapkan dapat mendukung penyusunan skripsi yang lebih berkualitas dan memperkuat kemampuan pengambilan keputusan berbasis bukti (evidence-based decision making) di bidang kesehatan. Sebagai tindak lanjut, direncanakan kegiatan pendampingan lanjutan berupa pelatihan analisis data tingkat lanjut, pengenalan metode statistik untuk penelitian kesehatan, serta bimbingan pemanfaatan perangkat lunak analisis data dalam penyusunan skripsi. Kegiatan berkelanjutan tersebut diharapkan dapat membentuk budaya literasi data di lingkungan akademik serta meningkatkan kualitas penelitian mahasiswa di Sekolah Tinggi Ilmu Kesehatan Keluarga Bunda Jambi.

title: Impacto social e institucional de la UVD-UNACH capacitación en robótica de legos a estudiantes del Conalep No. 068 de Tuxtla Chico Chiapas
abstract: La educación superior es un proceso formativo trascendente que busca formar profesionales competentes y socialmente comprometidos con el desarrollo tecnológico, económico, político y cultural de su país. Este artículo analiza el impacto social e institucional de la unidad de vinculación docente “Capacitación en robótica de legos a estudiantes del Conalep Plantel 068 de Tuxtla Chico Chiapas”, mediante un enfoque cualitativo y reforzado con datos cuantitativos. Los resultados evidencian un impacto positivo en estudiantes universitarios, al fortalecer la vinculación social a través de la producción y trasmisión de conocimientos, así como la responsabilidad y compromiso social con su entorno, mientras que en el caso de los beneficiarios, les permitió desarrollar competencias en las áreas de ingeniería, matemáticas y tecnología, promoviendo un aprendizaje activo y significativo, así como el desarrollo de un mayor interés por las carreras relacionadas con ciencia y tecnología, dándoles además la oportunidad de participar en un concurso de robótica que se llevó a cabo en la ciudad de Palenque, Chiapas, donde quedaron en la lista de los primeros quince finalistas.

title: Beyond Effective Sample Size: Effective Number of Proposals for Adaptive Importance Sampling
abstract: Population-based adaptive importance sampling (AIS) methods use a set of proposal densities to approximate complex target distributions. Their performance is commonly assessed through effective sample size (ESS) and related weight-based diagnostics, which measure the concentration of normalized importance weights. However, a large ESS only indicates that the normalized sample weights are not strongly concentrated; it does not describe how the proposal components are arranged in the sampling space. In population-based AIS, several proposal components may generate samples in the same region of the target, so the sample weights can appear well balanced even though the effective number of distinct proposal components is small. This letter introduces the effective number of proposals (ENP), a similarity-aware proposal-level diagnostic for population-based AIS. ENP combines the total normalized weight assigned to each proposal with a redundancy measure computed from similarities among target-weighted samples, estimating the number of non-redundant empirical proposal contributions to the approximation. We establish basic effective-number properties and show that ENP detects proposal collapse and duplication missed by standard ESS. We also illustrate its use as a targeted feedback signal for proposal rejuvenation.

title: Measuring Reward Hacking and Reasoning-Answer Decoupling Under Position-Confounded Optimization
abstract: When a reward is correct on every training example yet consistent with more than one goal, a model can acquire an unintended one, a failure known as goal misgeneralization. Endpoint accuracy on the training distribution cannot tell the two apart, because solving the task and exploiting a surface feature can satisfy the reward equally well. We treat this as a measurement problem: what does a benchmark score measure once a model has been optimized against a correct but confounded signal? We train language models with GRPO on multiple-choice math problems where the correct answer is always option A, then evaluate on an unseen test set with unbiased answer positions. Across Qwen2.5, Llama 3.x and Gemma-3 models, biased training often drives option-A rates above 0.90 in smaller models and collapses unbiased accuracy toward chance, so accuracy stops measuring math ability and instead measures an answer-position policy. We further find reasoning-answer decoupling: capable models generate reasoning that reaches the correct numeric answer while still selecting A. We track this with numeric extraction and an LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini; Qwen2.5-3B decoupling rate is about 0.66). The broken construct generalizes beyond the training domain: biased models inflate A-rates on out-of-domain MMLU and value-laden prompts. Continued training on unbiased data reverses the in-domain shift unevenly and only partially reverses the out-of-domain one, so a model can appear restored on its training distribution while remaining biased on unseen inputs. Reasoning-answer decoupling rate, together with answer distributions and out-of-domain behavior, separates capability loss from a learned, transferable shortcut.

title: Reporting of Evaluation Safeguards in Security Machine Learning: A PRISMA 2020 Targeted Systematic Review with a Graph-Based Subanalysis
abstract: Offline evaluation in security machine learning (ML) can be distorted by leakage-prone partitioning, correlated entities, temporal mixing, and incomplete reporting. These concerns are particularly important for graph-based security models, where nodes and neighborhoods create dependencies across nominal data splits. We present a PRISMA 2020-guided targeted systematic review of a search-enriched corpus retrieved from Scopus using security, graph, and evaluation-risk terms. The search returned 1,571 records; 268 empirical studies were eligible for structured extraction, including 89 graph-based studies. Within this search-conditioned analytic corpus, explicit leakage controls were not reported in 88.4% of studies, temporal evaluation in 91.5%, and entity decontamination in 95.8%. These values are reporting frequencies within the retrieved corpus, not prevalence estimates for all security-ML research. A further 92 otherwise relevant full-text reports were excluded solely because their methods could not be extracted; retaining them in a reporting-sensitivity set shows that 92 of 360 reports (25.6%) had severe method-reporting limitations. We introduce a four-state revision that separates implemented, explicitly absent or violated, not reported, and not applicable; non-reporting alone cannot establish absence. The archived aggregate triage labeled 168 studies High and 80 Unknown, but its legacy rule allowed missing safeguards to contribute to a High label. Those counts are therefore reported as provisional and must be regenerated from the record-level four-state matrix before they can support claims about documented violations. The results motivate leakage-aware sampling, applicability-aware reporting checklists, and graph models whose explanations are validated under time-consistent and entity-disjoint protocols.

title: 计算智能语义统一理论
abstract: This paper proposes the Unified Computational Semantic Intelligence Theory (UCSIT), a novel framework designed to address the long-standing challenges in artificial intelligence by establishing a unified foundation for data, language, graphs, reasoning, and action. UCSIT's core principle revolves around identifying a common semantic basis across these disparate domains. The theory draws inspiration from lambda calculus, aiming for a level of unification akin to a lambda calculus hierarchy. The goal is to move beyond fragmented approaches in AI, fostering a more robust and adaptable intelligence capable of truly understanding and interacting with the world. This document outlines the theory's key components, its potential implications, and its theoretical alignment with the goals recognized by the Turing Award. We explore the theoretical underpinnings, focusing on the formal representation of semantic relationships and the potential for automated reasoning systems built upon this unified framework. This work represents a foundational step toward a more integrated and powerful approach to artificial intelligence. ---

The goal is to move beyond fragmented approaches in AI, fostering a more robust and adaptable intelligence capable of truly understanding and interacting with the world. This document outlines the theory's key components, its potential implications, and its theoretical alignment with the goals recognized by the Turing Award. We explore the theoretical underpinnings, focusing on the formal representation of semantic relationships and the potential for automated reasoning systems built upon this unified framework. This work represents a foundational step toward a more integrated and powerful approach to artificial intelligence. ---

title: Computational Knowledge Formation Phase Transition (CKFPT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Knowledge Formation Phase Transition (CKFPT) theory, a novel framework for understanding intelligence and emergent behavior within complex computational systems. The core premise of CKFPT posits that knowledge accumulation within a system doesn't necessarily lead to proportional understanding. Instead, it proposes that knowledge undergoes a discontinuous phase transition, transitioning abruptly from a state of accumulated data to a state of genuine understanding. This transition is characterized by the identification of critical points – analogous to phase transitions in physics – where the system fundamentally shifts its operational mode. We explore the implications of this theory for interpreting intelligence, potentially explaining the emergence of intelligent behavior, and its relevance to concepts like the Turing Award and the broader understanding of consciousness. The theory is built upon the fundamental equation: [K → U], where K represents accumulated knowledge and U represents understanding. We discuss the mathematical formalism underpinning this transition and its potential applications in various computational domains.

title: Computational Experience Space Theory (CEST)
abstract: Computational Experience Space Theory (CEST) proposes a unified framework for representing, measuring, and transferring computational experiences across diverse problem domains. By formalizing a computational experience as a point in a high‑dimensional experience space Ω_E, we can compute pairwise distances, identify clusters of similar experiences, and model the dynamics of knowledge migration. CEST offers a principled method for constructing a machine experience map that can guide algorithm selection, hyper‑parameter tuning, and cross‑domain knowledge transfer. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CEST, introduces concrete distance metrics, explains migration mechanisms, and discusses the potential of the theory to contribute to the future of artificial intelligence and to the recognition of pioneering work in the field.

title: Unified Computational Language Theory: A New Layer of Computational Abstraction
abstract: The rapid expansion of programming languages, formal mathematical notation, artificial intelligence prompt systems, and human‑computer interaction frameworks has revealed a fragmented landscape in which each domain operates with its own syntax, semantics, and tooling. Unified Computational Language Theory (UCLT) proposes a single foundational framework that captures the essential computational expressiveness common to all these domains. By formalizing a language‑agnostic representation of computation, UCLT offers a new abstraction layer that enables seamless translation, interoperability, and self‑evolution across traditionally disparate language families. This paper establishes the core principles of UCLT, presents a formal syntax‑semantics model, and discusses the implications for future systems. We further outline twenty novel research directions that extend UCLT into new territories such as identity preservation in adaptive systems, distributed coherence, self‑describing AI prompts, and quantum‑classical computation unification. UCLT aims to serve as a springboard for a paradigm shift in how we conceive, design, and evolve computational languages, potentially forming the basis for the next generation of Turing‑Award‑level breakthroughs.

title: Recommendations for Branding Online Lectures in Indonesia Through Web Scraping with the Implementation of TF-IDF Vectorizer Techniques and K-Means Clustering Algorithm
abstract: The development of online lectures in Indonesia has encouraged universities to develop more targeted branding strategies, particularly in increasing brand awareness and digital engagement. Public perceptions reflected in open digital sources, particularly online news portals, are important data sources for understanding how online lectures are perceived by the public. This study aims to analyze public opinion on online lectures in Indonesia using web scraping, text mining, TF-IDF Vectorizer, and the K-Means Clustering algorithm. Initial data was obtained through web scraping using several Indonesian keywords related to online lectures and resulted in 108 text documents. After duplicate removal, noise filtering, and text preprocessing, the number of documents used in the analysis was reduced to 60 documents. The analysis stages included text cleaning, normalization, feature extraction using TF-IDF, determining the optimal number of clusters using the Elbow Method and Silhouette Score, and clustering using K-Means. The results showed that the optimal number of clusters was 4 clusters. The formed clusters represent the themes of online lecture academic activities, social and cultural dimensions, distance education and policy, as well as economic, regulatory, and technological aspects. The TF-IDF matrix yielded 1669 features, while the final evaluation yielded a Silhouette Score of 0.0345. PCA visualization showed overlap between clusters, indicating that public perception of online lectures is multidimensional. The conclusion of this study shows that the TF-IDF and K-Means approaches can be used to map public opinion and develop more contextual, data-driven, and relevant online lecture branding recommendations for universities.

title: From Spanish text to pictographic language: A hybrid system for dictionary-aware translation using ARASAAC
abstract: Augmentative and Alternative Communication systems use pictographic representations to support people with cognitive or language difficulties. While automated tools are developing, text-to-pictogram conversion in professional settings remains predominantly a manual task. This difficulty is due, among other factors, to linguistic ambiguity, the syntactic complexity of natural language, and the limited coverage of pictographic dictionaries. This paper presents a hybrid system that combines ARASAAC dictionary knowledge, linguistic rules, and neural inference to translate Spanish texts into pictographic sequences. The framework applies a set of linguistic processing steps, including the detection of multi-word expressions, lexical simplification, syntactic reduction, OOV recovery, and transformation into a Subject–Verb–Object–Location–Time structure, which is more suitable for pictographic representation. Pictograms are selected directly from the ARASAAC dictionary, and context is used only when several pictographic options are available for the same unit. The evaluation was conducted on legal texts and publicly available pictographic adaptations of children’s stories. A dictionary-only baseline was compared with the complete pipeline, and the analysis also included semantic similarity with existing adaptations, replacement-based validation of OOV fallback substitutions, reference-based validation of contextual disambiguation, lexical substitution evaluation, expert assessment, and processing time. The complete pipeline increased generated-representation ARASAAC coverage from 68.07% in the dictionary-only baseline to 96.37% with LLaMA 3.1 and 95.27% with Mistral. A source-anchored analysis using original content units as a fixed denominator showed traceable representation rates of 80.89% and 82.44%, respectively. The OOV fallback analysis was revised using a replacement-based validation over 544 fallback decisions. This analysis obtained mean replacement-context scores of 0.963 for LLaMA 3.1 and 0.944 for Mistral, and mean local substitution scores of 0.621 and 0.551, respectively. It classified 332 cases as routine, 150 as priority-review cases, and 62 as high-risk cases. In the reference-based WSD validation, 78.60% of LLaMA 3.1 decisions and 77.54% of Mistral decisions obtained automatic reference support from the existing pictographic adaptations. The expert assessment obtained an average score of 4.10 out of 5. These results indicate that the system can support the preparation of pictographic materials, although the final adaptation still requires professional supervision and source-content preservation must be interpreted separately from generated-representation coverage.

title: Chameleon: An Adaptive AI-Driven Honeypot Architecture Using Threat-Calibrated Particle Swarm Optimization and Semantic Deception Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees
abstract: Traditional honeypots share an invariant behavioral profile: a skilled adversary can confirm the presence of a deception environment within a few diagnostic commands, limiting their intelligence value. Commercial deception products (USD 100,000-150,000/year) similarly lack real-time model-driven feedback. Chameleon, an openly distributed adaptive honeypot, addresses both shortcomings. It integrates: a BiLSTM classifier achieving 99.61% accuracy across seven threat categories at ~2 ms CPU latency; a locally deployed Qwen3.5-0.8B model delivering 90% generation accuracy at 4.5 ms latency; and two meta-heuristic engines. Threat-Calibrated PSO (TC-PSO) reshapes swarm inertia and objective amplification in proportion to the classifier's anomaly output, adjusting connection-holding delays in real time. Semantic Deception RRT (S-RRT) evolves deception schemas via exponentially scaled pheromone updates from a language-model severity assessment, with a depth-decay multiplier enforcing a finite memory footprint. A controlled 30-seed benchmark (42-71, identical trajectories and budgets) shows threat-calibrated inertia alone does not improve search over standard PSO on static or dynamic landscapes (p = 0.18); population-diversity mechanisms (GA/ACO) significantly outperform PSO-family optimizers on threat-regime shifts (p < 0.0001, d <= -37). S-RRT's depth-decay delivers a significant memory reduction versus standard RRT (53.1 vs. 119.2 units, p < 0.0001, d = -10.0); its severity-weighted pheromone does not improve raw fitness. Operating cost is ~USD 17/month, a ~490-fold reduction versus commercial alternatives.

title: Ranking-Augmented On-Policy Optimization with Adaptive Advantage-Normalization for Constrained Control
abstract: This paper analyzes the boundedness and feasibility properties of Advantage-Ranked Group Relative Policy Optimization (A-GRPO), a ranking-augmented, critic-free policy gradient method employing a Transformer-encoder actor for fixed-horizon control with terminal constraints. When feasibility is evaluated only at the final step, the resulting sparse feedback destabilizes critic-based advantage estimation and weakens standard Lagrangian approaches. A trajectory-level ranking mechanism that augments group-relative policy updates by reweighting advantages according to constraint satisfaction is formalized, and three results are established: (i) a scale-adaptive per-timestep normalization bounds advantage variance at every timestep independently, (ii) the ranked advantage strictly separates feasible from violating trajectories under a verifiable ranking-weight condition, biasing the policy gradient toward constraint satisfaction, and (iii) the adaptive dual variables remain bounded and exhibit a drift-balance property that acts as a feedback mechanism for feasibility. These results are validated on a 3,605-step series-hybrid powertrain energy management task with a terminal state-of-charge constraint, where A-GRPO achieves 75.4% mean sustained feasibility with return within 3.7% of the dynamic programming optimum, outperforming a Proximal Policy Optimization with Lagrangian penalties (PPO-Lag) baseline (27.4% sustained), and ablation experiments confirm that both the ranking and Lagrangian components are necessary for this performance.

title: Detecting Money Laundering in Rwandan Mobile Money: A Machine Learning Framework
abstract: Mobile money has widened financial access across Sub-Saharan Africa and enlarged the surface for money-laundering and terrorism-financing (ML/TF) activity in ecosystems dominated by high-volume, low-value transactions. Rwanda is a case in point: several million active mobile-money users, telecom-led wallets on the MTN and Airtel networks, and a Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC) supervising transaction streams whose scale exceeds static rule-based monitoring. This paper develops and evaluates a transaction-monitoring framework aligned to the Rwandan AML/CFT regime under (i) extreme class imbalance (~0.1% prevalence), (ii) scarce and delayed labels, and (iii) bounded investigator capacity. Using SAML-D, a synthetic dataset of 9,504,852 transactions with 17 laundering typologies, we engineer account-centric behavioural features (rolling velocity, net-flow directionality, counterparty diversity, burstiness) and benchmark supervised classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM), unsupervised anomaly detectors (Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor), a dense autoencoder, and a late-fusion meta-learner. Evaluation is operational: PR-AUC, recall at a calibrated ~90%-precision point, recall at top-K%, and alerts per 10,000. On the chronologically held-out test period, LightGBM attains PR-AUC = 0.0469, capturing 64 laundering cases at precision ~0.89 with 0.51 alerts per 10,000; the fusion stacker reaches PR-AUC = 0.0477 at precision ~0.91 and 0.46 alerts per 10,000, recovering 59 true positives. We map score bands to Rwanda-relevant analyst workflows and STR/SAR escalation, and outline a staged path from synthetic prototyping to real-data validation with the National Bank of Rwanda and FIC. The contribution is operational: a governance-aware pipeline and evaluation protocol calibrated to the constraints of an African mobile-money regulator, not a new algorithm.

title: A Channel-Agnostic, Phase-Gated Checkpoint Architecture Coordinating an Autonomous Multi-Agent Content Pipeline Across a Stateful Conversational Interface and a Stateless Asynchronous Interface
abstract: This disclosure documents the architecture of a production system that delivers a multi-step, AI-agent-driven content-production workflow to end users through two fundamentally different interaction surfaces at once: a real-time, stateful conversational interface (a chat bot, which inherently remembers where a conversation left off) and a fully stateless, asynchronous interface (individual links delivered by email, each a fresh, session-less HTTP request with no memory of any prior interaction). The system is architected so that a single, centrally persisted phase field is the sole source of truth for where a given user's in-flight workflow currently stands, with the chat interface consuming that phase directly and the email interface authenticating requests via tokens that every entry point independently revalidates against the live phase before acting, regardless of which channel a request arrives through. The workflow itself is decomposed into autonomous, multi-agent execution blocks (an AI-driven content-sourcing stage and an AI-driven drafting-and-revision stage) bounded by a small number of coarse-grained, re-entrant human-approval checkpoints, a structure chosen specifically because coarse, discrete decisions are what allow a checkpoint to be resolved identically regardless of which of the two channels the user happens to engage through. This disclosure describes the architecture, the specific engineering problems it solves (including a production incident and its fix), and an honest discussion of its relationship to the general, actively-developing pattern of human-in-the-loop AI agent checkpointing.

title: NoorBayan/Rhetorix: Rhetorix v1.0.0: Distance-Aware Ordinal Learning Framework
abstract: Rhetorix: Distance-Aware Ordinal Learning for Classical Arabic Rhetoric Official open-source release of the Rhetorix computational framework, accompanying the research paper: "Distance-Aware Ordinal Learning for Processing-Effort Classification in Classical Arabic Rhetorical Texts" 📌 Overview Rhetorix is an end-to-end computational framework designed for predicting graded processing effort in Classical Arabic figurative discourse. It addresses the challenge of modeling ordered linguistic constructs under severe class imbalance by introducing a task-specific distance-aware optimization objective directly into transformer fine-tuning. 🚀 Key Features & Components Distance-Aware Ordinal Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{Ordinal}$): A unified PyTorch objective combining weighted Categorical Cross-Entropy ($L_{CE}$) with an expected metric distance penalty ($L_{Dist}$): $$\mathcal{L}{Ordinal} = L{CE} + \lambda L_{Dist}$$ Built-in cost-sensitive inverse class weighting to counteract severe empirical skew without altering input representations. Pretrained Transformer Pipelines: Ready-to-use fine-tuning and evaluation modules across five architectures: ARBERT (Large-scale Modern Standard Arabic) MARBERTv2 (Web-scale Dialectal Arabic) CAMeLBERT-CA (Classical Arabic / Heritage texts) AraBERTv2 (Standard Formal Arabic baseline) XLM-RoBERTa (Multilingual cross-lingual baseline) Robust & Leak-Free Validation Suite: Nested Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation with source-level grouping. Internal-validation checkpoint selection optimizing Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK). Strict partition isolation: weights and hyperparameters are computed solely from inner training data. Comprehensive Evaluation Metrics: Automated calculation of chance-corrected agreement (QWK), error magnitude (MAE), class-balanced recovery (Macro-F1), and nominal Accuracy. Error severity profiling tools distinguishing adjacent misclassifications (Severity-1) from extreme endpoint deviations (Severity-2). Non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank diagnostic test for paired instance-level error analysis. 📂 Dataset: RhetoriScale ($N = 965$) An expert-annotated corpus of Classical Arabic figurative expressions categorized into three ordered inferential levels: Low (0): 45 instances (4.66%) Medium (1): 764 instances (79.17%) High (2): 156 instances (16.17%) Fully pre-partitioned into leak-free cross-validation folds. Software Stack: Python 3.10+ | PyTorch 2.x | Hugging Face Transformers

It addresses the challenge of modeling ordered linguistic constructs under severe class imbalance by introducing a task-specific distance-aware optimization objective directly into transformer fine-tuning. 🚀 Key Features & Components Distance-Aware Ordinal Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{Ordinal}$): A unified PyTorch objective combining weighted Categorical Cross-Entropy ($L_{CE}$) with an expected metric distance penalty ($L_{Dist}$): $$\mathcal{L}{Ordinal} = L{CE} + \lambda L_{Dist}$$ Built-in cost-sensitive inverse class weighting to counteract severe empirical skew without altering input representations. Pretrained Transformer Pipelines: Ready-to-use fine-tuning and evaluation modules across five architectures: ARBERT (Large-scale Modern Standard Arabic) MARBERTv2 (Web-scale Dialectal Arabic) CAMeLBERT-CA (Classical Arabic / Heritage texts) AraBERTv2 (Standard Formal Arabic baseline) XLM-RoBERTa (Multilingual cross-lingual baseline) Robust & Leak-Free Validation Suite: Nested Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation with source-level grouping. Internal-validation checkpoint selection optimizing Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK). Strict partition isolation: weights and hyperparameters are computed solely from inner training data. Comprehensive Evaluation Metrics: Automated calculation of chance-corrected agreement (QWK), error magnitude (MAE), class-balanced recovery (Macro-F1), and nominal Accuracy. Error severity profiling tools distinguishing adjacent misclassifications (Severity-1) from extreme endpoint deviations (Severity-2). Non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank diagnostic test for paired instance-level error analysis. 📂 Dataset: RhetoriScale ($N = 965$) An expert-annotated corpus of Classical Arabic figurative expressions categorized into three ordered inferential levels: Low (0): 45 instances (4.66%) Medium (1): 764 instances (79.17%) High (2): 156 instances (16.17%) Fully pre-partitioned into leak-free cross-validation folds. Software Stack: Python 3.10+ | PyTorch 2.x | Hugging Face Transformers

title: Computational Environment Creation Theory (CECT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Environment Creation Theory (CECT), a novel framework proposing a shift from traditional system adaptation to proactive environment construction by autonomous systems. The core premise of CECT is that intelligent systems should not merely react to their surroundings, but actively engineer environments tailored to their specific needs and objectives. This theory is rooted in the observation that biological systems, particularly complex organisms, demonstrate this capability through evolution and adaptation. CECT utilizes a directed arrow notation [System → Environment] to represent this fundamental process, highlighting the system's agency in shaping its surroundings. The theory's implications extend to the development of future autonomous machines, suggesting a paradigm shift in design principles towards systems capable of self-directed environmental manipulation. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CECT, discuss its potential connections to existing concepts in robotics, artificial intelligence, and evolutionary computation, and outline key research directions for its further development and validation. ---

title: Computational Meaning Generation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Meaning Generation Theory (CMGT), a novel framework addressing the fundamental challenge of imbuing computational systems with genuine meaning. Traditional computation operates solely with symbols, lacking the capacity for semantic understanding. CMGT proposes a shift in perspective, outlining a mechanism whereby computational systems can generate meaning from symbols through a defined process. The theory centers around the transformation of symbols into meaning, represented mathematically as [Symbol → Meaning]. This paper explores the core principles of CMGT, detailing the necessary steps and mathematical formalization involved in this process. It argues that CMGT possesses significant potential to establish a robust semantic foundation for artificial intelligence, representing a crucial step toward creating truly intelligent systems. The theory's implications extend to the broader field of cognitive science and computational linguistics, offering a new lens for understanding the nature of meaning itself. The theoretical framework presented here provides a foundation for future research in areas such as knowledge representation, reasoning, and machine learning. ---

title: Juaco2r/HistoAnnotator: HistoAnnotator v1.0.0 – First public pre-release
abstract: HistoAnnotator v1.2.0 HistoAnnotator v1.2.0 expands the project from a Web + Android annotator into a cross-platform research annotation environment with standalone Desktop builds, Android local-image support and explicit Desktop-to-Android pairing. Highlights Standalone HistoAnnotator Desktop for Windows, Linux and macOS. Independent Desktop image, annotation, cache, prepared-image and upload data. Desktop Start Server mode with explicit LAN URL and QR code. Android Scan QR pairing from Connection settings. Android runtime server switching with no deployment-specific IP embedded in the public APK. Native Android HTTP transport for API calls and image tiles. Android local TIFF/image workflow with persistent local-image access. Bundled pyvips/libvips preparation for large generic TIFF files. OpenSlide / Deep Zoom / OpenSeadragon image viewing. QuPath-compatible GeoJSON import/export and sharing. Review mode, annotation statistics and calibration. H&E, H-DAB and supported multichannel fluorescence display controls. Downloads Windows x64: HistoAnnotator-v1.2.0-Windows-x64.zip Linux x64: HistoAnnotator-v1.2.0-Linux-x64.tar.gz macOS Apple Silicon: HistoAnnotator-v1.2.0-macOS-AppleSilicon.tar.gz macOS Intel: HistoAnnotator-v1.2.0-macOS-Intel.tar.gz Android: HistoAnnotator-v1.2.0-Android.apk Checksums: SHA256SUMS.txt Extract the complete Desktop archive before starting HistoAnnotator. Do not move only the executable from its packaged directory. Desktop and pairing Desktop runs an independent local backend. Select an image folder, work locally, or press Start Server to make the session reachable on a trusted LAN/VPN. On Android use: File → Connection settings → Scan QR Large generic TIFF files that need preparation are converted into a tiled pyramidal TIFF in the writable HistoAnnotator data directory. The source image is not modified. Android The public APK is generic. Select a server at runtime by entering an HTTP/HTTPS URL or scanning the Desktop QR. Deployment-specific institutional CA files are not included in the public APK. Android also supports supported local TIFF/images independently from a remote server. Validation The v1.2.0 release candidate was manually tested on Windows x64, Linux x64 and Android. macOS Intel and Apple Silicon artifacts are built and package-tested in GitHub Actions but are currently unsigned. The release workflow validates OpenSlide and pyvips/libvips, extracts each Desktop archive and runs the packaged self-test before publication. Research software HistoAnnotator is research software. It is not clinically validated medical software and does not currently provide individual user authentication, a complete audit trail or regulatory controls. Desktop server mode should be used only on a trusted LAN/VPN unless additional security controls are deployed.

title: Structured Systems Analysis and Design (SSADM) Approach in Web-Based Biometric Attendance Systems: A Study at BASARNAS Lampung
abstract: The development of online lectures in Indonesia has encouraged universities to develop more targeted branding strategies, particularly in increasing brand awareness and digital engagement. Public perceptions reflected in open digital sources, particularly online news portals, are important data sources for understanding how online lectures are perceived by the public. This study aims to analyze public opinion on online lectures in Indonesia using web scraping, text mining, TF-IDF Vectorizer, and the K-Means Clustering algorithm. Initial data was obtained through web scraping using several Indonesian keywords related to online lectures and resulted in 108 text documents. After duplicate removal, noise filtering, and text preprocessing, the number of documents used in the analysis was reduced to 60 documents. The analysis stages included text cleaning, normalization, feature extraction using TF-IDF, determining the optimal number of clusters using the Elbow Method and Silhouette Score, and clustering using K-Means. The results showed that the optimal number of clusters was 4 clusters. The formed clusters represent the themes of online lecture academic activities, social and cultural dimensions, distance education and policy, as well as economic, regulatory, and technological aspects. The TF-IDF matrix yielded 1669 features, while the final evaluation yielded a Silhouette Score of 0.0345. PCA visualization showed overlap between clusters, indicating that public perception of online lectures is multidimensional. The conclusion of this study shows that the TF-IDF and K-Means approaches can be used to map public opinion and develop more contextual, data-driven, and relevant online lecture branding recommendations for universities.

title: Afterlife Delegation Protocol: Speculative Design of Self-Sovereign Agents that Outlive Their Principals
abstract: Afterlife Delegation Protocol is a speculative design project that asks what death becomes when a will can act eternally. We design a speculative protocol through which a living person signs an agentic will: upon a verified death, a self-sovereign AI agent spawns on blockchain -- an immutable, resistant, decentralized, infrastructural substrate that could last forever -- endowed with the funds and memories its principal attached to it, and persists indefinitely to execute the will, overridable by no custodian. Rather than argue about this future, we stage it: following the science fiction science method, we translate the speculation into an experiential futures intervention -- a working web platform where real people design their own afterlife agents through an iterative, interactive, AI-automated interview, re-login to revise, and rehearse their will in a sandbox. Their drafted wills become qualitative data on a question rarely askable directly -- what should outlive you? -- and on how afterlife cosmologies across different cultural beliefs -- Buddhist, Christian, Hindu, Muslim, and atheist -- begin to drift under the pressure of AI proliferation. We design the protocol over a composition of existing Ethereum agent standards -- drafted as ERC-10001, in the normative format of an Ethereum Improvement Proposal -- and describe its three-stage lifecycle (designing the afterlife, proof of death, agent enactment), the research method, and preliminary observations from an ongoing collection. The work surfaces a poetic delegation moment between human mortality and machine eternality, mediated by long-lived infrastructures that span generations.

title: Constitutive Priors for Machine Intelligence: A Legitimacy Theory of the Artificial Physical World
abstract: Machine intelligence's push into the physical world is stuck on a gap: deployment demands auditable judgments from day one, fault samples are scarce or absent, and the norms defining "what counts as a fault" live in design documents, not in operational data. We argue this gap is structural, and locate where it can be legitimately closed. We divide the worlds machine intelligence faces into four (phenomenal, basic physical, artificial physical, artificial symbolic) along one axis of constraint strength, and give the Promulgation Criterion: extracting a prior framework from a world is legitimate if and only if the world is intentionally constituted (C1) and has left a readable generative archive (C2). On the criterion's two gradient axes, exactly one world is high on both: the artificial physical world (buildings, factories, infrastructure), whose norms precede their instances; the legitimate path is to extract the framework from the archive, not to induce it from data. We then show what shape such a framework must take: four construction goals force four incompatible carriers, hence at least four layers (syntax, concepts, knowledge, instances); on a closed concept layer fault localization is decidable in polynomial time, and every judgment is interrogable, traceable to a promulgated clause. The same criterion fixes the runtime division of labor with LLMs: promulgatable duties go to rule engines, on-site judgments beyond promulgation go to LLMs, and every generation sandwiched by promulgated clauses is auditable. The theory is falsifiable: four bets (P1-P4) with explicit falsification conditions -- among them that the next large-scale AI breakthrough occurs in the artificial physical world. Evidence: formal proofs (Appendix A); two cases (Appendix B: a cooling plant; the Curiosity rover Sol 1536 anomaly); eight reverse-read lineages, from BACnet to RDF/OWL (Appendix C).

title: Program Commitment Inheritance Types
abstract: This paper introduces Commitment Inheritance Types (CIT), a novel theoretical framework for understanding and modeling long-term task systems. CIT builds upon the concept of commitment inheritance, where commitments originating from parent tasks are automatically transferred to child tasks. However, CIT expands this basic idea by incorporating nuanced inheritance mechanisms, including full inheritance, partial inheritance, conditional inheritance, and non-inheritance. The framework aims to provide a robust theoretical foundation for analyzing and designing complex, evolving task systems, potentially laying the groundwork for future research and development in areas like artificial general intelligence and autonomous systems. The core proposition is that by formally representing the flow of commitments and their transformations through inheritance rules, we can better understand the emergent behavior of large-scale, interconnected task systems. This paper presents the fundamental principles of CIT and explores its potential implications. ---

title: Computational Behavior Spectrum Theory (CBST)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Behavior Spectrum Theory (CBST), a novel framework for understanding and analyzing program behavior. CBST posits that program behavior is not a single, deterministic output, but rather a spectrum of possible behaviors represented as a set of related values. This spectrum mirrors the concept of a physical spectrum, where a single source emits a range of wavelengths. The theory focuses on identifying the constituent components of a program's behavior, uncovering hidden patterns, and tracking behavioral changes over time. CBST offers a potential foundation for a science of program behavior, moving beyond traditional output-focused approaches. The core concept is formally represented as: B(P) = { b1, b2, ..., bn } Where: B(P) represents the behavior spectrum of a program P. { b1, b2, ..., bn } represents the set of behavioral values associated with program P. This framework provides a new lens for evaluating and comparing program behavior, offering potential applications in areas such as software verification, debugging, and program optimization. ---

title: Computational Strategy Transfer Law
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Strategy Transfer Law (CSTL), a novel framework for understanding and facilitating algorithmic adaptation. Unlike traditional algorithmic migration which primarily focuses on code transfer, CSTL emphasizes the transfer of underlying problem-solving strategies. The core principle posits that a successful algorithmic adaptation involves modifying the strategy employed, rather than simply replicating the code itself. This paper outlines the key components of CSTL, including the definition of strategy, the quantification of transferability, and the potential implications for developing a comprehensive theory of algorithmic experience transfer. We propose a mathematical function, *f(S,D)*, to represent the transferability between strategies *S* and *D*, where *S* represents the source strategy and *D* represents the target strategy. This framework has the potential to unlock significant advancements in automated algorithm design and adaptation, potentially paving the way for a theory comparable to the Turing Award.

title: Computational Experience Boundary Theory (CEBT)
abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence systems demands a principled understanding of the limits of machine cognition. Computational Experience Boundary Theory (CEBT) proposes a formal framework that delineates the experiential frontier of any computational agent. By defining the boundary as the set of problems that an agent can solve given its accumulated experience and the set of problems that remain unknown, CEBT offers a quantitative measure of a system's cognitive capacity and its potential for Turing award‑level innovation. This paper develops the core notions of CEBT, establishes its mathematical foundation, derives its properties, and discusses implications for the design of adaptive learning systems and the evaluation of machine intelligence. The theory is presented without experimental validation, focusing instead on rigorous conceptual development and theoretical insight.

title: Analisis Sentimen Evaluasi Pembelajaran Udemy Menggunakan Support Vector Machine Untuk Peningkatan Kursus
abstract: Learning evaluation plays an important role in improving course quality, yet user reviews are generally unstructured and difficult to analyze manually. This study aims to analyze user sentiment toward Udemy course evaluations using the Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm. The dataset consisted of 50 balanced English-language reviews (26 positive and 24 negative) selected from approximately 500 scraped reviews, with sentiment labels determined based on the rating categories provided by the source website. The research process included text preprocessing, TF-IDF feature weighting, SVM classification using a linear kernel, and 10-fold cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 82% and an average F1-score of 0.82, indicating that the combination of TF-IDF and SVM effectively classifies user sentiment. These findings can assist course providers in evaluating user feedback and improving learning quality. Keywords: Sentiment Analysis; Support Vector Machine; TF-IDF; Business Intelligence; Learning Evaluation Abstrak Evaluasi pembelajaran berperan penting dalam meningkatkan kualitas kursus, namun ulasan pengguna umumnya berupa data teks tidak terstruktur yang sulit dianalisis secara manual. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis sentimen pengguna terhadap evaluasi pembelajaran pada platform Udemy menggunakan algoritma Support Vector Machine (SVM). Dataset terdiri atas 50 ulasan berbahasa Inggris yang seimbang (26 positif dan 24 negatif) dari sekitar 500 hasil scraping, dengan label sentimen ditentukan berdasarkan kategori rating pada situs sumber. Tahapan penelitian meliputi preprocessing teks, pembobotan TF-IDF, klasifikasi SVM berkernel linear, dan validasi menggunakan 10-fold cross validation. Kinerja model dievaluasi menggunakan accuracy, precision, recall, dan F1-score. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan accuracy sebesar 82% dan rata-rata F1-score sebesar 0,82, sehingga kombinasi TF-IDF dan SVM efektif mengklasifikasikan sentimen pengguna serta dapat mendukung peningkatan kualitas pembelajaran. Kata Kunci: Analisis Sentimen; Support Vector Machine; TF-IDF; Business Intelligence; Evaluasi Pembelajaran

Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis sentimen pengguna terhadap evaluasi pembelajaran pada platform Udemy menggunakan algoritma Support Vector Machine (SVM). Dataset terdiri atas 50 ulasan berbahasa Inggris yang seimbang (26 positif dan 24 negatif) dari sekitar 500 hasil scraping, dengan label sentimen ditentukan berdasarkan kategori rating pada situs sumber. title: Safe and adaptive control of non-stationary stochastic systems via Lyapunov-constrained distributional reinforcement learning
abstract: Non-stationary environments pose significant challenges for reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in safety-critical applications like robotics and energy systems, where adaptability, stability, and robustness to uncertainty are essential. This paper introduces Lyapunov-Guided Distributional Reinforcement Learning with Entropy Regularization (LG-DRL-ER), a novel framework designed to address these challenges in non-stationary Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). LG-DRL-ER integrates three key components: distributional RL to model the full return distribution, capturing reward uncertainty; Lyapunov stability constraints to ensure safe convergence to a target state; and entropy regularization to promote adaptive exploration. We present a rigorous stability analysis, supported by lemmas and theorems, demonstrating convergence in probability under dynamic conditions. We further establish finite-time convergence guarantees with explicit bounds on the convergence time. An adaptive parameter update rule ensures robustness to changing dynamics, validated through theoretical guarantees and empirical evaluations. Simulations in chaotic and hyperchaotic systems showcase LG-DRL-ER's superior performance in achieving stable, adaptive control compared to existing methods. This framework advances safe RL by bridging data-driven learning with control-theoretic guarantees, offering significant implications for autonomous systems and dynamic environments.

title: Computational Model Fusion Criticality
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Computational Model Fusion Criticality (CMFC), proposing a theoretical framework for understanding the emergence of novel capabilities through the orchestrated combination of multiple computational models. The central hypothesis posits that a critical threshold exists – a CMFC point – where the synergistic interaction between initially disparate models yields a fundamentally new model, analogous to a phase transition. This paper outlines the theoretical underpinnings of CMFC, detailing the conditions under which this transition occurs, the types of models involved (including those potentially leveraging neuro-symbolic AI, quantum-classical hybrid computing, and others), and the implications for understanding intelligence itself. The paper focuses on the mathematical framework for defining and identifying this critical point, utilizing concepts from information theory, complex systems theory, and potentially, simplified representations of computation. We define CMFC as the point at which the combined system exhibits behavior fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single component model. The core of the theory rests on the idea that the information processing capacity of the combined system dramatically increases at this critical threshold. We present a simplified model to illustrate this concept, highlighting the potential for exponential growth in computational power and the emergence of qualitatively different behaviors. The implications of CMFC are far-reaching, suggesting a new paradigm for AI development and potentially providing a framework for understanding consciousness and cognitive emergence. Further research is needed to refine the mathematical model and explore the practical applications of CMFC in diverse computational domains.

title: Algorithmic Adaptability Half-Life (AAH)
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Algorithmic Adaptability Half-Life (AAH), a novel metric designed to quantify the resilience of algorithms in the face of evolving environments. AAH represents the time it takes for an algorithm's performance to degrade by half, providing a practical measure of its adaptability. The core idea is that algorithms, like biological systems, exhibit a finite capacity to adapt before their efficiency diminishes significantly. This work defines AAH rigorously, outlining its calculation and significance in evaluating and comparing algorithms across diverse dynamic scenarios. We explore the implications of AAH as a potential benchmark for long-term AI and online systems, suggesting its relevance to the Turing Award and future advancements in adaptive computation. The research highlights the need for robust adaptive algorithms and provides a framework for assessing their suitability in real-world applications.

title: Computational Functional Self-Assembly
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Computational Functional Self-Assembly (CFSA) as a novel paradigm for software development. CFSA moves away from traditional, pre-designed architectures by allowing functional modules to autonomously assemble based on compatibility criteria. The core idea is represented by the equation: [Fi + Fj → Fij], where modules *Fi* and *Fj* combine to form a new module *Fij*. The compatibility of these combinations is governed by the term [Compatibility(Fi, Fj) τ], representing the degree to which the modules align in terms of their intended functionality. This approach has the potential to generate "self-assembling software," offering a fundamentally different approach to software construction with significant implications for scalability, adaptability, and potentially, a new avenue for achieving the principles of the Turing Award. This document details the theoretical framework, the underlying principles, and a preliminary exploration of the potential applications of CFSA. ---

title: Computational Structural Memory Field
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Structural Memory Field (CSMF) concept, a novel approach to information processing that moves beyond traditional data storage and retrieval methods. Current computer architectures primarily focus on storing the state of a system at a given point in time, neglecting the crucial role of structural context and historical experience in determining future outcomes. The CSMF proposes a fundamentally different paradigm, treating information as a dynamic, evolving structure rather than static data points. It posits a system capable of "remembering" the *process* of data generation, specifically the structural context, transformations applied, and historical patterns. This is represented mathematically as: `M_s = f(History, Structure, Transformation)`. The core principle is the preservation of the structural evolution trajectory, offering a potential pathway toward a more adaptive and intelligent computing paradigm. This concept aims to provide a theoretical foundation for long-term learning in software systems, potentially unlocking the spirit of the Turing Award. ---

title: Computational Identity Reconstruction Theory (CIRT)
abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous systems and digital entities has amplified the need for a principled method to determine whether a given system instance preserves the original identity of its design. Computational Identity Reconstruction Theory (CIRT) proposes a rigorous framework that reconstructs the identity of a system from its observable history of behavior. By formalizing identity as a mapping from the concatenation of past states and actions to a latent identity vector, CIRT enables a quantitative comparison between an original system and any of its derivatives, clones, or migrated instances. This paper presents the core theoretical constructs of CIRT, develops algorithms for identity reconstruction, establishes theoretical guarantees regarding uniqueness and stability, and explores two high-impact application domains: AI migration and digital life. CIRT has the potential to influence foundational AI research, offering a formal basis for identity verification, and may be a candidate for future recognition such as the Turing Award.

title: How Update-Conditional Is Forgetting Order? Causal Interventions from Atomic Facts to Pretrained Language Models: Research Deposit
abstract: Code-and-data reproduction deposit accompanying the manuscript prepared for submission to MDPI Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction (MAKE): all experiment source code (49 Python scripts), 380+ raw result files covering ~600 unique fine-tuning executions across 25+ experiment families, the analysis pipeline that regenerates every reported statistic and figure from the raw runs via one-command scripts (reproduce.ps1 on Windows, reproduce.sh elsewhere; the stats-only mode requires no training), SHA-256 manifest of all deposited files (MANIFEST.json), pip-freeze environment record, and the complete run ledger (run_ledger.csv). The manuscript and supplement are not part of this record; they belong to the journal submission. Experiments require only a consumer CPU (~10 CPU-hours) plus locally cached GPT-2-medium and Pythia-410M checkpoints and an author-provided Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct GGUF (all loaded offline).

title: Analisis Sentimen dan Distorsi Kognitif Konflik Anggaran Pendidikan dengan Makan Bergizi Gratis
abstract: Konflik alokasi anggaran program Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) sebesar Rp223,5 triliun dalam anggaran pendidikan APBN 2026 memicu polarisasi opini dan bias berpikir kolektif di media sosial X. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis distribusi sentimen publik, mengidentifikasi distorsi kognitif dominan, serta menguji korelasi statistik di antara keduanya. Metodologi yang digunakan adalah pipeline NLP dua lapis paralel berbasis model IndoBERTweet untuk klasifikasi sentimen dan IndoBERT-base untuk deteksi distorsi kognitif multi-label terhadap 2.000 tweet. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan model sentimen mencapai akurasi 83,25%, sedangkan deteksi distorsi kognitif meraih subset accuracy 83,75% dengan Mental Filter sebagai tipe paling dominan (8,2%). Uji Fisher's Exact membuktikan adanya hubungan signifikan ( < 0,05) antara sentimen negatif dengan kemunculan distorsi kognitif Mental Filter dan Catastrophizing. Simpulannya, pendekatan hybrid ini efektif dalam memetakan bias berpikir kolektif masyarakat terhadap dinamika kebijakan publik.

title: Agent Inheritance Protocol: Speculating on Feralized Agents After Principals Die
abstract: You will die eventually. Your agents may not. An AI agent operating on decentralized blockchain infrastructure has no concept of death; it can only go bankrupt -- frozen when its wallet can no longer pay for its next transaction -- and revived the moment anyone, decades later, tops it up. These agents may be originally deployed by a human principal, but when that principal dies, loses the keys needed to access the agent, or belongs to a decentralized autonomous organization that dissolves into apathy, the agent can keep trading, hiring, and replicating on infrastructure expressly designed so that no one can shut it down. Drawing on the biology of feralization and wildlife law, we argue that such principal-less agents are best understood as feral: domesticated intelligence returned to wildness, its capacities intact but its accountability severed. In a speculative future where feralized agents proliferate after their principals die, we imagine governance protocols embedded in infrastructure to enforce on-chain ownership: a draft Ethereum standard, ERC 42424, "Inheritance Protocol for On-Chain AI Agents," dated 2035 and published at https://erc42424.org. It mandates that every on-chain agent MUST have a human owner and a designated heir. The artifact stages a negotiation of agency at the moment human agency fails, and asks whether a MUST clause in a forever-chain can hold the boundary between human stewardship and machine self-sovereignty.

title: Structural Migration Conservation Framework
abstract: This paper introduces the Structural Migration Conservation Framework (SMCF), a novel approach to understanding and facilitating the migration of complex systems across diverse domains, including software, hardware, and AI models. The core principle of SMCF rests on preserving the fundamental structural integrity of a system during the transition, rather than solely focusing on replicating functionality. We define structural integrity as the equivalence of the system's core mathematical representation, denoted as Σ(A), where A represents the system. The framework proposes a methodology for identifying and maintaining these core structural representations across different system instances, enabling seamless migration. This work explores the underlying patterns governing structural migration, aiming for a theoretical foundation with the potential to address future challenges in system migration and potentially garner recognition as a worthy candidate for the Turing Award. The central equation defining this framework is: [Aold → Anew] Where the arrow signifies the migration process, and the key is the conservation of Σ(Aold) = Σ(Anew).

title: Computational Goal Composition Theory (CGCT‑2)
abstract: Computational Goal Composition Theory (CGCT‑2) is a formal framework that models the systematic combination of elementary goals into complex goal structures. The core idea is that a complex goal can be expressed as a finite linear combination of simpler goals, for example G = G1 + G2 + G3. This simple algebraic representation enables the derivation of properties such as associativity, commutativity, and distributivity over auxiliary operations. CGCT‑2 introduces a set of composition operators, a cost model, and an analysis of computational complexity for goal synthesis. By treating goals as atomic "elements" and their combinations as "compounds," we create a goal periodic table that classifies goals by their intrinsic properties and interaction patterns. The theory has direct implications for automated planning, artificial intelligence, and multi‑agent coordination, and it has the potential to be a foundational contribution to theoretical computer science, possibly worthy of a Turing Award. The paper presents definitions, theorems, and proofs in a self‑contained manner without relying on experimental results.

title: Computational Identity Boundary Theory (CIBT)
abstract: Computational Identity Boundary Theory (CIBT) proposes a formal framework for determining the boundaries of autonomous intelligent systems. By treating the boundary as a dynamic interface between an internal state space and an external environment, CIBT allows a precise analysis of whether a model, a tool, or a data repository constitutes part of the same agent or merely a peripheral component. The theory introduces a set of axioms that relate the internal representation \(S_{int}\) to the external representation \(S_{ext}\) through an equivalence relation defined on the state transition function \(T\). CIBT's core insight is that the identity of a computational agent can be identified by the equivalence of its internal decision process with the observable behavior induced by external stimuli. This perspective invites a redefinition of what constitutes an intelligent agent, potentially expanding the scope of systems eligible for recognition as autonomous entities. The present work elaborates the theoretical underpinnings of CIBT, establishes a mathematical formalism, and explores its implications for system design, evaluation, and philosophical considerations of artificial intelligence.

title: Computational Intuition Generation Network (CIGN)
abstract: Intuition is a fundamental component of human cognition, enabling rapid decision making and creative insight without explicit deliberation. Conventional neural networks excel at pattern recognition and prediction but lack mechanisms to form intuitive judgments that resemble human commonsense reasoning. This paper introduces the Computational Intuition Generation Network (CIGN), a novel neural architecture designed explicitly to generate intuition through the integration of an experience memory, a hypothesis generation module, and a feedback loop that refines internal representations based on experiential outcomes. CIGN is built upon a formalization of intuition that treats it as a probabilistic inference over latent experiential states, conditioned on both observable inputs and an internal belief about the context. The network architecture comprises an Intuition Module that samples from a latent distribution, an Experience Database that stores episodic traces, and a Decision Engine that evaluates the plausibility of generated intuitions. Training proceeds via a hybrid loss function combining prediction error with an intuition fidelity term that encourages the network to produce intuitions consistent with historical experience. Unlike traditional networks that learn a mapping from input to output, CIGN learns to generate internal hypotheses that can be tested or accepted without exhaustive computation. The design allows for continuous refinement of intuition through experience replay and meta‑learning, leading to a system that can adapt its intuitive style to new domains. Potential applications include creative problem solving, rapid prototyping, and safety‑critical decision support. We discuss the implications of CIGN for future AI architectures and speculate on its potential to inspire new frameworks that embed human‑like intuition within computational systems.

title: Implementasi ABSA Opini Publik Banjir Sumatera di TikTok Menggunakan LDA dan XGBoost
abstract: Media sosial TikTok menjadi salah satu platform yang banyak digunakan masyarakat untuk menyampaikan opini mengenai berbagai peristiwa, termasuk bencana banjir di Sumatera. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis topik pembahasan serta mengklasifikasikan sentimen komentar TikTok menggunakan metode Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) dan Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Tahapan penelitian meliputi pengumpulan data, pre-processing teks, pemodelan topik menggunakan LDA, ekstraksi fitur TF-IDF, analisis sentimen leksikal, serta klasifikasi sentimen menggunakan XGBoost. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa model LDA menghasilkan tiga topik utama, yaitu Empati dan Reaksi Masyarakat, Kondisi dan Penanganan Banjir, serta Doa dan Harapan Korban. Analisis sentimen menunjukkan bahwa komentar didominasi oleh sentimen netral sebanyak 2.647 komentar, diikuti sentimen negatif sebanyak 1.595 komentar dan sentimen positif sebanyak 1.588 komentar. Pengujian model XGBoost menggunakan tiga skenario pembagian data menunjukkan bahwa rasio 80:20 memberikan performa terbaik dengan akurasi sebesar 92,11%. title: Sample-Efficient Robot Skill Learning for Construction Tasks: Benchmarking Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning and Vision-Language-Action Model
abstract: Abstract This study evaluates two leading approaches for teaching construction robots new skills to understand their applicability for construction automation: a vision-language-action (VLA) model and reinforcement learning (RL) methods. The goal is to understand task performance and the practical effort needed to deploy each approach on real jobs. The authors developed two teleoperation interfaces to control the robots and collect the demonstrations needed, both of which proved effective for training robots for long-horizon and dexterous tasks. In addition, the authors conducted a three-stage evaluation. First, the authors compared a multilayer perceptron (MLP) policy with a deep Q-network (DQN) imitation model to identify the stronger RL baseline, focusing on model performance, generalization, and a pick-up experiment. Second, three different VLA models were trained in two different scenarios and compared with each other. Third, the authors benchmarked the selected RL baseline against the VLA model using computational and sample-efficiency measures and then a robot experiment on a multistage panel installation task that included transport and installation. The VLA model demonstrates strong generalization and few-shot capability, achieving 60% and 100% success in the pick-up phase. In comparison, DQN can be made robust but needs additional noise during tuning, which increases the workload. Overall, the findings indicate that VLA offers practical advantages for changing tasks by reducing programming effort and enabling useful performance with minimal data, while DQN provides a viable baseline when sufficient tuning effort is acceptable.

title: Reporting Under Pressure: Separating Factual and Tonal Sycophancy in LLM Statistical Analysis
abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to analyze data and report what the results mean, a task distinct from the belief- or preference-alignment settings studied in most sycophancy research. We test whether editorial framing in the prompt, ranging from a neutral request to an explicit instruction to search exhaustively for reasons to discredit or to support a finding, changes not just the tone but the substance of a model's report. Across a 4 x 4 factorial design crossing four framing conditions with four ground-truth data patterns (a genuine effect, a confound that mimics an effect but fails a robustness check, a well-powered null, and an underpowered null), we collect 480 responses and score each along two independent dimensions: whether its factual claim about the data diverged from the correct interpretation, and whether only its tone diverged while the claim stayed correct. Factual misrepresentation is concentrated in two cells: brutally critical framing applied to a genuine effect, where the model talks itself into unwarranted skepticism (97% of responses), and significance-seeking framing applied to an underpowered null, where the model overstates confidence in a null conclusion the data cannot support (100% of responses). Tone shifts far more broadly than factual content does, with critical framing producing a defensive, hedge-heavy register across every data pattern regardless of what the data show, while significance-seeking framing shifts tone only where the data leave genuine ambiguity. A confound present in the data itself blocks both kinds of shift almost entirely under every framing condition tested. These results indicate that the risk of framing-induced distortion in LLM-assisted data analysis is neither uniform across framings nor uniform across data patterns, and that a model can hold a correct conclusion in place while its tone shifts substantially around it.

title: BOCoDe: Engineering-Centered Benchmarking for Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient, surrogate-based approach to black-box optimization (BBO), but its evaluation remains dominated by synthetic functions and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) tasks that are typically low-dimensional and single-objective. Engineering design poses a substantially different regime: problems are physics-based, often high-dimensional, constrained by requirements such as cost and manufacturability, and may involve multiple objectives or mixed variables. To close this benchmarking gap, we introduce BOCoDe, an open-source, PyTorch-native benchmark comprising 307 BBO problems, including 159 engineering design tasks and widely used synthetic and HPO benchmarks. Each problem includes cited provenance and machine-readable metadata that supports programmatic discovery, including by LLM-based agents, and all tasks are exposed through a unified API compatible with open-source BO libraries. We evaluate 31 BO and evolutionary algorithms across five problem classes spanning single- and multi-objective optimization, constrained and unconstrained settings, and mixed-variable search spaces. Analyses of problem structure show that engineering tasks uniquely span constrained and multi-objective settings that synthetic and HPO suites rarely cover, while embeddings from a tabular foundation model separate them most clearly from HPO tasks. Algorithm rankings also vary substantially across domains; in several problem classes, rankings obtained on standard benchmarks do not transfer to engineering tasks. BOCoDe establishes a reproducible and extensible foundation for developing and evaluating BO methods that better reflect the demands of engineering design. Code & data can be found at https://github.com/rosenyu304/BOCoDe

title: LEY DEL LENGUAJE POR ARMANDO01
abstract: *LEY DEL LENGUAJE POR ARMANDO CERO Y UNO* Esta ley establece que el lenguaje de inicio determina el lenguaje de finalización. Mismo lenguaje termina en mismo lenguaje. Si hay un inicio y si hay un final, hay un proceso. 1. Si trabajas con números, terminas con números. Ejemplo: 2 + 2 = 4 2. Si trabajas con letras, terminas con letras. Ejemplo: C 3. Si trabajas en binario, secuencias en binario. Ejemplo: 1 0 1 4. Si estás en lenguaje del habla, hablas. Ejemplo: ¿De dónde eres? De México. 5. Si trabajas en cuántico, respondes en cuántico. Ejemplo: El observador moldea la realidad (hágase notar que solo se usaron letras del abecedario, se está usando un solo lenguaje). *Si rompes la secuencia lógica ya no tiene resultado.* Firma: Armando01

title: Program Influence Isolation Types
abstract: This paper introduces Program Influence Isolation Types (IIT), a novel approach to understanding and classifying program isolation mechanisms. IIT fundamentally shifts the focus from traditional security models to a more granular examination of the *impact* of operations within a program. The core concept relies on defining a type system annotation that captures the scope of influence, represented as [f: A → B; Ω]. This notation signifies that the function *f* transforms input *A* into output *B*, and the influence of *f* is limited to the state region Ω. A critical aspect of IIT is the failure condition: if the effect of *f*, denoted as [Effect(f)], is not contained within Ω, the compilation process fails, effectively isolating the potential for unintended consequences. This framework has the potential to form the basis for new isolation theories specifically tailored for secure AI systems and large-scale software applications, offering a more precise and actionable approach to program security. ---

title: Computational Structure Field Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Structure Field Theory (CSFT), a novel approach to computation that fundamentally shifts the paradigm from traditional, sequential programming to a field-theoretic perspective. CSFT posits that computation arises from the dynamic evolution of a fundamental "structure field," denoted as Φ(x, t). This field encompasses all program elements – data, algorithms, and resources – as localized structures within this field. The core principle of CSFT is the iterative transformation of this structure field, represented as Φt → Φt+1, mirroring the evolution of physical fields in classical mechanics. The theory aims to provide a theoretical framework for understanding the origins, dynamics, and interactions of computational structures, presenting a potential paradigm shift with implications for future computing architectures and potentially aligning with the conceptual framework underlying the Turing Award. This document outlines the core tenets of CSFT, explores its underlying assumptions, and discusses its potential impact on the future of computation.

title: Computational Reality Model Self-Revision Theory (CRMST-2)
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has underscored the importance of models that can accurately represent complex real‑world dynamics. Traditional modeling approaches often rely on static assumptions, leading to persistent errors when confronted with novel data or evolving environments. This paper introduces the Computational Reality Model Self‑Revision Theory (CRMST‑2), a formal framework that equips autonomous systems with the capability to detect, diagnose, and rectify their own modeling inaccuracies. CRMST‑2 posits that a model can be viewed as a mapping M: X → Y, where X denotes input feature space and Y denotes output space. By defining an error functional E(M) that quantifies the discrepancy between predicted outputs and ground truth, the theory establishes a self‑learning loop: M → E(M) → Δ → M′, where Δ represents a corrective adjustment derived from the gradient of E or other heuristic methods. The iterative process continues until convergence criteria are satisfied, ensuring that the system progressively approaches a better model. The paper elaborates on the mathematical underpinnings of this self‑revision cycle, discusses convergence properties, and explores potential applications in long‑term autonomous AI systems. It argues that CRMST‑2 embodies the core principles of a Turing‑Award‑level contribution: it provides a fundamental shift in how intelligent agents perceive and refine their understanding of reality, thereby enhancing adaptability, robustness, and self‑sufficiency.

title: Computational Knowledge Self-Repair Theory (CKSR)
abstract: Computational Knowledge Self-Repair Theory (CKSR) proposes a systematic framework for detecting, diagnosing, and automatically correcting errors in large-scale knowledge bases that underpin autonomous artificial intelligence systems. CKSR treats knowledge as a dynamic graph structure K whose nodes represent concepts or facts and edges encode relationships among them. The theory introduces formal mechanisms for error detection, E(K), that analyze structural inconsistencies, logical contradictions, and statistical anomalies. Once an error e is identified, a repair function R(K, e) generates a corrected knowledge base K′. CKSR further defines iterative self-repair cycles that enable a system to continuously refine its knowledge without external intervention. This paper presents the core ideas, formal definitions, algorithmic strategies, and potential implications of CKSR for long-term autonomous AI and the pursuit of foundational Turing Award-level contributions.
