title: Klasifikasi Surat Otomatis pada Sistem Pengarsipan Surat Digital Menggunakan TF-IDF dan Naïve Bayes
abstract: The letter archiving process in the Riangkemie Village Government is still done manually, requiring long search times and potentially causing errors in classification. This study aims to develop a digital letter archiving system capable of automatically classifying letters using the Naive Bayes algorithm. The dataset used was 1,008 letter data that were processed through preprocessing and TF-IDF weighting stages, then divided into training data and test data with a ratio of 80:20. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score and tested the effectiveness of archive searches on the system. The results showed that the model achieved an accuracy of 98.51% with high precision, recall, and F1-score values for each letter category. In addition, the system was able to speed up the archive search process with an average search time of 0.39 seconds. These results indicate that the proposed method is effective in improving classification accuracy and efficiency of digital letter archive management.

title: If it bleeds, it leads? Evaluating whether LLMs can identify what is newsworthy
abstract: Journalists have always had to make the challenging decision about which stories to focus on and which stories to ignore. This paper investigates whether AI can assist journalists in identifying newsworthy stories from large databases. We first build a dataset of Canadian lobbying registrations, each labeled as "newsworthy" or "not newsworthy" based on whether a journalist covered it in a published article or not. We then systematically evaluate several AI models' ability to identify the one newsworthy registration within a batch of ten. The best models identify a single newsworthy registration with 22% accuracy, rising to 48% when allowed to select three, and to 52% when provided previous headline examples. Our results suggest that a filtering approach silently discards real stories, whereas allowing the model to rank registrations by newsworthiness ensures no information is lost. We conclude that while AI holds real potential to help identify leads, this is not possible without further investment in evaluation infrastructure, and even then, there is an important role for journalists to identify what AI misses, as it cannot replace their editorial judgment entirely.

title: StateSight: Benchmarking Latent Spatial-State Reconstruction in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used for multimodal question answering, yet their ability to reconstruct latent spatial structure from a single image remains difficult to isolate. Broad benchmarks often combine perception, optical character recognition, domain knowledge, linguistic priors, and reasoning in the same evaluation. We introduce StateSight, a procedurally generated benchmark for cube-net opposite-face reasoning, occluded cube-tower counting, and 4-neighbor connected-component counting. Each task family contains 300 single-image prompts with deterministic oracle labels and exact-match scoring. OpenAI GPT-5.5, using the API model identifier gpt-5.5, achieved 59.3%, 33.3%, and 28.3% accuracy across the three tasks, while Claude Sonnet 5 achieved 53.3%, 18.7%, and 7.3%. All final direct runs had zero format errors. A 30-participant human baseline on 60 items exceeded both models on every task, with mean accuracies of 80.8%, 68.8%, and 64.3%. Visible-derivation analysis identified recurring errors in image-state reconstruction and reasoning procedure. We also introduce StateSight-Steps, a companion dataset of 900 interleaved image-text examples and 3,600 deterministic intermediate visual states. The results show that format-valid responses can mask failures to recover the spatial structure required for verifiable visual inference.

title: A Posterior-Dynamics Framework for Imaging Inverse Problems with Pretrained Diffusion Priors
abstract: Pretrained diffusion models represent image distributions through a continuum of progressively smoothed distributions. This multiscale structure organizes generation from global structure to fine detail and supports high-quality, diverse samples. We exploit the same multiscale diffusion prior for linear imaging inverse problems. Rather than using the pretrained model only as a denoiser in an outer iteration, we define a surrogate likelihood whose center is aligned with the clean-image coordinate and whose covariance accounts for residual diffusion uncertainty. This construction defines an explicit surrogate posterior path, from which we derive continuous posterior dynamics. A tunable Langevin component supports target tracking and allows the amount of posterior exploration to be adapted to the application. We prove endpoint consistency and a finite-horizon tracking bound and, in the exact-score setting, first-order weak accuracy. For computation, we derive the Posterior-Dynamics Implicit--Explicit sampler (PD-IMEX), a stable method using one score evaluation per diffusion scale and an implicit data-consistency update. Experiments on deblurring, super-resolution, and inpainting show strong reconstruction quality at 100 score evaluations, coarse-grid stability, and controllable fidelity--diversity behavior.

title: Computational Self-Discovered Mathematics (CSDM)
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Computational Self-Discovered Mathematics (CSDM), a paradigm shift in how we conceive of computational systems. The core idea is that future computing systems will not merely execute algorithms but will actively *discover* mathematical structures. This process will be driven by observation of data and the subsequent construction of mathematical objects to model and understand that data. title: Computational Abstraction Formation Mechanism (CAFM)
abstract: This paper investigates the computational mechanisms underlying the formation of abstraction in artificial intelligence. Abstraction, a cornerstone of human intelligence, allows us to represent complex realities with simplified models, facilitating reasoning and problem-solving. This research proposes a framework, the Computational Abstraction Formation Mechanism (CAFM), designed to mimic the process by which humans develop concepts, theories, and ultimately, abstract representations from raw sensory data. The CAFM utilizes a layered approach, transforming objects into concepts through pattern recognition, and subsequently developing theories based on those concepts. The core of the system involves iterative cycles of data analysis, hypothesis generation, and refinement, mirroring the cognitive processes associated with abstraction. This work explores the potential of such a system to contribute to the field of artificial general intelligence and, potentially, to unlock new paradigms in scientific discovery. The framework presented here provides a theoretical foundation for building intelligent systems capable of autonomous abstraction, a critical step toward achieving true machine understanding. ---

title: Computational Knowledge Boundary Shift (CKBS)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Knowledge Boundary Shift (CKBS) theory, a novel framework for understanding and modeling the expansion of cognitive reach within complex systems. The core premise of CKBS is that knowledge boundaries, represented as [Bt], are not static but rather undergo continuous, directional shifts over time, denoted as [Bt → Bt+1]. This shift represents a fundamental process of system evolution, driven by the acquisition of new information and the subsequent re-evaluation of existing cognitive structures. The theory posits that the rate and direction of these shifts are governed by a complex interplay of factors, including environmental stimuli, internal feedback mechanisms, and the inherent architecture of the system. We explore the mathematical formalism underlying CKBS, defining key variables and relationships, and propose a model for quantifying the dynamics of knowledge boundary movement. The theoretical implications of CKBS are significant, potentially offering a new perspective on intelligence, learning, and adaptation, with the possibility of contributing to the development of robust and adaptable AI systems. Furthermore, we discuss the theoretical alignment with the Turing Award and its potential as a foundational theory for intelligent growth.

title: Program Behavioral Elasticity Theory (PBET)
abstract: This paper introduces Program Behavioral Elasticity Theory (PBET), a novel theoretical framework designed to quantify and understand the robustness of software systems. PBET focuses on a system's ability to maintain consistent behavior when subjected to changes in its input, workload, or surrounding environment. The core concept is defined by the elasticity ratio: EP = (ΔBehavior / ΔEnvironment). A low elasticity value (EP ≈ 0) indicates a system's inherent stability and resistance to deviation. This theory lays the groundwork for a new mathematical approach to software resilience, potentially leading to the development of the "Turing Award" level of theoretical breakthroughs in the field. This document outlines the foundational principles of PBET, explores its implications for software design and verification, and suggests future research directions. ---

title: Computational Intuition Universe Theory (CIUT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Intuition Universe Theory (CIUT), a novel framework that seeks to formalize intuition as a structured, computable entity. We posit that all possible intuitions form a universal set Ω_I, within which each intuition is represented as a vector of features (s_1, s_2, ..., s_K). The theory explores the topology of intuition space, proposes a metric to quantify distances between intuitions, and establishes a computational model that simulates the evolution of intuition through iterative refinement processes. By integrating concepts from information theory, cognitive science, and algorithmic information, CIUT offers a rigorous foundation for understanding intuition as an emergent, high-level abstraction. The implications for artificial intelligence are discussed, highlighting how CIUT can guide the design of systems that emulate human-like intuition and potentially elevate intelligence research to a level worthy of Turing Award recognition.

title: Analisis Sentimen Berbasis Aspek untuk Mendukung Pengambilan Keputusan pada Industri Perhotelan
abstract: Guest reviews on Online Travel Agents have become an important source for assessing hotel service quality, yet conventional sentiment analysis only produces an overall score and fails to capture opinions on specific service aspects, making it difficult to determine improvement priorities. This study aims to build an Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) framework that turns reviews into actionable service-improvement recommendations. Reviews from several platforms were collected, labeled, and classified using a fine-tuned IndoBERT model to identify seven service aspects along with their sentiment polarity, after which the results were summarized and presented through an interactive monitoring dashboard. The proposed model achieved 92.83% accuracy, 92.89% weighted F1, and 74.55% macro F1. These results show that the proposed framework delivers more interpretable and targeted insights than conventional sentiment analysis, thereby supporting data-driven decision-making for service improvement in the hospitality industry. Keywords: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis; IndoBERT; Hotel Reviews; Monitoring Dashboard; Online Travel Agent Abstrak Ulasan tamu di Online Travel Agent menjadi sumber penting untuk menilai kualitas layanan hotel, namun analisis sentimen konvensional hanya menghasilkan skor keseluruhan dan gagal menangkap opini pada aspek layanan tertentu, sehingga sulit menentukan prioritas perbaikan. Penelitian ini bertujuan membangun kerangka kerja Analisis Sentimen Berbasis Aspek (ABSA) yang mengubah ulasan menjadi rekomendasi perbaikan layanan yang dapat ditindaklanjuti. Ulasan dari beberapa platform dikumpulkan, dilabeli, lalu diklasifikasikan menggunakan model IndoBERT yang disempurnakan untuk mengenali tujuh aspek layanan beserta polaritas sentimennya, kemudian hasilnya diringkas dan disajikan melalui dashboard pemantauan interaktif. Model yang diusulkan mencapai akurasi 92,83%, F1 tertimbang 92,89%, dan F1 makro 74,55%. Hasil ini menunjukkan bahwa kerangka kerja yang diusulkan memberikan wawasan yang lebih interpretatif dan tepat sasaran dibanding analisis sentimen konvensional, sehingga mendukung pengambilan keputusan perbaikan layanan berbasis data di industri perhotelan.

title: Translating finite-domain integer constraint models to CP/SMT/ILP/PB/SAT solvers with CPMpy
abstract: Constraint solving is a declarative approach for solving combinatorial satisfaction and optimization problems. The user specifies their problem through constraints and decision variables, and a generic solver is used to find a solution. Several constraint-solving technologies exist, and certain solvers perform well on certain problems. Therefore, it is useful to try different solvers given a particular application. However, each solving paradigm supports different types of constraints and decision variables. Our goal is to translate high-level constraint satisfaction and optimization problems into any lower-level formalism, including CP, SMT QF-LIA, ILP, PB and (Max)SAT. This allows for comparing different solving technologies for a particular problem, without requiring a user to manually remodel it for each solving paradigm. We define a high-level language of logical and arithmetic operations, and useful additional functions and constraints, which are known as global constraints in the CP community. We then present a modular framework for transforming our high-level modeling language to CP/SMT/ILP/PB and (Max)SAT solvers. While many transformations are partly described in the literature, we observe that they can be implemented through a modular waterfall of smaller components, where lower-level paradigms reuse the transformations of higher-level paradigms. Two recurring challenges are handling the negation of arbitrary subexpressions and avoiding the introduction of auxiliary variables. Additionally, we take special care linearizing non-linear operators for ILP, PB and SAT-solvers. The transformation waterfall is implemented and evaluated in the open-source CPMpy library. Our results show that constraint models significantly change throughout the transformations, and that optimizations to the linearization of constraints are essential for ILP and PB solvers.

title: Qudit-ADAPT-VQE: an adaptive variational algorithm with counterdiabatic-inspired improvements for qudits
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms based on qudits have attracted significant attention in recent years. However, as in their qubit-based counterparts, challenges such as barren plateaus and the design of efficient ansatz remain major obstacles. In this work, we propose to address these issues through a qudit implementation of the ADAPT-VQE algorithm, which constructs the ansatz iteratively. Specifically, we introduce an operator pool inspired by adiabatic evolution enhanced with counterdiabatic driving for ansatz construction and employ it to solve Max 3-Cut. We show that the warm-start strategy inherent to ADAPT-VQE, together with an ansatz construction based on counterdiabatic operators, achieves higher accuracy and lower native gates implementation than approaches on fixed ansatz. Furthermore, we show that, in qudit-based quantum computing, ADAPT-VQE with a counterdiabatic operator pool can navigate rough optimization landscapes with local traps through the burrowing mechanism, suggesting robustness against barren plateau effects and providing a scalable framework for variational quantum algorithms with qudits.

title: Does Heavy-Tailed Gradient Noise Explain the CIFAR-10 Gap in Byzantine-Robust, Differentially Private Federated Learning? An Empirical Stress Test of Byz-Clip21-SGD2M
abstract: Byz-Clip21-SGD2M (Islamov et al., 2026) provides high-probability convergence guarantees for federated learning under simultaneous Byzantine adversaries and differential-privacy (DP) noise, relaxing the bounded-gradient assumption behind the tight privacy-robustness-utility trade-off of Allouah et al. (2023b) to standard L-smoothness and σ-sub-Gaussian gradient noise. Its own empirical validation is MNIST-only, and its Conclusion lists heavy-tailed gradient noise as future work; we stress-test both the algorithm and its sub-Gaussian premise at CIFAR-10 scale. Using the established Hill-estimator/kurtosis tail-index methodology of Şimşekli et al. (2019) and follow-ons — applied here, not proposed as new — we find CIFAR-10's gradient noise consistently heavier-tailed than MNIST's across every statistic and configuration checked. Isolating ablations show the Byzantine-robustness mechanism itself performs comparably on both datasets, so the degradation is not robustness-specific; a dedicated DP-aware search over the clipping threshold τ, spanning the source paper's own privacy-budget grid, fails to recover non-degenerate CIFAR-10 accuracy even as DP noise is driven toward zero. This rules out both "DP noise alone explains the gap" and "the fixed-τ protocol was miscalibrated"; the evidence instead points to CIFAR-10's own clean-training convergence difficulty, plausibly linked to its heavier tail, as the dominant factor. A seed scale-up (CIFAR-10 sweep to n=10/cell, ablation to n=10/arm) with paired Wilcoxon testing confirms this: no CIFAR-10 condition differs significantly from any other, and the ablation's recovery to CIFAR-10's clean ceiling is statistically indistinguishable (p=1.000), not a small-sample artifact. An independent, unpaired Mann-Whitney U test further corroborates the hyperparameter-transfer gap under matched hyperparameters and round budget (U=100, p=0.000183). We also close this paper's previously most significant open limitation: we implement and unit-test the source paper's two external baselines, Safe-DSHB (Allouah et al., 2023b) and Byz-Clip-SGD (Islamov et al., 2026), from its appendix pseudocode, and run both under the identical protocol used for Byz-Clip21-SGD2M throughout. Under shared, non-independently-tuned hyperparameters, both baselines match or nominally exceed Byz-Clip21-SGD2M on several MNIST conditions — an exploratory finding, not confirmatory (the source paper's own independently-tuned comparison reaches the opposite conclusion, and none of these comparisons survive multiple-comparison correction). We then ran the independently-tuned comparison this gap called for (30-point (γ, τ) grid per baseline, matching the source paper's own tuning range): it erases the MNIST advantage seen under shared hyperparameters entirely (all 12 comparisons now p ≥ 0.06) without producing a Byz-Clip21-SGD2M advantage either, since our tuning remains a simplified, single-condition probe rather than the source paper's per-ε, DP-aware protocol — so whether Byz-Clip21-SGD2M has a genuine MNIST edge under equally careful tuning stays open. On CIFAR-10, all three algorithms are statistically indistinguishable and collapse to chance together, a more direct finding independent of any tuning caveat: the CIFAR-10 gap is not specific to Byz-Clip21-SGD2M. We report every known gap in our replication honestly, including a corrected theoretical positioning relative to Allouah et al.'s tight dimension-dependent lower bound and two corrections to our own earlier internal pilot analysis.

title: Computational Strategy Formation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Strategy Formation Theory (CSFT), a novel framework for understanding intelligent behavior beyond traditional machine learning paradigms. CSFT posits that systems don't merely learn optimal parameters; instead, they actively *formulate strategies* – explicit, rule-based approaches to problem-solving – based on experience. The core principle is expressed as: Experience → Strategy. This theory investigates the underlying mechanisms responsible for strategy genesis, addressing a critical gap in current AI research. CSFT aims to unify concepts related to planning, learning, and search within a single, computationally-driven framework, offering potential insights relevant to the Turing Award. The theory emphasizes the importance of representing and executing strategies rather than solely optimizing numerical parameters. This approach provides a more robust and interpretable model for complex decision-making systems. ---

title: Computational Structure Migration Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Structure Migration Theory (CSMT), a novel framework designed to automate the process of transferring software structures between disparate environments. The core premise of CSMT is that software structures possess inherent adaptability and can successfully migrate to novel contexts. The theory posits a system capable of autonomously identifying the optimal migration strategy, minimizing a defined "MigrationLoss" function. This function quantifies the discrepancy between the source and target environments, incorporating factors such as architectural differences, computational resource constraints, and operational dependencies. The theoretical framework suggests a potential pathway towards unifying critical areas within software engineering, namely cross-hardware compilation, software porting, and model deployment. The system iteratively explores potential transformation strategies, represented by a variable *T*, aiming to achieve the lowest possible MigrationLoss. This process leverages a search algorithm to discover the optimal transformation, offering a potentially scalable and robust solution for complex migration scenarios. The presented theory lays a foundational framework for future research and development in automated software migration.

title: Title: Computational Experience Explanation Theory (CEET)
abstract: Computational Experience Explanation Theory (CEET) proposes a systematic framework for answering the fundamental question: "Why did this experience arise?" CEET unifies three core concepts—experience, reasoning, and explanation—into a coherent computational architecture. Experience is represented as a high‑dimensional vector E = (e_1, e_2, ..., e_n) capturing observable data, internal states, and contextual cues. Reasoning is modelled as a transformation R = f(E) = (r_1, r_2, ..., r_m) that extracts latent causal relationships and inference paths from experience. Explanation is expressed as a symbolic or probabilistic narrative Exp = g(R) = (exp_1, exp_2, ..., exp_k) that translates reasoning into human‑interpretable accounts. The CEET pipeline leverages a layered architecture comprising data acquisition, feature extraction, probabilistic inference, causal modeling, and narrative synthesis. This paper details the mathematical formalism underlying each layer, presents algorithmic procedures for mapping experience to explanation, and discusses implications for artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and human‑computer interaction. The theory's potential to bridge experiential data and explanatory insight positions CEET as a candidate for high‑impact contributions, potentially meriting recognition such as a Turing Award.

The CEET pipeline leverages a layered architecture comprising data acquisition, feature extraction, probabilistic inference, causal modeling, and narrative synthesis. This paper details the mathematical formalism underlying each layer, presents algorithmic procedures for mapping experience to explanation, and discusses implications for artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and human‑computer interaction. The theory's potential to bridge experiential data and explanatory insight positions CEET as a candidate for high‑impact contributions, potentially meriting recognition such as a Turing Award.

title: Computational Rule Evolution Theory (CRET)
abstract: Computational Rule Evolution Theory (CRET) proposes a novel framework in which computational rules are treated as dynamic entities that undergo processes analogous to biological evolution. Unlike classical static logic or algorithmic systems, CRET allows a rule set R to transform over time according to a transition operator R_t → R_{t+1}. The theory formalizes mutation, selection, and recombination mechanisms within a rule space and introduces a differential equation model for the frequency of individual rule components. By mapping rule sets onto a fitness landscape, CRET captures how adaptive pressures steer rule evolution, leading to increasingly efficient or specialized computational behaviors. Illustrative examples include Boolean rule evolution, grid‑world navigation, and adaptive control of physical systems. The implications for self‑evolving software are profound: software can be conceived as a living system of rules that autonomously refines its own architecture, potentially yielding new classes of autonomic, self‑repairing, or self‑optimizing programs. CRET opens pathways toward a self‑evolving software theory, with the potential to contribute to the next generation of adaptive computing systems and to the broader field of artificial life.

title: Prior-art Note v1.0
abstract: Prior-art Note v1.0 is a companion document to Method Definition v1.0 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21931565). It documents the prior-art boundary of the defined practical AI-learning method by distinguishing established pedagogical and AI-tutoring mechanisms from the specific six-function method configuration fixed in the Method Definition. The Note reviews representative historical and contemporary precedents, including intelligent tutoring systems, instruction-programmed LLM tutors, learner-steering approaches, evidence-based checking and remediation, and transfer. It does not claim worldwide novelty or the absence of undocumented earlier implementations. The central finding is a bounded non-finding, assigned moderate rather than high confidence: within the reviewed public source set, no single documented precedent was identified that established all six mandatory functions together with the same allocation of control and the Minimal Profile defined in Method Definition v1.0. The deposit contains the canonical English version and an authorized Russian translation in both PDF and Markdown formats, together with SHA-256 checksums.

title: Large Language Model Assisted Operational Monitoring for Battery Energy Storage System Integrated Power Distribution Networks
abstract: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are increasingly used in distribution networks for voltage regulation and demand response, which increases the volume and complexity of operational telemetry available to grid operators. This paper presents an AI-enabled monitoring framework that connects a large language model (LLM) interface with a structured telemetry database for BESS-integrated distribution system analysis. Operator questions are submitted in natural language and translated into validated SQL queries using predefined database schema information and approved KPI views. Retrieved measurements, including bus voltages, state of charge, active power, and reactive power, are evaluated against engineering constraints for voltage limits, BESS operation, and demand response tracking. The framework is validated using hardware-in-the-loop co-simulation data from a BESS-equipped distribution feeder operating under reactive power-based voltage control and price-driven demand response. Case studies show that the framework generates valid database queries, identifies repeated voltage violations, detects reactive power overshoot, and evaluates active-power tracking performance. The results show that LLM-assisted monitoring can connect structured grid telemetry with automated engineering assessment for BESS operation analysis.

title: HOIMask: Towards Generative Masked Modeling for Human Object Interaction Generation
abstract: Diffusion-based methods have dominated the HOI generation, as they enable critical contact fusions or signals to guide the diffusion process. However, they often result in high artifacts and unstable interaction quality due to error accumulation during iterative denoising. In this work, we propose HOIMask, the first generative masked framework for modeling HOI motion in discrete space. HOIMask first encodes both motion sequences and contact-aware signals into discrete 2D human and object token maps via HOI Vector Quantization (VQ), preserving fine-grained spatial-temporal structure beyond conventional 1D representations. On this basis, a generative masked modeling framework is employed to jointly capture human-object interaction dynamics, leveraging a transformer architecture designed to model complex spatial-temporal and interaction dependencies. To generate more coherent and physically plausible motions, we further introduce a novel contact-aware reconstruction guidance in discrete space during inference, which fuses contact signals to optimize HOI tokens that forces the generated motion with higher spatio-temporal consistency. With craftily designed motion interaction tokens, dedicated architecture and guidance strategy, HOIMask outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods, generating more realistic and semantically aligned HOI motions. Please refer to https://jyhflash.github.io/HOIMask/ for more results.

title: MA-CERD: A Gold Benchmark Dataset for Counterfactual Requirements and Evidence Change Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: MA-CERD (Multi-Agent Constraint-and-Evidence Reasoning Dataset) is a Gold benchmark dataset for evaluating reasoning under counterfactual requirement and evidence changes in multi-agent systems. The release contains 1,000 adjudicated Gold records constructed from 100 base cases and atomic semantic interventions. Each record captures the required relation, handling decision, impact set, preservation set, and provenance required to assess whether a system responds correctly to a changed requirement or evidence condition while preserving unaffected elements. Gold construction combines three separated evidence layers: O1 explicit-rule evidence, O2 blind human semantic review with third-party adjudication of disagreements, and O3 deterministic simulator-based shadow execution. The final release includes schema definitions, data dictionaries, family-level splits, privacy checks, evaluation utilities, intended-use documentation, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. The benchmark is intended for research on requirements evolution, change-impact reasoning, evidence-aware decision support, multi-agent systems, and leakage-resistant evaluation. It does not constitute operational validation, certified simulator fidelity, deployment readiness, or real-world safety assurance.

title: Dual Verification Computing
abstract: Dual Verification Computing (DVC) proposes a novel framework for verifying computational systems, moving beyond traditional notions of correctness and focusing on the simultaneous satisfaction of both correctness and acceptability. The core principle of DVC rests on the requirement that any computational action must simultaneously satisfy two verification conditions: $V_1 = \text{Correctness}$ and $V_2 = \text{Acceptability}$. Only when both conditions are true can the action be considered valid and executed. This approach has the potential to significantly expand the scope of program verification, potentially leading to a new paradigm of computing centered around systems that are not only correct but also demonstrably acceptable to their intended users and contexts. This document outlines the foundational concepts of DVC, explores its implications for system design and verification, and suggests avenues for future research. ---

title: Volume 42: Neural Networks & Informational Constraints
abstract: ABSTRACT Neural networks—both biological and artificial—represent one of the most profound manifestations of informational organization in nature and technology. This volume presents a comprehensive analysis of neural networks through the lens of the ICQER (Informational Constraints Quantum Event Realism) framework, demonstrating that neurons, synapses, and network architectures function fundamentally as constraint-driven informational systems. By examining neural computation as constraint propagation and optimization, we reveal how learning, memory, adaptation, and emergent intelligence arise from the dynamic interplay of local and global informational constraints. The volume is structured across ten sections that systematically develop the ICQER perspective on neural networks. Beginning with foundational principles, we establish neurons and synapses as constraint nodes and channels, and network architectures as constraint topologies. The analysis then progresses through constraint propagation mechanisms, demonstrating how forward and backward information flow represent informational shaping and optimization processes. Learning is reinterpreted as constraint optimization, unifying supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement paradigms under a single ICQER framework. Biological neural networks are examined in depth, highlighting how plasticity, network topology, and temporal dynamics embody constraint modulation in living systems. The emergence of intelligence and cognition is explained as a system-level resolution of constraints into coherent informational patterns, with hierarchical constraint organization enabling complex, multilevel processing. Temporal dynamics—including oscillations, synchronization, and predictive coding—are presented as manifestations of time-dependent constraints that enable memory, anticipation, and adaptive behavior. The volume addresses practical applications through sections on optimization and constraint engineering, demonstrating how ICQER principles guide the design of robust, efficient, and adaptable neural systems. Hybrid networks and neuromorphic computing are explored as embodiments of constraint-driven computation across biological and artificial substrates. Finally, we identify key challenges and open questions, including multi-scale constraint interactions, the bridge between biological and artificial systems, and the minimal constraint requirements for emergent cognition and consciousness. This volume bridges neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and complex systems theory, providing both theoretical foundations and practical insights for understanding, designing, and optimizing neural networks across domains. The ICQER framework illuminates the underlying principles that unify diverse neural systems, offering a roadmap for future research in both natural and artificial intelligence.

title: Unified Computational Intuition Theory (UCIT)
abstract: The Unified Computational Intuition Theory (UCIT) proposes that a key component of intelligent behavior is the ability to form compressed high‑dimensional representations of complex structures and to make rapid judgments based on these representations. UCIT integrates empirical learning, pattern recognition, expert judgment, scientific insight, and creativity into a single theoretical framework. By formalizing the relationship between experience, compression, and structure, UCIT aims to provide a mathematical foundation for future artificial intelligence systems that can autonomously generate, modify, and discover computational rules. This paper presents the core concepts of UCIT, develops a formal model using plain‑text mathematical notation, discusses its potential to become a foundational theory in AI, and introduces twenty novel research directions that build upon the core idea of computational rule generation.

title: Computational Reality Model Generation Theory (CRMGT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Reality Model Generation Theory (CRMGT), a novel framework for understanding how intelligent systems can autonomously create internal models of their environments. While traditional machine learning approaches emphasize passive pattern extraction from data, CRMGT proposes that an adaptive system should actively generate and refine a structured representation of reality that guides perception, reasoning, and action. The theory is formalized through a set of equations and algorithmic procedures that describe the transformation from sensory input to an evolving internal reality model. We discuss the theoretical foundations, propose a concrete implementation strategy, and explore the implications of CRMGT for the development of general artificial intelligence. The potential of this theory to contribute to the next generation of intelligent systems, and possibly to be recognized with the Turing Award, is also examined.
